This, at least, was what Sara gathered from his letters. It is true that any other business scheme, however magnificent, would have had little appeal for her or for the schoolroom. But “diamond mines” sounded so like the Arabian Nights that no one could be indifferent. Sara thought them enchanting, and painted pictures, for Ermengarde and Lottie, of maze-like passages in the bowels of the earth, where sparkling stones studded the walls and roofs and ceilings, and strange, dark men dug them out with heavy picks. Ermengarde delighted in the story, and Lottie insisted on having it retold to her every evening. Lavinia was very spiteful about it, and told Jessie she didn’t believe such things as diamond mines existed.

6.1.oldText: “My mama has a diamond ring which cost forty pounds,” she said. “And it is not a big one, either. If there were mines full of diamonds, people would be so rich it would be ridiculous.”

6.2.oldText: “Perhaps Sara will be so rich that she will be ridiculous,” giggled Jessie.

6.3.oldText: “She’s ridiculous without being rich,” Lavinia sniffed.

6.4.oldText: “I believe you hate her,” said Jessie.

6.5.oldText: “No, I don’t,” snapped Lavinia. “But I don’t believe in mines full of diamonds.”

6.6.oldText: “Well, people have to get them from somewhere,” said Jessie. “Lavinia,” with a new giggle, “what do you think Gertrude says?”

6.7.oldText: “I don’t know, I’m sure; and I don’t care if it’s something more about that everlasting Sara.”

6.8.oldText: “Well, it is. One of her ‘pretends’ is that she is a princess. She plays it all the time — even in school. She says it makes her learn her lessons better. She wants Ermengarde to be one too, but Ermengarde says she is too fat.”

6.9.oldText: “She IS too fat,” said Lavinia. “And Sara is too thin.”

6.11.oldText: “She says it has nothing to do with what you look like, or what you have. It has only to do with what you THINK of, and what you DO.”

6.12.oldText: “I suppose she thinks she could be a princess if she were a beggar,” said Lavinia. “Let’s start calling her Your Royal Highness.”

6.13.oldText: Lessons for the day were over, and they were sitting before the schoolroom fire, enjoying the time they liked best. It was the time when Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia were taking their tea in the sitting room reserved for themselves. At this hour a great deal of talking was done, and a great many secrets changed hands — particularly if the younger pupils behaved themselves well, and didn’t squabble or run about noisily, which it must be confessed they usually did. When they made an uproar, the older girls usually stepped in with scolding and shakes. They were expected to keep order, and there was a danger that if they didn’t, Miss Minchin or Miss Amelia would appear and put an end to the festivities. Even as Lavinia spoke, the door opened and Sara entered with Lottie, whose habit was to trot everywhere after her like a little dog.

6.14.oldText: “There she is, with that horrid child!” exclaimed Lavinia in a whisper. “If she’s so fond of her, why doesn’t she keep her in her own room? She’ll start howling about something in five minutes.”

6.15.oldText: It happened that Lottie had been seized with a sudden urge to play in the schoolroom, and had begged her adopted parent to come with her. She joined a group of little ones playing in a corner. Sara curled up in the window seat, opened a book, and began to read. It was a book about the French Revolution, and she was soon lost in a horrifying picture of the prisoners in the Bastille — men who had spent so many years in dungeons that when they were dragged out by their rescuers, their long, gray hair and beards almost hid their faces. They had forgotten that an outside world existed at all, and were like beings in a dream.

6.16.oldText: She was so far away from the schoolroom that it was not pleasant to be dragged back suddenly by a howl from Lottie. Never did she find anything as difficult as keeping herself from losing her temper when she was suddenly disturbed while absorbed in a book. People who are fond of books know the feeling of irritation that sweeps over them at such a moment. The temptation to be unreasonable and snappish is not easy to manage.

6.17.oldText: “It makes me feel as if someone had hit me,” Sara had told Ermengarde once in confidence. “And as if I want to hit back. I have to remember things quickly to keep from saying something ill-tempered.”

6.18.oldText: She had to remember things quickly when she laid her book on the window seat and jumped down from her comfortable corner.

6.19.oldText: Lottie had been sliding across the schoolroom floor, and, having first irritated Lavinia and Jessie by making a noise, had ended by falling down and hurting her fat knee. She was screaming and dancing up and down in the middle of a group of friends and enemies, who were taking turns coaxing and scolding her.

6.20.oldText: “Stop this minute, you crybaby! Stop this minute!” Lavinia commanded.

6.21.oldText: “I’m not a crybaby ... I’m not!” wailed Lottie. “Sara, Sa — ra!”

6.22.oldText: “If she doesn’t stop, Miss Minchin will hear her,” cried Jessie. “Lottie darling, I’ll give you a penny!”

6.23.oldText: “I don’t want your penny,” sobbed Lottie. And she looked down at her fat knee, and, seeing a drop of blood on it, burst into tears again.

6.24.oldText: Sara flew across the room and, kneeling down, put her arms around her.

6.25.oldText: “Now, Lottie,” she said. “Now, Lottie, you PROMISED Sara.”

6.26.oldText: “She said I was a crybaby,” wept Lottie.

6.27.oldText: Sara patted her, but spoke in the steady voice Lottie knew.

6.28.oldText: “But if you cry, you will be one, Lottie pet. You PROMISED.” Lottie remembered she had promised, but she preferred to lift up her voice.

6.29.oldText: “I haven’t any mama,” she announced. “I haven’t — a bit — of mama.”

6.30.oldText: “Yes, you have,” said Sara, cheerfully. “Have you forgotten? Don’t you know that Sara is your mama? Don’t you want Sara for your mama?”

6.31.oldText: Lottie cuddled up to her with a comforted sniff.

6.32.oldText: “Come and sit in the window seat with me,” Sara went on, “and I’ll whisper a story to you.”

6.33.oldText: “Will you?” whimpered Lottie. “Will you — tell me — about the diamond mines?”

6.34.oldText: “The diamond mines?” burst out Lavinia. “Nasty, little spoiled thing, I should like to SLAP her!”

6.35.oldText: Sara got quickly to her feet. It must be remembered that she had been very deeply absorbed in the book about the Bastille, and she had had to pull several things back into her mind quickly when she realized she must go and take care of her adopted child. She was not an angel, and she was not fond of Lavinia.

6.36.oldText: “Well,” she said, with some fire, “I should like to slap YOU — but I don’t want to slap you!” restraining herself. “At least I both want to slap you — and I should LIKE to slap you — but I WON’T slap you. We are not little gutter children. We are both old enough to know better.”

6.38.oldText: “Ah, yes, your royal highness,” she said. “We are princesses, I believe. At least one of us is. The school ought to be very fashionable now that Miss Minchin has a princess for a pupil.”

6.39.oldText: Sara started toward her. She looked as if she were going to box her ears. Perhaps she was. Her trick of pretending things was the joy of her life. She never spoke of it to girls she wasn’t fond of. Her new “pretend” about being a princess was very near to her heart, and she was shy and sensitive about it. She had meant it to be rather a secret, and here was Lavinia mocking it before nearly the whole school. She felt the blood rush up into her face and tingle in her ears. She just barely caught herself. If you were a princess, you did not fly into rages. Her hand dropped, and she stood quite still for a moment. When she spoke, it was in a quiet, steady voice. She held her head up, and everyone listened to her.

6.40.oldText: “It’s true,” she said. “Sometimes I do pretend I am a princess. I pretend I am a princess so that I can try to behave like one.”

6.41.oldText: Lavinia could not think of exactly the right thing to say. Several times she had found that she couldn’t think of a satisfying reply when dealing with Sara. The reason was that, somehow, the rest always seemed to be vaguely on Sara’s side. She saw now that they were pricking up their ears with interest. The truth was, they liked princesses, and they all hoped they might hear something more definite about this one. So they drew nearer to Sara.

6.42.oldText: Lavinia could only invent one remark, and it fell rather flat.

6.43.oldText: “Dear me,” she said, “I hope, when you come to the throne, you won’t forget us!”

6.44.oldText: “I won’t,” said Sara. And she didn’t utter another word, but stood quite still and stared at her steadily as she watched her take Jessie’s arm and turn away.

6.45.oldText: After this, the girls who were jealous of her used to speak of her as “Princess Sara” whenever they wanted to be especially scornful, and those who were fond of her gave her the name among themselves as a term of affection. No one called her “princess” instead of “Sara,” but her admirers were much pleased with the picturesqueness and grandeur of the title. And Miss Minchin, hearing of it, mentioned it more than once to visiting parents, feeling that it rather suggested a kind of royal boarding school.

6.46.oldText: To Becky it seemed the most fitting thing in the world. The friendship begun on the foggy afternoon when she had jumped up terrified from her sleep in the comfortable chair had ripened and grown — though it must be admitted that Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia knew very little about it. They were aware that Sara was “kind” to the scullery maid, but they knew nothing of certain delightful moments snatched at risk when, the upstairs rooms being set in order with lightning speed, Sara’s sitting room was reached, and the heavy coal box set down with a sigh of joy. At such times stories were told in installments, and things of a satisfying nature were either produced and eaten, or quickly tucked into pockets to be eaten at night, when Becky went upstairs to her attic to bed.

6.47.oldText: “But I has to eat ’em careful, miss,” she said once. “’Cos if I leaves crumbs the rats come out to get ’em.”

6.48.oldText: “Rats!” exclaimed Sara, in horror. “Are there RATS there?”

6.49.oldText: “Lots of ’em, miss,” Becky answered in quite a matter-of-fact way. “There mostly is rats an’ mice in attics. You gets used to the noise they makes scuttling about. I’ve got so I don’t mind ’em s’ long as they don’t run over my piller.”

6.51.oldText: “You gets used to anythin’ after a bit,” said Becky. “You have to, miss, if you’re born a scullery maid. I’d rather have rats than cockroaches.”

6.52.oldText: “So would I,” said Sara. “I suppose you might make friends with a rat in time, but I don’t believe I should like to make friends with a cockroach.”

6.53.oldText: Sometimes Becky did not dare to spend more than a few minutes in the bright, warm room. When this was the case, perhaps only a few words could be exchanged, and a small purchase slipped into the old-fashioned pocket Becky carried under her dress skirt, tied around her waist with a band of tape. The search for and discovery of satisfying things to eat that could be packed into small space added a new interest to Sara’s life. When she drove or walked out, she used to look into shop windows eagerly. The first time it occurred to her to bring home two or three little meat pies, she felt that she had hit upon a discovery. When she showed them, Becky’s eyes quite sparkled.

6.54.oldText: “Oh, miss!” she murmured. “Them will be nice an’ fillin’. It’s fillin’ness that’s best. Sponge cake’s a ’evenly thing, but it melts away like — if you understand, miss. These’ll just STAY in yer stummick.”

6.55.oldText: “Well,” Sara hesitated, “I don’t think it would be good if they stayed there always, but I do believe they will be satisfying.”

6.56.oldText: They were satisfying — and so were beef sandwiches, bought at a cook-shop — and so were rolls and Bologna sausage. In time, Becky began to lose her hungry, tired feeling, and the coal box did not seem so unbearably heavy.

6.57.oldText: However heavy it was, and whatever the temper of the cook, and the hardness of the work piled on her shoulders, she always had the chance of the afternoon to look forward to — the chance that Miss Sara would be in her sitting room. In fact, the mere sight of Miss Sara would have been enough without meat pies. If there was time only for a few words, they were always friendly, cheerful words that put heart into one. And if there was time for more, then there was an installment of a story to be told, or some other thing one remembered afterward and sometimes lay awake in one’s bed in the attic to think over. Sara — who was only doing what she unconsciously liked better than anything else, Nature having made her for a giver — had not the least idea what she meant to poor Becky, and how wonderful a benefactor she seemed. If Nature has made you for a giver, your hands are born open, and so is your heart. Though there may be times when your hands are empty, your heart is always full, and you can give things out of that — warm things, kind things, sweet things — help and comfort and laughter — and sometimes cheerful, kind laughter is the best help of all.

6.58.oldText: Becky had scarcely known what laughter was through all her poor, hard-driven little life. Sara made her laugh, and laughed with her. And, though neither of them quite knew it, the laughter was as “fillin’” as the meat pies.

6.59.oldText: A few weeks before Sara’s eleventh birthday, a letter came to her from her father, which did not seem to be written in such boyish high spirits as usual. He was not very well, and was clearly weighed down by the business connected with the diamond mines.

6.60.oldText: “You see, little Sara,” he wrote, “your daddy isn’t a businessman at all, and figures and documents bother him. He doesn’t really understand them, and all this seems so enormous. Perhaps if I weren’t feverish I should not be awake, tossing about, half the night and spending the other half in troubled dreams. If my little missus were here, I dare say she would give me some solemn, good advice. You would, wouldn’t you, Little Missus?”

6.61.oldText: One of his many jokes had been to call her his “little missus” because she had such an old-fashioned air.

6.62.oldText: He had made wonderful preparations for her birthday. Among other things, a new doll had been ordered in Paris, and her wardrobe was to be, indeed, a marvel of splendid perfection. When she had replied to the letter asking if the doll would be an acceptable present, Sara had been very quaint.

6.63.oldText: “I am getting very old,” she wrote. “You see, I shall never live to have another doll given me. This will be my last doll. There is something solemn about it. If I could write poetry, I am sure a poem about ‘A Last Doll’ would be very nice. But I cannot write poetry. I have tried, and it made me laugh. It did not sound like Watts or Coleridge or Shakespeare at all. No one could ever take Emily’s place, but I should respect the Last Doll very much. And I am sure the school would love it. They all like dolls, though some of the big ones — the almost fifteen ones — pretend they are too grown-up.”

6.64.oldText: Captain Crewe had a splitting headache when he read this letter in his bungalow in India. The table before him was heaped with papers and letters that were alarming him and filling him with anxious dread. But he laughed as he had not laughed for weeks.

6.65.oldText: “Oh,” he said, “she’s better fun every year she lives. God grant this business may right itself and leave me free to run home and see her. What wouldn’t I give to have her little arms round my neck this minute! What WOULDN’T I give!”

6.66.oldText: The birthday was to be celebrated with great festivities. The schoolroom was to be decorated, and there was to be a party. The boxes containing the presents were to be opened with great ceremony, and a glittering feast was to be spread in Miss Minchin’s special room. When the day arrived, the whole house was in a whirl of excitement. How the morning passed, nobody quite knew, because there seemed to be such preparations to be made. The schoolroom was being decked with garlands of holly. The desks had been moved away, and red covers had been put on the benches arranged round the room against the wall.

6.67.oldText: When Sara went into her sitting room in the morning, she found on the table a small, dumpy package, tied up in a piece of brown paper. She knew it was a present, and she thought she could guess whom it came from. She opened it quite tenderly. It was a square pincushion, made of not-quite-clean red flannel, and black pins had been stuck carefully into it to form the words, “Menny hapy returns.”

6.68.oldText: “Oh!” cried Sara, with a warm feeling in her heart. “What pains she has taken! I like it so — it — it makes me feel sad.”

6.69.oldText: But the next moment she was puzzled. On the underside of the pincushion was attached a card, bearing in neat letters the name “Miss Amelia Minchin.”

6.71.oldText: “Miss Amelia!” she said to herself. “How CAN it be!”

6.72.oldText: And just at that very moment she heard the door being cautiously pushed open, and saw Becky peeping round it.

6.73.oldText: There was an affectionate, happy grin on her face, and she shuffled forward and stood nervously pulling at her fingers.

6.74.oldText: “Do yer like it, Miss Sara?” she said. “Do yer?”

6.75.oldText: “Like it?” cried Sara. “You darling Becky, you made it all yourself.”

6.76.oldText: Becky gave a hysterical but joyful sniff, and her eyes looked quite moist with delight.

6.77.oldText: “It ain’t nothin’ but flannin, an’ the flannin ain’t new. But I wanted to give yer somethin’ an’ I made it of nights. I knew yer could PRETEND it was satin with diamond pins in. _I_ tried to when I was makin’ it. The card, miss,” rather doubtfully, “’t warn’t wrong of me to pick it up out o’ the dust-bin, was it? Miss ’Meliar had throwed it away. I hadn’t no card o’ my own, an’ I knowed it wouldn’t be a proper presink if I didn’t pin a card on — so I pinned Miss ’Meliar’s.”

6.78.oldText: Sara flew at her and hugged her. She could not have told herself or anyone else why there was a lump in her throat.

6.79.oldText: “Oh, Becky!” she cried out, with a queer little laugh, “I love you, Becky — I do, I do!”

6.80.oldText: “Oh, miss!” breathed Becky. “Thank yer, miss, kindly. It ain’t good enough for that. The — the flannin wasn’t new.”

7.0.oldText: When Sara entered the holly-decorated schoolroom that afternoon, she did so at the head of a kind of procession. Miss Minchin, in her grandest silk dress, led her by the hand. A manservant followed, carrying the box that held the Last Doll, a housemaid carried a second box, and Becky brought up the rear, carrying a third and wearing a clean apron and a new cap. Sara would have much preferred to walk in the usual way, but Miss Minchin had sent for her, and after an interview in her private sitting room, had announced her wishes.

7.1.oldText: “This is not an ordinary occasion,” she said. “I do not want it treated as one.”

7.2.oldText: So Sara was led grandly in. She felt shy when, as she entered, the older girls stared at her and nudged each other’s elbows, and the little ones began to squirm joyfully in their seats.

7.3.oldText: “Silence, young ladies!” said Miss Minchin, at the murmur that rose up. “James, place the box on the table and remove the lid. Emma, put yours upon a chair. Becky!” she added suddenly and severely.

7.4.oldText: Becky had quite forgotten herself in her excitement, and was grinning at Lottie, who was wriggling with delighted expectation. The disapproving voice startled her so much that she almost dropped her box, and her frightened, bobbing curtsy of apology was so funny that Lavinia and Jessie giggled.

7.5.oldText: “It is not your place to look at the young ladies,” said Miss Minchin. “You forget yourself. Put your box down.”

7.7.oldText: “You may leave us,” Miss Minchin announced to the servants with a wave of her hand.

7.8.oldText: Becky stepped aside respectfully to let the higher-ranked servants pass out first. She could not help casting a longing glance at the box on the table. Something made of blue satin was peeping out from between the folds of tissue paper.

7.9.oldText: “If you please, Miss Minchin,” said Sara suddenly, “may Becky stay?”

7.10.oldText: It was a bold thing to do. Miss Minchin gave something like a slight jump. Then she lifted her eyeglass and looked at her star pupil with a troubled expression.

7.13.oldText: “I want her to stay because I know she will love seeing the presents,” she explained. “She is a little girl, too, you know.”

7.14.oldText: Miss Minchin was scandalized. She glanced from one figure to the other.

7.15.oldText: “My dear Sara,” she said, “Becky is the scullery maid. Scullery maids — er — are not little girls.”

7.16.oldText: It really had not occurred to her to think of them in that way. Scullery maids were machines who carried coal scuttles and made fires.

7.17.oldText: “But Becky is,” said Sara. “And I know she would enjoy herself. Please let her stay — because it is my birthday.”

7.18.oldText: Miss Minchin replied with great dignity:

7.19.oldText: “Since you ask it as a birthday favor — she may stay. Rebecca, thank Miss Sara for her great kindness.”

7.20.oldText: Becky had been backing into the corner, twisting the hem of her apron in delighted suspense. She came forward, bobbing curtsies, and between Sara’s eyes and her own there passed a glance of friendly understanding, while her words tumbled over each other.

7.21.oldText: “Oh, if you please, miss! I’m that grateful, miss! I did want to see the doll, miss, that I did. Thank you, miss. And thank you, ma’am,” — turning and making an alarmed bob to Miss Minchin — “for letting me take the liberty.”

7.22.oldText: Miss Minchin waved her hand again — this time toward the corner near the door.

7.23.oldText: “Go and stand there,” she commanded. “Not too near the young ladies.”

7.24.oldText: Becky went to her place, grinning. She did not care where she was sent, so long as she had the luck of being inside the room, instead of being downstairs in the scullery, while these wonderful things were going on. She did not even mind when Miss Minchin cleared her throat ominously and spoke again.

7.25.oldText: “Now, young ladies, I have a few words to say to you,” she announced.

7.26.oldText: “She’s going to make a speech,” whispered one of the girls. “I wish it were over.”

7.27.oldText: Sara felt rather uncomfortable. As this was her party, the speech was probably about her. It is not pleasant to stand in a schoolroom and have a speech made about you.

7.28.oldText: “You are aware, young ladies,” the speech began — for it was a speech — “that dear Sara is eleven years old today.”

7.30.oldText: “Several of you have also been eleven years old, but Sara’s birthdays are rather different from other little girls’ birthdays. When she is older, she will be heiress to a large fortune, which it will be her duty to spend in a worthy manner.”

7.31.oldText: “The diamond mines,” giggled Jessie in a whisper.

7.32.oldText: Sara did not hear her, but as she stood with her green-gray eyes fixed steadily on Miss Minchin, she felt herself growing rather hot. When Miss Minchin talked about money, she always somehow felt that she hated her — and, of course, it was disrespectful to hate grown-up people.

7.33.oldText: “When her dear papa, Captain Crewe, brought her from India and gave her into my care,” the speech continued, “he said to me, in a joking way, ‘I am afraid she will be very rich, Miss Minchin.’ My reply was, ‘Her education at my seminary, Captain Crewe, shall be such as will adorn the largest fortune.’ Sara has become my most accomplished pupil. Her French and her dancing are a credit to the seminary. Her manners — which have made you call her Princess Sara — are perfect. She shows her kindness by giving you this afternoon’s party. I hope you appreciate her generosity. I want you to express your appreciation by saying aloud all together, ‘Thank you, Sara!’”

7.34.oldText: The whole schoolroom rose to its feet, just as it had on the morning Sara remembered so well.

7.35.oldText: “Thank you, Sara!” it said, and it must be admitted that Lottie jumped up and down. Sara looked rather shy for a moment. She made a curtsy — and it was a very nice one.

7.36.oldText: “Thank you,” she said, “for coming to my party.”

7.37.oldText: “Very pretty indeed, Sara,” said Miss Minchin approvingly. “That is what a real princess does when the people applaud her. Lavinia” — scathingly — “the sound you just made was extremely like a snort. If you are jealous of your fellow pupil, I beg you to express your feelings in a more lady-like manner. Now I will leave you to enjoy yourselves.”

7.38.oldText: The instant she had swept out of the room, the spell her presence always cast upon them was broken. The door had barely closed before every seat was empty. The little girls jumped or tumbled out of theirs; the older ones wasted no time in leaving theirs. There was a rush toward the boxes. Sara had bent over one of them with a delighted face.

7.39.oldText: “These are books, I know,” she said.

7.40.oldText: The little children broke into a disappointed murmur, and Ermengarde looked horrified.

7.41.oldText: “Does your papa send you books for a birthday present?” she exclaimed. “Why, he’s as bad as mine. Don’t open them, Sara.”

7.42.oldText: “I like them,” Sara laughed, but she turned to the biggest box. When she took out the Last Doll, it was so magnificent that the children let out delighted gasps of joy, and actually drew back to gaze at it in breathless wonder.

7.43.oldText: “She is almost as big as Lottie,” someone gasped.

7.45.oldText: “She’s dressed for the theater,” said Lavinia. “Her cloak is lined with ermine.”

7.46.oldText: “Oh,” cried Ermengarde, darting forward, “she has an opera-glass in her hand — a blue-and-gold one!”

7.47.oldText: “Here is her trunk,” said Sara. “Let’s open it and look at her things.”

7.48.oldText: She sat down on the floor and turned the key. The children crowded clamoring around her, as she lifted tray after tray and revealed their contents. The schoolroom had never been in such an uproar. There were lace collars and silk stockings and handkerchiefs; there was a jewel case containing a necklace and a tiara that looked exactly as if they were made of real diamonds; there was a long sealskin coat and muff; there were ball gowns and walking dresses and visiting dresses; there were hats and tea gowns and fans. Even Lavinia and Jessie forgot that they were too old to care about dolls, and let out cries of delight as they snatched up things to look at them.

7.49.oldText: “Suppose,” Sara said, as she stood by the table, putting a large black-velvet hat on the calmly smiling owner of all these splendors — “suppose she understands human talk and feels proud of being admired.”

7.50.oldText: “You are always supposing things,” said Lavinia, her air very superior.

7.51.oldText: “I know I am,” answered Sara, undisturbed. “I like it. There is nothing so nice as supposing. It’s almost like being a fairy. If you suppose anything hard enough, it seems as if it were real.”

7.52.oldText: “It’s all very well to suppose things if you have everything,” said Lavinia. “Could you suppose and pretend if you were a beggar and lived in a garret?”

7.53.oldText: Sara stopped arranging the Last Doll’s ostrich plumes, and looked thoughtful.

7.54.oldText: “I BELIEVE I could,” she said. “If one were a beggar, one would have to suppose and pretend all the time. But it might not be easy.”

7.55.oldText: She often thought afterward how strange it was that just as she had finished saying this — at that very moment — Miss Amelia came into the room.

7.56.oldText: “Sara,” she said, “your papa’s solicitor, Mr. Barrow, has come to see Miss Minchin, and since she must talk to him alone and the refreshments are laid out in her parlor, you had all better go and have your feast now, so that my sister can have her interview here in the schoolroom.”

7.57.oldText: Refreshments were not likely to be turned down at any hour, and many pairs of eyes gleamed. Miss Amelia arranged the procession into proper order, and then, with Sara at her side leading it, she led them away. The Last Doll was left sitting upon a chair, the glories of her wardrobe scattered about her — dresses and coats hanging on chair backs, piles of lace-frilled petticoats lying on the seats.

7.58.oldText: Becky, who was not expected to share in the refreshments, made the mistake of lingering a moment to look at these beauties — it really was a mistake.

7.59.oldText: “Go back to your work, Becky,” Miss Amelia had said; but Becky had stopped to pick up reverently first a muff and then a coat, and while she stood gazing at them adoringly, she heard Miss Minchin at the doorway. Struck with terror at the thought of being accused of taking liberties, she rashly darted under the table, where the tablecloth hid her.

7.60.oldText: Miss Minchin came into the room, accompanied by a sharp-featured, dry little gentleman, who looked rather upset. Miss Minchin herself also looked rather upset, it must be admitted, and she stared at the dry little gentleman with an irritated and puzzled expression.

7.61.oldText: She sat down with stiff dignity, and waved him to a chair.

7.62.oldText: “Please, be seated, Mr. Barrow,” she said.

7.63.oldText: Mr. Barrow did not sit down right away. His attention seemed caught by the Last Doll and the things around her. He adjusted his eyeglasses and looked at them in nervous disapproval. The Last Doll herself did not seem to mind in the least. She simply sat upright and returned his gaze indifferently.

7.64.oldText: “A hundred pounds,” Mr. Barrow remarked shortly. “All expensive material, and made at a Parisian dressmaker’s. He spent money lavishly enough, that young man.”

7.65.oldText: Miss Minchin felt offended. This seemed to be a criticism of her best patron, and was a liberty.

7.67.oldText: “I beg your pardon, Mr. Barrow,” she said stiffly. “I do not understand.”

7.68.oldText: “Birthday presents,” said Mr. Barrow in the same critical manner, “to a child eleven years old! Mad extravagance, I call it.”

7.69.oldText: Miss Minchin drew herself up even more rigidly.

7.70.oldText: “Captain Crewe is a man of fortune,” she said. “The diamond mines alone —”

7.71.oldText: Mr. Barrow whirled around at her. “Diamond mines!” he burst out. “There are none! Never were!”

7.74.oldText: “At any rate,” answered Mr. Barrow, quite snappishly, “it would have been much better if there never had been any.”

7.75.oldText: “No diamond mines?” gasped Miss Minchin, catching at the back of a chair and feeling as if a splendid dream were fading away from her.

7.76.oldText: “Diamond mines spell ruin more often than they spell wealth,” said Mr. Barrow. “When a man is in the hands of a very dear friend and is not a businessman himself, he had better steer clear of his dear friend’s diamond mines, or gold mines, or any other kind of mines that dear friends want his money to put into. The late Captain Crewe —”

7.77.oldText: Here Miss Minchin stopped him with a gasp.

7.78.oldText: “The LATE Captain Crewe!” she cried out. “The LATE! You don’t mean to tell me that Captain Crewe is —”

7.79.oldText: “He’s dead, ma’am,” Mr. Barrow answered with jerky bluntness. “Died of jungle fever and business troubles combined. The jungle fever might not have killed him if he had not been driven mad by the business troubles, and the business troubles might not have finished him if the jungle fever had not helped along. Captain Crewe is dead!”

7.80.oldText: Miss Minchin dropped into her chair again. The words he had spoken filled her with alarm.

7.81.oldText: “What WERE his business troubles?” she said. “What WERE they?”

7.82.oldText: “Diamond mines,” answered Mr. Barrow, “and dear friends — and ruin.”

7.85.oldText: “Lost every penny. That young man had too much money. The dear friend was mad on the subject of the diamond mine. He put all his own money into it, and all of Captain Crewe’s as well. Then the dear friend ran away — Captain Crewe was already stricken with fever when the news reached him. The shock was too much for him. He died delirious, raving about his little girl — and didn’t leave a penny.”

7.86.oldText: Now Miss Minchin understood, and never had she received such a blow in her life. Her star pupil, her star patron, swept away from the Select Seminary at one stroke. She felt as if she had been outraged and robbed, and as if Captain Crewe and Sara and Mr. Barrow were equally to blame.

7.87.oldText: “Do you mean to tell me,” she cried out, “that he left NOTHING! That Sara will have no fortune! That the child is a beggar! That she is left on my hands as a little pauper instead of an heiress?”

7.88.oldText: Mr. Barrow was a shrewd businessman, and felt it was wise to make his own freedom from responsibility quite clear without any delay.

7.89.oldText: “She is certainly left a beggar,” he replied. “And she is certainly left on your hands, ma’am — since she has not a relation in the world that we know of.”

7.90.oldText: Miss Minchin started forward. She looked as if she were about to open the door and rush out of the room to stop the festivities going on so joyfully and rather noisily at that moment over the refreshments.

7.91.oldText: “It is monstrous!” she said. “She’s in my sitting room at this very moment, dressed in silk gauze and lace petticoats, giving a party at my expense.”

7.92.oldText: “She’s giving it at your expense, madam, if she’s giving it,” said Mr. Barrow calmly. “Barrow & Skipworth are not responsible for anything. There never was a cleaner sweep made of a man’s fortune. Captain Crewe died without paying OUR last bill — and it was a big one.”

7.93.oldText: Miss Minchin turned back from the door in even greater outrage. This was worse than anyone could have imagined.

7.94.oldText: “That is what has happened to me!” she cried. “I was always so sure of his payments that I went to all sorts of ridiculous expenses for the child. I paid the bills for that ridiculous doll and her ridiculous extravagant wardrobe. The child was to have anything she wanted. She has a carriage and a pony and a maid, and I’ve paid for all of them since the last cheque came.”

7.95.oldText: Mr. Barrow clearly did not intend to stay and listen to the story of Miss Minchin’s grievances after he had made the position of his firm clear and laid out the bare dry facts. He felt no particular sympathy for angry keepers of boarding schools.

7.96.oldText: “You had better not pay for anything more, ma’am,” he remarked, “unless you want to give presents to the young lady. No one will reimburse you. She hasn’t a brass farthing to call her own.”

7.97.oldText: “But what am I to do?” demanded Miss Minchin, as if she felt it was entirely his duty to fix the matter. “What am I to do?”

7.98.oldText: “There isn’t anything to do,” said Mr. Barrow, folding up his eyeglasses and slipping them into his pocket. “Captain Crewe is dead. The child is left a pauper. Nobody is responsible for her but you.”

7.99.oldText: “I am not responsible for her, and I refuse to be made responsible!”

7.100.oldText: Miss Minchin became quite white with rage.

7.102.oldText: “I have nothing to do with that, madam,” he said indifferently. “Barrow & Skipworth are not responsible. Very sorry the thing has happened, of course.”

7.103.oldText: “If you think she is going to be dumped on me, you are greatly mistaken,” Miss Minchin gasped. “I have been robbed and cheated; I will turn her out into the street!”

7.104.oldText: If she had not been so furious, she would have been smart enough not to say so much. She saw herself stuck with a child raised in luxury, a child she had always resented, and she lost all self-control.

7.105.oldText: Mr. Barrow walked calmly toward the door.

7.106.oldText: “I wouldn't do that, madam,” he commented. “It wouldn't look good. It would be an unpleasant story to spread about the school. A pupil thrown out, penniless and without friends.”

7.107.oldText: He was a clever businessman, and he knew what he was saying. He also knew that Miss Minchin was a businesswoman, and would be sharp enough to see the truth. She could not afford to do something that would make people call her cruel and hard-hearted.

7.108.oldText: “Better keep her and put her to use,” he added. “She's a clever child, I believe. You can get a great deal out of her as she grows older.”

7.109.oldText: “I will get a great deal out of her before she grows older!” exclaimed Miss Minchin.

7.110.oldText: “I am sure you will, ma'am,” said Mr. Barrow, with a small, sinister smile. “I am sure you will. Good morning!”

7.111.oldText: He bowed himself out and shut the door, and it must be admitted that Miss Minchin stood for a few moments and glared at it. What he had said was quite true. She knew it. She had absolutely no way to recover her losses. Her star pupil had melted into nothing, leaving only a friendless, penniless little girl. The money she herself had spent was gone and could not be regained.

7.112.oldText: And as she stood there, breathless with her sense of injury, a burst of cheerful voices reached her ears from her own private room, which had been given over to the feast. She could at least put a stop to that.

7.113.oldText: But as she started toward the door, it was opened by Miss Amelia, who, when she caught sight of the changed, angry face, fell back a step in alarm.

7.114.oldText: “What IS the matter, sister?” she blurted out.

7.115.oldText: Miss Minchin's voice was almost fierce when she answered:

7.118.oldText: “Sara!” she stammered. “Why, she's with the children in your room, of course.”

7.119.oldText: “Has she a black dress in her splendid wardrobe?”—in bitter sarcasm.

7.120.oldText: “A black dress?” Miss Amelia stammered again. “A BLACK one?”

7.121.oldText: “She has dresses of every other color. Has she a black one?”

7.122.oldText: Miss Amelia began to turn pale.

7.123.oldText: “No—ye-es!” she said. “But it is too short for her. She has only the old black velvet, and she has outgrown it.”

7.124.oldText: “Go and tell her to take off that ridiculous pink silk gauze, and put the black one on, whether it is too short or not. She is finished with finery!”

7.125.oldText: Then Miss Amelia began to wring her plump hands and cry.

7.126.oldText: “Oh, sister!” she sniffed. “Oh, sister! What CAN have happened?”

7.128.oldText: “Captain Crewe is dead,” she said. “He has died without a penny. That spoiled, pampered, dreamy child is left a pauper on my hands.”

7.129.oldText: Miss Amelia sat down quite heavily in the nearest chair.

7.130.oldText: “Hundreds of pounds I have spent on nonsense for her. And I shall never see a penny of it back. Put a stop to that ridiculous party of hers. Go and make her change her dress at once.”

7.131.oldText: “I?” panted Miss Amelia. “M-must I go and tell her now?”

7.132.oldText: “This very moment!” was the fierce answer. “Don't sit staring like a goose. Go!”

7.133.oldText: Poor Miss Amelia was used to being called a goose. She knew, in fact, that she was rather a goose, and that geese were left to do many disagreeable things. It was a rather embarrassing thing to walk into a room full of delighted children, and tell the girl who had given the feast that she had suddenly been turned into a little beggar, and must go upstairs and put on an old black dress that was too small for her. But the thing had to be done. This was clearly not the time when questions could be asked.

7.134.oldText: She rubbed her eyes with her handkerchief until they looked quite red. After that she got up and went out of the room, without daring to say another word. When her older sister looked and spoke as she had done just now, the wisest thing to do was obey orders without any comment. Miss Minchin walked across the room. She spoke to herself out loud without realizing she was doing it. During the past year, the story of the diamond mines had suggested all kinds of possibilities to her. Even the owners of seminaries might make fortunes in stocks, with the help of the owners of mines. And now, instead of looking forward to gains, she was left to look back on losses.

7.135.oldText: “Princess Sara, indeed!” she said. “The child has been pampered as if she were a QUEEN.” She was sweeping angrily past the corner table as she said it, and the next moment she was startled by the sound of a loud, sobbing sniff that came from under the cover.

7.136.oldText: “What is that!” she exclaimed angrily. The loud, sobbing sniff was heard again, and she stooped and lifted the hanging folds of the table cover.

7.137.oldText: “How DARE you!” she cried out. “How dare you! Come out immediately!”

7.138.oldText: It was poor Becky who crawled out, her cap knocked sideways, and her face red from holding back her crying.

7.139.oldText: “If you please, ma'am—it's me, ma'am,” she explained. “I know I shouldn't have. But I was looking at the doll, ma'am—and I got frightened when you came in—and slipped under the table.”

7.140.oldText: “You have been there the whole time, listening,” said Miss Minchin.

7.141.oldText: “No, ma'am,” Becky protested, bobbing curtsies. “Not listening—I thought I could slip out without you noticing, but I couldn't, and I had to stay. But I didn't listen, ma'am—I wouldn't, not for anything. But I couldn't help hearing.”

7.142.oldText: Suddenly it almost seemed as if she lost all fear of the terrible lady in front of her. She burst into fresh tears.

7.143.oldText: “Oh, please, ma'am,” she said; “I expect you'll dismiss me, ma'am—but I'm so sorry for poor Miss Sara—I'm so sorry!”

7.145.oldText: Becky curtsied again, the tears streaming openly down her cheeks.

7.146.oldText: “Yes, ma'am; I will, ma'am,” she said, trembling. “But oh, I just wanted to ask you: Miss Sara—she's been such a rich young lady, and she's been waited on, hand and foot. What will she do now, ma'am, without any maid? If—if, oh please, would you let me wait on her after I've finished my pots and kettles? I'd do them so quickly—if you'd just let me wait on her now that she's poor. Oh,” bursting out again, “poor little Miss Sara, ma'am—who used to be called a princess.”

7.147.oldText: Somehow, this made Miss Minchin feel angrier than ever. That even the kitchen maid should take the side of this child—whom she now realized more fully than ever she had never liked—was too much. She actually stamped her foot.

7.148.oldText: “No—certainly not,” she said. “She will wait on herself, and on other people too. Leave the room this instant, or you'll lose your job.”

7.149.oldText: Becky threw her apron over her head and fled. She ran out of the room and down the steps into the scullery, and there she sat down among her pots and kettles, and wept as if her heart would break.

7.150.oldText: “It's exactly like the ones in the stories,” she wailed. “Those poor princess ones who were driven out into the world.”

7.151.oldText: Miss Minchin had never looked quite so still and hard as she did when Sara came to her, a few hours later, in answer to the message she had sent.

7.152.oldText: Even by then, it seemed to Sara as if the birthday party had either been a dream, or a thing that had happened years ago, and had happened in the life of quite another little girl.

7.153.oldText: Every sign of the celebration had been swept away. The holly had been removed from the schoolroom walls, and the benches and desks had been put back in their places. Miss Minchin's sitting room looked as it always did—every trace of the feast was gone, and Miss Minchin had put on her usual dress. The pupils had been ordered to put away their party dresses; and once that was done, they had returned to the schoolroom and huddled together in groups, whispering and talking excitedly.

7.154.oldText: “Tell Sara to come to my room,” Miss Minchin had said to her sister. “And explain to her clearly that I will not have any crying or unpleasant scenes.”

7.155.oldText: “Sister,” replied Miss Amelia, “she is the strangest child I ever saw. She has actually made no fuss at all. You remember she made none when Captain Crewe went back to India. When I told her what had happened, she just stood quite still and looked at me without making a sound. Her eyes seemed to get bigger and bigger, and she went quite pale. When I had finished, she still stood staring for a few seconds, and then her chin began to shake, and she turned and ran out of the room and upstairs. Several of the other children began to cry, but she did not seem to hear them, or to be aware of anything except what I was saying. It made me feel quite strange not to get an answer; and when you tell someone something sudden and shocking, you expect them to say SOMETHING—whatever it is.”

7.156.oldText: Nobody but Sara herself ever knew what happened in her room after she ran upstairs and locked her door. In fact, she herself barely remembered anything except that she walked up and down, repeating over and over again to herself, in a voice that did not seem to be her own, “My papa is dead! My papa is dead!”

7.157.oldText: Once she stopped in front of Emily, who sat watching her from her chair, and cried out wildly, “Emily! Do you hear? Do you hear—papa is dead? He is dead in India—thousands of miles away.”

7.158.oldText: When she came into Miss Minchin's sitting room in answer to the summons, her face was white and her eyes had dark rings around them. Her mouth was set as if she did not want it to reveal what she had suffered and was still suffering. She did not look in the least like the rose-colored butterfly child who had flitted from one of her treasures to another in the decorated schoolroom. She looked instead a strange, desolate, almost grotesque little figure.

7.159.oldText: She had put on, without Mariette's help, the cast-aside black-velvet dress. It was too short and tight, and her slim legs looked long and thin, showing themselves below the brief skirt. Since she had not found a piece of black ribbon, her short, thick, black hair tumbled loosely about her face and contrasted sharply with its paleness. She held Emily tightly in one arm, and Emily was wrapped in a piece of black material.

7.160.oldText: “Put down your doll,” said Miss Minchin. “What do you mean by bringing her here?”

7.161.oldText: “No,” Sara answered. “I will not put her down. She is all I have. My papa gave her to me.”

7.162.oldText: She had always made Miss Minchin feel secretly uncomfortable, and she did so now. She did not speak with rudeness so much as with a cold steadiness that Miss Minchin found difficult to deal with—perhaps because she knew she was doing a heartless and inhuman thing.

7.163.oldText: “You will have no time for dolls in the future,” she said. “You will have to work and improve yourself and make yourself useful.”

7.164.oldText: Sara kept her big, strange eyes fixed on her, and said not a word.

7.165.oldText: “Everything will be very different now,” Miss Minchin went on. “I suppose Miss Amelia has explained things to you.”

7.166.oldText: “Yes,” answered Sara. “My papa is dead. He left me no money. I am quite poor.”

7.167.oldText: “You are a beggar,” said Miss Minchin, her temper rising as she remembered what all this meant. “It appears that you have no relatives and no home, and no one to take care of you.”

7.169.oldText: “What are you staring at?” demanded Miss Minchin sharply. “Are you so stupid that you cannot understand? I am telling you that you are quite alone in the world, and have no one to do anything for you, unless I choose to keep you here out of charity.”

7.170.oldText: “I understand,” answered Sara, in a low tone; and there was a sound as if she had swallowed down something that rose in her throat. “I understand.”

7.171.oldText: “That doll,” cried Miss Minchin, pointing to the splendid birthday gift seated nearby—“that ridiculous doll, with all her absurd, extravagant things—I actually paid the bill for her!”

7.173.oldText: “The Last Doll,” she said. “The Last Doll.” And her small, mournful voice had a strange sound.

7.174.oldText: “The Last Doll, indeed!” said Miss Minchin. “And she is mine, not yours. Everything you own is mine.”

7.175.oldText: “Please take her away from me, then,” said Sara. “I do not want her.”

7.176.oldText: If she had cried and sobbed and seemed frightened, Miss Minchin might almost have had more patience with her. She was a woman who liked to dominate and feel her power, and as she looked at Sara's pale little steady face and heard her proud little voice, she felt as if her authority was being treated as nothing.

7.177.oldText: “Don't put on grand airs,” she said. “The time for that sort of thing is past. You are not a princess any longer. Your carriage and your pony will be sent away—your maid will be dismissed. You will wear your oldest and plainest clothes—your extravagant ones are no longer suited to your station. You are like Becky—you must work for your living.”

7.178.oldText: To her surprise, a faint gleam of light came into the child's eyes—a hint of relief.

7.179.oldText: “Can I work?” she said. “If I can work, it will not matter so much. What can I do?”

7.180.oldText: “You can do whatever you are told,” was the answer. “You are a sharp child, and pick things up readily. If you make yourself useful, I may let you stay here. You speak French well, and you can help with the younger children.”

7.181.oldText: “May I?” exclaimed Sara. “Oh, please let me! I know I can teach them. I like them, and they like me.”

7.182.oldText: “Don't talk nonsense about people liking you,” said Miss Minchin. “You will have to do more than teach the little ones. You will run errands and help in the kitchen as well as in the schoolroom. If you don't please me, you will be sent away. Remember that. Now go.”

7.183.oldText: Sara stood still for just a moment, looking at her. In her young soul, she was thinking deep and strange things. Then she turned to leave the room.

7.184.oldText: “Stop!” said Miss Minchin. “Don't you intend to thank me?”

7.185.oldText: Sara paused, and all the deep, strange thoughts surged up in her chest.

7.187.oldText: “For my kindness to you,” replied Miss Minchin. “For my kindness in giving you a home.”

7.188.oldText: Sara took two or three steps toward her. Her thin little chest heaved up and down, and she spoke in a strange, fierce way that did not sound like a child.

7.189.oldText: “You are not kind,” she said. “You are NOT kind, and it is NOT a home.” And she had turned and run out of the room before Miss Minchin could stop her or do anything but stare after her with stony anger.

7.190.oldText: She went up the stairs slowly, panting for breath, and she held Emily tightly against her side.

7.191.oldText: “I wish she could talk,” she said to herself. “If she could speak—if she could speak!”

7.192.oldText: She meant to go to her room and lie down on the tiger-skin, with her cheek on the great cat's head, and look into the fire and think and think and think. But just before she reached the landing, Miss Amelia came out of the door and closed it behind her, and stood in front of it, looking nervous and awkward. The truth was that she felt secretly ashamed of the thing she had been ordered to do.

7.193.oldText: “You—you are not to go in there,” she said.

7.194.oldText: “Not go in?” exclaimed Sara, and she fell back a step.

7.195.oldText: “That is not your room now,” Miss Amelia answered, blushing a little.

7.196.oldText: Somehow, all at once, Sara understood. She realized that this was the beginning of the change Miss Minchin had spoken of.

7.197.oldText: “Where is my room?” she asked, hoping very much that her voice did not shake.

7.198.oldText: “You are to sleep in the attic next to Becky.”

7.199.oldText: Sara knew where it was. Becky had told her about it. She turned, and climbed up two flights of stairs. The last one was narrow, and covered with shabby strips of old carpet. She felt as if she were walking away and leaving far behind her the world in which that other child, who no longer seemed like herself, had lived. This child, in her short, tight old dress, climbing the stairs to the attic, was quite a different creature.

7.200.oldText: When she reached the attic door and opened it, her heart gave a dreary little thump. Then she shut the door and stood against it and looked around her.

7.201.oldText: Yes, this was another world. The room had a slanting roof and was whitewashed. The whitewash was dingy and had fallen off in places. There was a rusty grate, an old iron bedstead, and a hard bed covered with a faded coverlet. Some pieces of furniture too worn to be used downstairs had been sent up. Under the skylight in the roof, which showed nothing but an oblong piece of dull gray sky, there stood an old battered red footstool. Sara went to it and sat down. She seldom cried. She did not cry now. She laid Emily across her knees and put her face down upon her and her arms around her, and sat there, her little black head resting on the black drapery, not saying one word, not making one sound.

7.202.oldText: And as she sat in this silence, there came a low tap at the door—such a low, humble one that she did not at first hear it, and indeed was not roused until the door was timidly pushed open and a poor tear-smeared face peeped round it. It was Becky's face, and Becky had been crying secretly for hours and rubbing her eyes with her kitchen apron until she looked strange indeed.

7.203.oldText: “Oh, miss,” she said under her breath. “Might I—would you allow me—just to come in?”

7.204.oldText: Sara lifted her head and looked at her. She tried to begin a smile, and somehow she could not. Suddenly—and it was all because of the loving sadness of Becky's streaming eyes—her face looked more like a child's, not so much too old for her years. She held out her hand and gave a little sob.

7.205.oldText: “Oh, Becky,” she said. “I told you we were just the same—only two little girls—just two little girls. You see how true it is. There's no difference now. I'm not a princess anymore.”

7.206.oldText: Becky ran to her and caught her hand, and hugged it to her chest, kneeling beside her and sobbing with love and pain.

7.207.oldText: “Yes, miss, you are,” she cried, and her words were all broken. “Whatever happens to you—whatever—you'd be a princess all the same—and nothing could ever make you anything different.”

8.1.oldText: “My papa is dead!” she kept whispering to herself. “My papa is dead!”

8.4.oldText: “She must begin as she is to go on,” Miss Minchin said to Miss Amelia. “She must be taught at once what to expect.”

8.7.oldText: “You will begin your new duties, Sara,” she said, “by sitting with the younger children at a smaller table. You must keep them quiet, see that they behave well, and make sure they do not waste their food. You should have been down earlier. Lottie has already spilled her tea.”

8.8.oldText: That was the beginning, and from day to day more duties were piled on her. She taught the younger children French and listened to their other lessons, and these were the lightest of her chores. They found she could be used in countless ways. She could be sent on errands at any time and in any weather. She could be told to do things other people had skipped. The cook and the housemaids took their cue from Miss Minchin, and rather enjoyed bossing around the “young one” who had been fussed over for so long. They were not the best class of servants. They had neither good manners nor good tempers, and it was often convenient to have someone nearby to blame.

8.12.oldText: “If I do not remind myself of the things I have learned, I might forget them,” she said to herself. “I am almost a kitchen maid, and if I am a kitchen maid who knows nothing, I shall be like poor Becky. I wonder if I could quite forget, and start dropping my H's, and not remember that Henry the Eighth had six wives.”

8.14.oldText: “I will not have her forming close friendships and talking to the other children,” that lady said. “Girls love a grievance, and if she begins to tell romantic stories about herself, she will become a poor, mistreated heroine, and parents will get the wrong impression. It is better that she live a separate life — one suited to her circumstances. I am giving her a home, and that is more than she has any right to expect from me.”

8.16.oldText: “To think she was the girl with the diamond mines,” Lavinia commented. “She looks awful. And she's stranger than ever. I never liked her much, but I can't bear that way she has now of looking at people without speaking — just as if she was figuring them out.”

8.17.oldText: “I am,” said Sara promptly when she heard about it. “That's what I look at some people for. I like to know about them. I think them over afterwards.”

8.20.oldText: “Soldiers don't complain,” she would say between her small, tight teeth. “I am not going to do it. I will pretend this is part of a war.”

8.22.oldText: The first, it must be admitted, was Becky — just Becky. Throughout that whole first night in the garret, she had felt a vague comfort knowing that on the other side of the wall, where the rats scuffled and squeaked, there was another young human being. And during the nights that followed, the comfort grew. They had little chance to speak to each other during the day. Each had her own tasks, and any attempt at conversation would have been seen as loitering and wasting time. “Don't mind me, miss,” Becky whispered the first morning, “if I don't say nothin' polite. Some'un'd be down on us if I did. I means ‘please' an' ‘thank you' an' ‘beg pardon,' but I dassn't take time to say it.”

8.27.oldText: Ermengarde was too slow a girl to handle such a moment. She could not think of anything to say. She knew what had happened, but somehow she had never imagined Sara could look like this — so odd and poor and almost like a servant. It made her quite miserable, and she could do nothing but break into a short, hysterical laugh and exclaim — pointlessly, as if without meaning anything — “Oh, Sara, is that you?”

8.28.oldText: “Yes,” answered Sara, and suddenly a strange thought passed through her mind and made her face flush. She held the pile of clothes in her arms, with her chin resting on top of it to keep it steady. Something in the look of her direct, steady eyes made Ermengarde lose her wits even more. She felt as if Sara had turned into a new kind of girl she had never known. Perhaps it was because Sara had suddenly grown poor and had to mend things and work like Becky.

8.30.oldText: “I don't know,” Sara replied. “How are you?”

8.31.oldText: “I'm — I'm quite well,” said Ermengarde, overwhelmed with shyness. Then suddenly she thought of something to say that seemed more personal. “Are you — are you very unhappy?” she said in a rush.

8.33.oldText: “What do you think?” she said. “Do you think I am very happy?” And she marched past her without another word.

8.36.oldText: “She is like the others,” she had thought. “She does not really want to talk to me. She knows no one does.”

8.38.oldText: “If she would rather not talk to me,” Sara thought, “I will keep out of her way. Miss Minchin makes that easy enough.”

8.40.oldText: “What are you crying for, Ermengarde?” she asked.

8.41.oldText: “I'm not crying,” answered Ermengarde, in a muffled, shaky voice.

8.42.oldText: “You are,” said Jessie. “A great big tear just rolled down the bridge of your nose and dropped off the end of it. And there goes another.”

8.43.oldText: “Well,” said Ermengarde, “I'm miserable — and no one need interfere.” And she turned her plump back, took out her handkerchief, and boldly hid her face in it.

8.45.oldText: “Nobody goes there but me,” she thought quickly, “but someone has lit a candle.”

8.47.oldText: “Ermengarde!” cried Sara. She was so startled she was almost frightened. “You will get into trouble.”

8.49.oldText: “I know I shall — if I'm found out,” she said. “But I don't care — I don't care a bit. Oh, Sara, please tell me. What is the matter? Why don't you like me any more?”

8.50.oldText: Something in her voice made the familiar lump rise in Sara's throat. It was so affectionate and simple — so like the old Ermengarde who had asked her to be “best friends.” It sounded as if she had not meant what she had seemed to mean during the past few weeks.

8.51.oldText: “I do like you,” Sara answered. “I thought — you see, everything is different now. I thought you — were different.”

8.53.oldText: “Why, it was you who were different!” she cried. “You didn't want to talk to me. I didn't know what to do. It was you who were different after I came back.”

8.55.oldText: “I am different,” she explained, “though not in the way you think. Miss Minchin does not want me to talk to the girls. Most of them don't want to talk to me. I thought — perhaps — you didn't either. So I tried to keep out of your way.”

8.56.oldText: “Oh, Sara,” Ermengarde almost wailed in her hurt dismay. And then, after one more look, they rushed into each other's arms. It must be admitted that Sara's small black head lay for some minutes on the shoulder covered by the red shawl. When Ermengarde had seemed to abandon her, she had felt horribly lonely.

8.58.oldText: “I couldn't bear it any more,” she said. “I dare say you could live without me, Sara, but I couldn't live without you. I was nearly dead. So tonight, when I was crying under the bedclothes, I suddenly thought of creeping up here and just begging you to let us be friends again.”

8.59.oldText: “You are nicer than I am,” said Sara. “I was too proud to try to make friends. You see, now that hard times have come, they have shown that I am not a nice child. I was afraid they would. Perhaps” — wrinkling her forehead wisely — “that is what they were sent for.”

8.60.oldText: “I don't see any good in them,” said Ermengarde stoutly.

8.61.oldText: “Neither do I — to be honest,” admitted Sara, frankly. “But I suppose there might be good in things, even if we don't see it. There might” — doubtfully — “be good in Miss Minchin.”

8.63.oldText: “Sara,” she said, “do you think you can bear living here?”

8.65.oldText: “If I pretend it's quite different, I can,” she answered. “Or if I pretend it is a place in a story.”

8.67.oldText: “Other people have lived in worse places. Think of the Count of Monte Cristo in the dungeons of the Chateau d'If. And think of the people in the Bastille!”

8.68.oldText: “The Bastille,” half whispered Ermengarde, watching her and beginning to be fascinated. She remembered stories of the French Revolution which Sara had been able to fix in her mind by telling them dramatically. No one but Sara could have done it.

8.70.oldText: “Yes,” she said, hugging her knees, “that will be a good place to pretend about. I am a prisoner in the Bastille. I have been here for years and years — and years — and everybody has forgotten about me. Miss Minchin is the jailer — and Becky” — a sudden new light joining the glow in her eyes — “Becky is the prisoner in the next cell.”

8.72.oldText: “I shall pretend that,” she said. “And it will be a great comfort.”

8.74.oldText: “And will you tell me all about it?” she said. “May I creep up here at night, whenever it is safe, and hear the things you have made up during the day? It will feel as if we were more ‘best friends' than ever.”

8.75.oldText: “Yes,” answered Sara, nodding. “Hard times test people, and mine has tested you and proved how nice you are.”

9.0.oldText: The third person in the trio was Lottie. She was a small thing and did not know what hardship meant, and she was very confused by the change she saw in her young adopted mother. She had heard rumors that strange things had happened to Sara, but she could not understand why she looked different — why she wore an old black dress and came into the schoolroom only to teach instead of sitting in her place of honor and learning lessons herself. There had been much whispering among the little ones when they had discovered that Sara no longer lived in the rooms where Emily had so long sat in state. Lottie's biggest problem was that Sara said so little when one asked her questions. At seven, mysteries must be made very clear if you are to understand them.

9.1.oldText: “Are you very poor now, Sara?” she had asked privately the first morning her friend took charge of the small French class. “Are you as poor as a beggar?” She thrust a fat hand into the slim one and opened round, tearful eyes. “I don't want you to be as poor as a beggar.”

9.2.oldText: She looked as if she were about to cry. Sara hurriedly comforted her.

9.3.oldText: “Beggars have nowhere to live,” she said bravely. “I have a place to live in.”

9.4.oldText: “Where do you live?” Lottie persisted. “The new girl sleeps in your room, and it isn't pretty any more.”

9.5.oldText: “I live in another room,” said Sara.

9.6.oldText: “Is it a nice one?” Lottie asked. “I want to go and see it.”

9.7.oldText: “You must not talk,” said Sara. “Miss Minchin is looking at us. She will be angry with me for letting you whisper.”

9.8.oldText: She had already discovered that she was held responsible for everything that anyone objected to. If the children were not paying attention, if they talked, if they were restless, she was the one who would be scolded.

9.9.oldText: But Lottie was a determined little person. If Sara would not tell her where she lived, she would find out some other way. She talked to her small companions, hung around the older girls, and listened when they were gossiping. Acting on certain bits of information they had unconsciously let slip, she set off late one afternoon on a voyage of discovery, climbing stairs she had never known existed, until she reached the attic floor. There she found two doors near each other, and opening one of them, she saw her beloved Sara standing on an old table and looking out a window.

9.10.oldText: “Sara!” she cried, horrified. “Mamma Sara!” She was horrified because the attic was so bare and ugly and seemed so far away from the rest of the world. Her short legs had felt as if they had climbed hundreds of stairs.

9.11.oldText: Sara turned at the sound of her voice. It was her turn to be horrified. What would happen now? If Lottie began to cry and anyone happened to hear, they were both lost. She jumped down from her table and ran to the child.

9.12.oldText: “Don't cry and make a noise,” she begged. “I'll be scolded if you do, and I have been scolded all day. It's — it's not such a bad room, Lottie.”

9.13.oldText: “Isn't it?” Lottie gasped, and as she looked round it she bit her lip. She was still a spoiled child, but she was fond enough of her adopted mother to make an effort to control herself for her sake. Then somehow it was quite possible that any place Sara lived in might turn out to be nice. “Why isn't it, Sara?” she almost whispered.

9.14.oldText: Sara hugged her close and tried to laugh. There was a sort of comfort in the warmth of the plump little body. She had had a hard day and had been staring out of the windows with hot eyes.

9.15.oldText: “You can see all sorts of things you can't see downstairs,” she said.

9.16.oldText: “What sort of things?” demanded Lottie, with that curiosity Sara could always wake up even in bigger girls.

9.17.oldText: “Chimneys — quite close to us — with smoke curling up in wreaths and clouds and going up into the sky — and sparrows hopping about and talking to each other just as if they were people — and other attic windows where heads might pop out any minute, and you can wonder who they belong to. And it all feels so high up — as if it were another world.”

9.18.oldText: “Oh, let me see it!” cried Lottie. “Lift me up!”

9.19.oldText: Sara lifted her up, and they stood on the old table together and leaned on the edge of the flat window in the roof, and looked out.

9.20.oldText: Anyone who has not done this does not know what a different world they saw. The slates spread out on either side of them and slanted down into the rain gutters. The sparrows, being at home up there, twittered and hopped about quite without fear. Two of them perched on the nearest chimney top and quarreled fiercely until one pecked the other and drove him away. The garret window next to theirs was shut, because the house next door was empty.

9.21.oldText: “I wish someone lived there,” Sara said. “It is so close that if there was a little girl in the attic, we could talk to each other through the windows and climb over to see each other, if we were not afraid of falling.”

9.22.oldText: The sky seemed so much closer than when one saw it from the street that Lottie was enchanted. From the attic window, among the chimney pots, the things happening in the world below seemed almost unreal. One scarcely believed in the existence of Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia and the schoolroom, and the rolling of wheels in the square seemed a sound from another world.

9.23.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” cried Lottie, cuddling into her protecting arm. “I like this attic — I like it! It is nicer than downstairs!”

9.24.oldText: “Look at that sparrow,” whispered Sara. “I wish I had some crumbs to throw to him.”

9.25.oldText: “I have some!” came in a little shriek from Lottie. “I have part of a bun in my pocket. I bought it with my penny yesterday, and I saved a bit.”

9.26.oldText: When they threw out a few crumbs, the sparrow jumped and flew away to a nearby chimney top. He was clearly not used to friends in attics, and unexpected crumbs startled him. But when Lottie stayed quite still and Sara chirped very softly — almost as if she were a sparrow herself — he saw that the thing that had alarmed him meant hospitality after all. He put his head on one side, and from his perch on the chimney looked down at the crumbs with twinkling eyes. Lottie could scarcely keep still.

9.27.oldText: “Will he come? Will he come?” she whispered.

9.28.oldText: “His eyes look as if he will,” Sara whispered back. “He is thinking and thinking whether he dares. Yes, he will! Yes, he is coming!”

9.29.oldText: He flew down and hopped towards the crumbs, but stopped a few inches away from them, putting his head on one side again, as if weighing the chances that Sara and Lottie might turn out to be big cats and pounce on him. At last his heart told him they were really nicer than they looked, and he hopped nearer and nearer, darted at the biggest crumb with a lightning peck, grabbed it, and carried it away to the other side of his chimney.

9.30.oldText: “Now he knows,” said Sara. “And he will come back for the others.”

9.31.oldText: He did come back, and even brought a friend, and the friend went away and brought a relative, and between them they made a hearty meal, twittering and chattering and exclaiming, stopping every now and then to put their heads on one side and examine Lottie and Sara. Lottie was so delighted that she quite forgot her first shocked impression of the attic. In fact, when she was lifted down from the table and returned to earthly things, as it were, Sara was able to point out many beauties in the room that she herself would not have suspected existed.

9.32.oldText: “It is so little and so high above everything,” she said, “that it is almost like a nest in a tree. The slanting ceiling is so funny. Look — you can scarcely stand up at this end of the room. And when morning begins to come, I can lie in bed and look right up into the sky through that flat window in the roof. It is like a square patch of light. If the sun is going to shine, little pink clouds float about, and I feel as if I could touch them. And if it rains, the drops patter and patter as if they were saying something nice. Then if there are stars, you can lie and try to count how many fit into the patch. It takes such a lot. And just look at that tiny, rusty grate in the corner. If it was polished and there was a fire in it, just think how nice it would be. You see, it's really a beautiful little room.”

9.33.oldText: She was walking round the small place, holding Lottie's hand and making gestures that described all the beauties she was making herself see. She quite made Lottie see them too. Lottie could always believe in the things Sara made pictures of.

9.34.oldText: “You see,” she said, “there could be a thick, soft blue Indian rug on the floor, and in that corner there could be a soft little sofa, with cushions to curl up on. And just over it there could be a shelf full of books, so that one could reach them easily. And there could be a fur rug before the fire, and hangings on the wall to cover up the whitewash, and pictures. They would have to be little ones, but they could be beautiful. And there could be a lamp with a deep rose-colored shade. And a table in the middle, with things to have tea with. And a little fat copper kettle singing on the hob. And the bed could be quite different. It could be made soft and covered with a lovely silk coverlet. It could be beautiful. And perhaps we could coax the sparrows until we made such friends with them that they would come and peck at the window and ask to be let in.”

9.35.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” cried Lottie. “I should like to live here!”

9.36.oldText: When Sara had persuaded her to go downstairs again, and, after setting her on her way, had come back to her attic, she stood in the middle of it and looked about her. The magic of her imaginings for Lottie had died away. The bed was hard and covered with its dingy quilt. The whitewashed wall showed its broken patches, the floor was cold and bare, the grate was broken and rusty, and the battered footstool, tilted sideways on its damaged leg, was the only seat in the room. She sat down on it for a few minutes and let her head drop into her hands. The mere fact that Lottie had come and gone again made things seem a little worse — just as perhaps prisoners feel a little more lonely after visitors come and go, leaving them behind.

9.37.oldText: “It's a lonely place,” she said. “Sometimes it's the loneliest place in the world.”

9.38.oldText: She was sitting like that when her attention was caught by a slight sound near her. She lifted her head to see where it came from, and if she had been a nervous child she would have leapt off the battered footstool in a great hurry. A large rat was sitting up on his hind legs and sniffing the air with an interested look. Some of Lottie's crumbs had dropped on the floor, and their scent had drawn him out of his hole.

9.39.oldText: He looked so odd and so like a gray-whiskered dwarf or gnome that Sara was rather fascinated. He looked at her with his bright eyes, as if he were asking a question. He was clearly so doubtful that one of the child's strange thoughts came into her mind.

9.40.oldText: “I dare say it is rather hard to be a rat,” she mused. “Nobody likes you. People jump and run away and scream out, ‘Oh, a horrid rat!' I shouldn't like people to scream and jump and say, ‘Oh, a horrid Sara!' the moment they saw me. And set traps for me, and pretend they were dinner. It's so different to be a sparrow. But nobody asked this rat if he wanted to be a rat when he was made. Nobody said, ‘Wouldn't you rather be a sparrow?'”

9.41.oldText: She had sat so quietly that the rat had begun to take courage. He was very much afraid of her, but perhaps he had a heart like the sparrow's, and it told him that she was not the sort of thing that pounced. He was very hungry. He had a wife and a large family in the wall, and they had had frightfully bad luck for several days. He had left the children crying bitterly, and he felt he would risk a good deal for a few crumbs, so he cautiously dropped onto his feet.

9.42.oldText: “Come on,” said Sara. “I'm not a trap. You can have them, poor thing! Prisoners in the Bastille used to make friends with rats. Suppose I make friends with you.”

9.43.oldText: How animals understand things I do not know, but it is certain that they do understand. Perhaps there is a language that is not made of words, and everything in the world understands it. Perhaps there is a soul hidden in everything, and it can always speak, without making a sound, to another soul. But whatever the reason, the rat knew from that moment that he was safe — even though he was a rat. He knew that this young human being sitting on the red footstool would not jump up and terrify him with wild, sharp noises, or throw heavy objects at him which, even if they did not crush him, would send him limping back to his hole. He was really a very nice rat, and meant no harm at all. When he had stood on his hind legs and sniffed the air, with his bright eyes fixed on Sara, he had hoped that she would understand this, and would not begin by hating him as an enemy. When the mysterious thing that speaks without words told him that she would not, he went softly toward the crumbs and began to eat them. As he ate, he glanced now and then at Sara, just as the sparrows had done, and his look was so apologetic that it touched her heart.

9.44.oldText: She sat and watched him without moving. One crumb was much larger than the others — in fact, it could scarcely be called a crumb. It was clear that he wanted that piece very much, but it lay quite near the footstool and he was still rather timid.

9.45.oldText: “I believe he wants it to carry to his family in the wall,” Sara thought. “If I do not stir at all, perhaps he will come and get it.”

9.46.oldText: She scarcely allowed herself to breathe, she was so deeply interested. The rat shuffled a little nearer and ate a few more crumbs, then he stopped and sniffed delicately, giving a side glance at the person on the footstool. Then he darted at the piece of bun with something very like the sudden boldness of the sparrow, and the instant he had it he fled back to the wall, slipped down a crack in the baseboard, and was gone.

9.47.oldText: “I knew he wanted it for his children,” said Sara. “I do believe I could make friends with him.”

9.48.oldText: A week or so later, on one of the rare nights when Ermengarde found it safe to sneak up to the attic, when she tapped on the door with the tips of her fingers, Sara did not come to her for two or three minutes. There was such a silence in the room at first that Ermengarde wondered if Sara could have fallen asleep. Then, to her surprise, she heard her give a little, low laugh and speak coaxingly to someone.

9.49.oldText: “There!” Ermengarde heard her say. “Take it and go home, Melchisedec! Go home to your wife!”

9.50.oldText: Almost at once Sara opened the door, and when she did, she found Ermengarde standing on the threshold with alarmed eyes.

9.51.oldText: “Who — who are you talking to, Sara?” she gasped out.

9.52.oldText: Sara drew her in cautiously, but she looked as if something pleased and amused her.

9.53.oldText: “You must promise not to be frightened — not to scream the least bit, or I can't tell you,” she answered.

9.54.oldText: Ermengarde felt almost ready to scream on the spot, but managed to control herself. She looked all round the attic and saw no one. And yet Sara had certainly been speaking to someone. She thought of ghosts.

9.55.oldText: “Is it — something that will frighten me?” she asked timidly.
