But strange men were dangerous things to be near. He lay close and flat near the entrance of his home, just managing to peep through the crack with a bright, alarmed eye. How much he understood of the talk he heard, I am not in the least able to say; but even if he had understood it all, he would probably still have been greatly mystified.

14.2.oldText: The secretary, who was light and young, slipped through the skylight as silently as Ram Dass had done, and he caught a last glimpse of Melchisedec's vanishing tail.

14.3.oldText: “Was that a rat?” he asked Ram Dass in a whisper.

14.4.oldText: “Yes; a rat, Sahib,” answered Ram Dass, also whispering. “There are many in the walls.”

14.5.oldText: “Ugh!” exclaimed the young man. “It is a wonder the child is not terrified of them.”

14.6.oldText: Ram Dass made a gesture with his hands. He also smiled respectfully. He was in this place as the trusted spokesman for Sara, even though she had only spoken to him once.

14.7.oldText: “The child is the little friend of all things, Sahib,” he answered. “She is not like other children. I see her when she does not see me. I slip across the slates and look at her many nights to make sure she is safe. I watch her from my window when she does not know I am near. She stands on the table there and looks out at the sky as if it were speaking to her. The sparrows come at her call. The rat she has fed and tamed in her loneliness. The poor slave of the house comes to her for comfort. There is a little child who comes to her in secret; there is one older who worships her and would listen to her forever if she might. This I have seen when I have crept across the roof. By the mistress of the house—who is an evil woman—she is treated like an outcast; but she has the bearing of a child of royal blood!”

14.8.oldText: “You seem to know a great deal about her,” the secretary said.

14.9.oldText: “Each day of her life, I know,” answered Ram Dass. “Her going out I know, and her coming in; her sadness and her poor joys; her coldness and her hunger. I know when she is alone until midnight, learning from her books; I know when her secret friends sneak up to her and she is happier—as children can be, even in the middle of poverty—because they come and she may laugh and talk with them in whispers. If she were ill, I should know, and I would come and serve her if it could be done.”

14.10.oldText: “You are sure no one comes near this place but herself, and that she will not return and surprise us. She would be frightened if she found us here, and the Sahib Carrisford's plan would be spoiled.”

14.11.oldText: Ram Dass crossed silently to the door and stood close to it.

14.12.oldText: “No one comes up here but herself, Sahib,” he said. “She has gone out with her basket and may be gone for hours. If I stand here, I can hear any step before it reaches the last flight of the stairs.”

14.13.oldText: The secretary took a pencil and a notebook from his breast pocket.

14.14.oldText: “Keep your ears open,” he said; and he began to walk slowly and softly round the miserable little room, making rapid notes in his notebook as he looked at things.

14.15.oldText: First he went to the narrow bed. He pressed his hand on the mattress and let out an exclamation.

14.16.oldText: “As hard as a stone,” he said. “That will have to be changed some day when she is out. A special trip can be made to bring it across. It cannot be done tonight.” He lifted the cover and examined the one thin pillow.

14.17.oldText: “Coverlet dingy and worn, blanket thin, sheets patched and ragged,” he said. “What a bed for a child to sleep in—and in a house that calls itself respectable! There has not been a fire in that grate for many a day,” he added, glancing at the rusty fireplace.

14.18.oldText: “Never since I have seen it,” said Ram Dass. “The mistress of the house is not one who remembers that anyone other than herself might be cold.”

14.19.oldText: The secretary was writing quickly in his notebook. He looked up from it as he tore off a leaf and slipped it into his breast pocket.

14.20.oldText: “It is a strange way of doing the thing,” he said. “Who planned it?”

14.21.oldText: Ram Dass made a modestly apologetic bow.

14.22.oldText: “It is true that the first thought was mine, Sahib,” he said; “though it was nothing but a fancy. I am fond of this child; we are both lonely. It is her way to share her visions with her secret friends. Being sad one night, I lay close to the open skylight and listened. The vision she described told what this miserable room might be if it had comforts in it. She seemed to see it as she talked, and she grew cheered and warmed as she spoke. Then she came to this fancy; and the next day, the Sahib being ill and wretched, I told him of the thing to amuse him. It seemed then but a dream, but it pleased the Sahib. To hear of the child's doings entertained him. He became interested in her and asked questions. At last he began to please himself with the thought of making her visions into real things.”

14.23.oldText: “You think that it can be done while she sleeps? Suppose she woke up,” the secretary suggested; and it was clear that whatever the plan referred to was, it had caught and pleased his fancy as well as the Sahib Carrisford's.

14.24.oldText: “I can move as if my feet were of velvet,” Ram Dass replied; “and children sleep soundly—even the unhappy ones. I could have entered this room in the night many times, and without making her turn on her pillow. If the other bearer passes the things to me through the window, I can do it all and she will not stir. When she wakes she will think a magician has been here.”

14.25.oldText: He smiled as if his heart warmed under his white robe, and the secretary smiled back at him.

14.26.oldText: “It will be like a story from the Arabian Nights,” he said. “Only an Easterner could have planned it. It does not belong to London fogs.”

14.27.oldText: They did not stay very long, to the great relief of Melchisedec, who, since he probably did not understand their conversation, found their movements and whispers ominous. The young secretary seemed interested in everything. He wrote down things about the floor, the fireplace, the broken footstool, the old table, the walls—which last he touched with his hand again and again, seeming much pleased when he found that a number of old nails had been driven in various places.

14.28.oldText: “You can hang things on them,” he said.

14.30.oldText: “Yesterday, when she was out,” he said, “I came in, bringing with me small, sharp nails which can be pressed into the wall without blows from a hammer. I placed many in the plaster where I may need them. They are ready.”

14.31.oldText: The Indian gentleman's secretary stood still and looked round him as he pushed his notebook back into his pocket.

14.32.oldText: “I think I have made enough notes; we can go now,” he said. “The Sahib Carrisford has a warm heart. It is a thousand pities that he has not found the lost child.”

14.33.oldText: “If he should find her, his strength would be restored to him,” said Ram Dass. “His God may lead her to him yet.”

14.34.oldText: Then they slipped through the skylight as silently as they had entered it. And after he was quite sure they had gone, Melchisedec was greatly relieved, and after a few minutes felt it was safe to come out of his hole again and scuffle about in the hope that even such alarming human beings as these might have happened to carry crumbs in their pockets and dropped one or two of them.

15.0.oldText: When Sara had passed the house next door, she had seen Ram Dass closing the shutters, and she had caught a glimpse of this room too.

15.1.oldText: “It is a long time since I saw a nice place from the inside,” was the thought that crossed her mind.

15.2.oldText: There was the usual bright fire glowing in the fireplace, and the Indian gentleman was sitting in front of it. His head was resting in his hand, and he looked as lonely and unhappy as ever.

15.3.oldText: “Poor man!” said Sara. “I wonder what you are supposing.”

15.4.oldText: And this was what he was “supposing” at that very moment.

15.5.oldText: “Suppose,” he was thinking, “suppose—even if Carmichael traces the people to Moscow—the little girl they took from Madame Pascal's school in Paris is NOT the one we are searching for. Suppose she turns out to be quite a different child. What steps shall I take next?”

15.6.oldText: When Sara went into the house, she met Miss Minchin, who had come downstairs to scold the cook.

15.7.oldText: “Where have you wasted your time?” she demanded. “You have been out for hours.”

15.8.oldText: “It was so wet and muddy,” Sara answered. “It was hard to walk, because my shoes were so bad and kept slipping.”

15.9.oldText: “Make no excuses,” said Miss Minchin, “and tell no lies.”

15.10.oldText: Sara went in to the cook. The cook had received a harsh scolding and was in a terrible mood as a result. She was only too glad to have someone to take her anger out on, and Sara was a convenient target, as usual.

15.11.oldText: “Why didn't you stay all night?” she snapped.

15.12.oldText: Sara laid her purchases on the table.

15.14.oldText: The cook looked them over, grumbling. She was in a very nasty mood indeed.

15.15.oldText: “May I have something to eat?” Sara asked rather faintly.

15.16.oldText: “Tea is over and done with,” was the answer. “Did you expect me to keep it hot for you?”

15.17.oldText: Sara stood silent for a second.

15.18.oldText: “I had no dinner,” she said next, and her voice was quite low. She made it low because she was afraid it would tremble.

15.19.oldText: “There's some bread in the pantry,” said the cook. “That's all you'll get at this time of day.”

15.20.oldText: Sara went and found the bread. It was old and hard and dry. The cook was in too mean a mood to give her anything to eat with it. It was always safe and easy to take her spite out on Sara. It really was hard for the child to climb the three long flights of stairs leading up to her attic. She often found them long and steep when she was tired, but tonight it seemed as if she would never reach the top. Several times she had to stop to rest. When she reached the top landing, she was glad to see the glimmer of a light coming from under her door. That meant Ermengarde had managed to creep up to pay her a visit. There was some comfort in that. It was better than going into the room alone and finding it empty and bleak. Just the presence of plump, comfortable Ermengarde, wrapped in her red shawl, would warm it a little.

15.21.oldText: Yes—Ermengarde was there when she opened the door. She was sitting in the middle of the bed with her feet tucked safely under her. She had never become close with Melchisedec and his family, although they rather fascinated her. When she found herself alone in the attic, she always preferred to sit on the bed until Sara arrived. In fact, this time she had had time to grow rather nervous, because Melchisedec had appeared and sniffed about a great deal, and once had made her let out a stifled squeak by sitting up on his hind legs and, while he looked at her, sniffing pointedly in her direction.

15.22.oldText: “Oh, Sara,” she cried out, “I'm glad you've come. Melchy WOULD keep sniffing about. I tried to coax him to go back, but he wouldn't for the longest time. I like him, you know—but it does frighten me when he sniffs right at me. Do you think he ever WOULD jump?”

15.24.oldText: Ermengarde crawled forward on the bed to look at her.

15.25.oldText: “You DO look tired, Sara,” she said. “You are quite pale.”

15.26.oldText: “I AM tired,” said Sara, dropping onto the lopsided footstool. “Oh, there's Melchisedec, poor thing. He's come to ask for his supper.”

15.27.oldText: Melchisedec had come out of his hole as if he had been listening for her footstep. Sara was quite sure he knew it. He came forward with an affectionate, expectant expression as Sara put her hand in her pocket and turned it inside out, shaking her head.

15.28.oldText: “I'm very sorry,” she said. “I haven't a single crumb left. Go home, Melchisedec, and tell your wife there was nothing in my pocket. I'm afraid I forgot, because the cook and Miss Minchin were so cross.”

15.29.oldText: Melchisedec seemed to understand. He shuffled off resignedly, if not contentedly, back to his home.

15.30.oldText: “I didn't expect to see you tonight, Ermie,” Sara said. Ermengarde hugged herself in the red shawl.

15.31.oldText: “Miss Amelia has gone out to spend the night with her old aunt,” she explained. “No one else ever comes and looks into the bedrooms after we are in bed. I could stay here until morning if I wanted to.”

15.32.oldText: She pointed toward the table under the skylight. Sara had not looked toward it as she came in. A number of books were piled on it. Ermengarde's gesture was a glum one.

15.33.oldText: “Papa has sent me some more books, Sara,” she said. “There they are.”

15.34.oldText: Sara looked round and got up at once. She ran to the table and, picking up the top volume, turned over its pages quickly. For the moment she forgot her troubles.

15.35.oldText: “Ah,” she cried out, “how beautiful! Carlyle's French Revolution. I have SO wanted to read that!”

15.36.oldText: “I haven't,” said Ermengarde. “And papa will be so cross if I don't. He'll expect me to know all about it when I go home for the holidays. What SHALL I do?”

15.37.oldText: Sara stopped turning over the pages and looked at her with an excited flush on her cheeks.

15.38.oldText: “Look here,” she cried, “if you'll lend me these books, I'll read them—and tell you everything that's in them afterward—and I'll tell it so that you'll remember it, too.”

15.39.oldText: “Oh, goodness!” exclaimed Ermengarde. “Do you think you can?”

15.40.oldText: “I know I can,” Sara answered. “The little ones always remember what I tell them.”

15.41.oldText: “Sara,” said Ermengarde, hope gleaming in her round face, “if you'll do that, and make me remember, I'll—I'll give you anything.”

15.42.oldText: “I don't want you to give me anything,” said Sara. “I want your books—I want them!” And her eyes grew big, and her chest heaved.

15.43.oldText: “Take them, then,” said Ermengarde. “I wish I wanted them—but I don't. I'm not clever, and my father is, and he thinks I ought to be.”

15.44.oldText: Sara was opening one book after another. “What are you going to tell your father?” she asked, a slight doubt dawning in her mind.

15.45.oldText: “Oh, he needn't know,” answered Ermengarde. “He'll think I've read them.”

15.46.oldText: Sara put down her book and shook her head slowly. “That's almost like telling lies,” she said. “And lies—well, you see, they're not just wicked—they're VULGAR. Sometimes”—thoughtfully—“I've thought perhaps I might do something wicked—I might suddenly fly into a rage and kill Miss Minchin, you know, when she was treating me badly—but I COULDN'T be vulgar. Why can't you tell your father I read them?”

15.47.oldText: “He wants ME to read them,” said Ermengarde, a little discouraged by this unexpected turn of things.

15.48.oldText: “He wants you to know what is in them,” said Sara. “And if I can tell it to you in an easy way and make you remember it, I should think he'd like that.”

15.49.oldText: “He'll like it if I learn anything in ANY way,” said rueful Ermengarde. “You would, if you were my father.”

15.50.oldText: “It's not your fault that—” Sara began. She pulled herself up and stopped rather suddenly. She had been about to say, “It's not your fault that you are stupid.”

15.52.oldText: “That you can't learn things quickly,” Sara amended. “If you can't, you can't. If I can—well, I can. That's all.”

15.53.oldText: She always felt very tender toward Ermengarde and tried not to let her feel too strongly the difference between being able to learn anything at once and not being able to learn anything at all. As she looked at her plump face, one of her wise, old-fashioned thoughts came to her.

15.54.oldText: “Perhaps,” she said, “being able to learn things quickly isn't everything. Being kind is worth a great deal to other people. If Miss Minchin knew everything on earth and was the way she is now, she'd still be a horrible thing, and everybody would hate her. Lots of clever people have done harm and have been wicked. Look at Robespierre—”

15.55.oldText: She stopped and studied Ermengarde's face, which was beginning to look puzzled. “Don't you remember?” she demanded. “I told you about him not long ago. I think you've forgotten.”

15.56.oldText: “Well, I don't remember ALL of it,” admitted Ermengarde.

15.57.oldText: “Well, you wait a minute,” said Sara, “and I'll take off my wet things and wrap myself in the bed cover and tell you all over again.”

15.58.oldText: She took off her hat and coat and hung them on a nail against the wall, and she changed her wet shoes for an old pair of slippers. Then she jumped on the bed and, drawing the bed cover around her shoulders, sat with her arms around her knees. “Now, listen,” she said.

15.59.oldText: She plunged into the bloody records of the French Revolution and told such stories of it that Ermengarde's eyes grew round with alarm and she held her breath. But although she was rather frightened, there was a delightful thrill in listening, and she was not likely to forget Robespierre again, or to have any doubts about the Princesse de Lamballe.

15.60.oldText: “You know they put her head on a pike and danced around it,” Sara explained. “And she had beautiful flowing blonde hair. And when I think of her, I never see her head on her body, but always on a pike, with those furious people dancing and howling.”

15.61.oldText: It was agreed that Mr. St. John would be told the plan they had made, and for now the books would be left in the attic.

15.62.oldText: “Now let's tell each other things,” said Sara. “How are you getting on with your French lessons?”

15.63.oldText: “So much better since the last time I came up here and you explained the conjugations. Miss Minchin couldn't understand why I did my exercises so well that first morning.”

15.65.oldText: “She doesn't understand why Lottie is doing her sums so well,” she said. “But it's because she creeps up here too, and I help her.” She glanced round the room. “The attic would be rather nice—if it wasn't so dreadful,” she said, laughing again. “It's a good place to pretend in.”

15.66.oldText: The truth was that Ermengarde knew nothing of the sometimes almost unbearable side of life in the attic, and she did not have a vivid enough imagination to picture it for herself. On the rare occasions that she could reach Sara's room, she only saw the side of it that was made exciting by things that were “pretended” and stories that were told. Her visits had the flavor of adventures. And although Sara sometimes looked rather pale, and there was no denying she had grown very thin, her proud little spirit would not allow her to complain. She had never confessed that at times she was almost ravenous with hunger, as she was tonight. She was growing rapidly, and her constant walking and running about would have given her a sharp appetite even if she had had plenty of regular meals of a far more nourishing kind than the unappetizing, low-quality food snatched at whatever odd times suited the kitchen. She was growing used to a certain gnawing feeling in her young stomach.

15.67.oldText: “I suppose soldiers feel like this when they are on a long and weary march,” she often said to herself. She liked the sound of the phrase, “long and weary march.” It made her feel rather like a soldier. She also had a quaint sense of being a hostess in the attic.

15.68.oldText: “If I lived in a castle,” she argued, “and Ermengarde was the lady of another castle, and she came to see me, with knights and squires and vassals riding with her, and pennants flying, when I heard the trumpets sounding outside the drawbridge I should go down to receive her, and I should spread feasts in the banquet hall and call in minstrels to sing and play and tell romances. When she comes into the attic I can't spread feasts, but I can tell stories, and not let her know about disagreeable things. I dare say poor lady-of-the-castle had to do that in times of famine, when their lands had been pillaged.” She was a proud, brave little lady of the castle, and she generously offered the one form of hospitality she could—the dreams she dreamed, the visions she saw, the imaginings that were her joy and comfort.

15.69.oldText: And so, as they sat together, Ermengarde did not know that she was faint as well as ravenous, and that while she talked, every now and then she wondered if her hunger would let her sleep when she was left alone. She felt as if she had never been quite so hungry before.

15.70.oldText: “I wish I was as thin as you, Sara,” Ermengarde said suddenly. “I believe you are thinner than you used to be. Your eyes look so big, and look at the sharp little bones sticking out of your elbow!”

15.71.oldText: Sara pulled down her sleeve, which had pushed itself up.

15.72.oldText: “I always was a thin child,” she said bravely, “and I always had big green eyes.”

15.73.oldText: “I love your strange eyes,” said Ermengarde, looking into them with affectionate admiration. “They always look as if they see such a long way. I love them—and I love them to be green—even though they usually look black.”

15.74.oldText: “They are cat's eyes,” laughed Sara. “But I can't see in the dark with them—because I have tried, and I couldn't—I wish I could.”

15.75.oldText: It was just at this minute that something happened at the skylight which neither of them saw. If either of them had happened to turn and look, she would have been startled by the sight of a dark face that peered cautiously into the room and disappeared as quickly and almost as silently as it had appeared. Not QUITE as silently, however. Sara, who had sharp ears, suddenly turned a little and looked up at the roof.

15.76.oldText: “That didn't sound like Melchisedec,” she said. “It wasn't scratchy enough.”

15.78.oldText: “Didn't you think you heard something?” asked Sara.

15.80.oldText: “Perhaps I didn't,” said Sara. “But I thought I did. It sounded as if something was on the slates—something that dragged softly.”

15.81.oldText: “What could it be?” said Ermengarde. “Could it be—robbers?”

15.82.oldText: “No,” Sara began cheerfully. “There is nothing to steal—”

15.83.oldText: She broke off in the middle of her words. They both heard the sound that stopped her. It was not on the slates, but on the stairs below, and it was Miss Minchin's angry voice. Sara sprang off the bed and put out the candle.

15.84.oldText: “She is scolding Becky,” she whispered, as she stood in the darkness. “She is making her cry.”

15.85.oldText: “Will she come in here?” Ermengarde whispered back, panic-stricken.

15.86.oldText: “No. She will think I am in bed. Don't move.”

15.87.oldText: It was very seldom that Miss Minchin climbed the last flight of stairs. Sara could only remember her doing it once before. But now she was angry enough to come at least part of the way up, and it sounded as if she was driving Becky in front of her.

15.88.oldText: “You impudent, dishonest child!” they heard her say. “Cook tells me she has missed things over and over.”

15.89.oldText: “'T warn't me, mum,” said Becky sobbing. “I was 'ungry enough, but 't warn't me—never!”

15.90.oldText: “You deserve to be sent to prison,” said Miss Minchin's voice. “Picking and stealing! Half a meat pie, indeed!”

15.91.oldText: “'T warn't me,” wept Becky. “I could 'ave eat a whole un—but I never laid a finger on it.”

15.92.oldText: Miss Minchin was out of breath from her temper and from climbing the stairs. The meat pie had been meant for her special late supper. It became clear that she boxed Becky's ears.

15.93.oldText: “Don't tell lies,” she said. “Go to your room this instant.”

15.94.oldText: Both Sara and Ermengarde heard the slap, and then they heard Becky run in her shuffling shoes up the stairs and into her attic. They heard her door shut, and they knew she had thrown herself down on her bed.

15.95.oldText: “I could 'ave e't two of 'em,” they heard her cry into her pillow. “An' I never took a bite. 'Twas cook give it to her policeman.”

15.96.oldText: Sara stood in the middle of the room in the darkness. She was clenching her little teeth and opening and shutting her stretched-out hands fiercely. She could scarcely stand still, but she dared not move until Miss Minchin had gone down the stairs and all was quiet.

15.97.oldText: “The wicked, cruel thing!” she burst out. “The cook takes things herself and then says Becky steals them. She DOESN'T! She DOESN'T! She's so hungry sometimes that she eats crusts out of the ash barrel!” She pressed her hands hard against her face and burst into passionate little sobs, and Ermengarde, hearing this unusual thing, was struck with awe. Sara was crying! The unconquerable Sara! It seemed to mean something new—some mood she had never known. Suppose—suppose—a new dreadful possibility presented itself all at once to her kind, slow, little mind. She crept off the bed in the dark and felt her way to the table where the candle stood. She struck a match and lit the candle. When she had lit it, she bent forward and looked at Sara, with her new thought growing into definite fear in her eyes.

15.98.oldText: “Sara,” she said in a timid, almost awe-struck voice, “are—are—you never told me—I don't want to be rude, but—are YOU ever hungry?”

15.99.oldText: It was too much just at that moment. The barrier broke down. Sara lifted her face from her hands.

15.100.oldText: “Yes,” she said in a new, passionate way. “Yes, I am. I'm so hungry now that I could almost eat you. And it makes it worse to hear poor Becky. She's hungrier than I am.”

15.102.oldText: “Oh, oh!” she cried sorrowfully. “And I never knew!”

15.103.oldText: “I didn't want you to know,” Sara said. “It would have made me feel like a street beggar. I know I look like a street beggar.”

15.104.oldText: “No, you don't—you don't!” Ermengarde broke in. “Your clothes are a little strange—but you couldn't look like a street beggar. You haven't a street-beggar face.”

15.105.oldText: “A little boy once gave me a sixpence for charity,” said Sara, with a short little laugh in spite of herself. “Here it is.” And she pulled out the thin ribbon from her neck. “He wouldn't have given me his Christmas sixpence if I hadn't looked as if I needed it.”

15.106.oldText: Somehow the sight of the dear little sixpence was good for both of them. It made them laugh a little, although they both had tears in their eyes.

15.107.oldText: “Who was he?” asked Ermengarde, looking at it as if it were not just an ordinary silver sixpence.

15.108.oldText: “He was a darling little thing going to a party,” said Sara. “He was one of the Large Family—the little one with the round legs—the one I call Guy Clarence. I suppose his nursery was crammed with Christmas presents and hampers full of cakes and things, and he could see I had nothing.”

15.109.oldText: Ermengarde gave a little jump backward. The last sentences had reminded her of something in her troubled mind and given her a sudden inspiration.

15.110.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” she cried. “What a silly thing I am not to have thought of it!”

15.112.oldText: “Something splendid!” said Ermengarde, in an excited rush. “This very afternoon my nicest aunt sent me a box. It is full of good things. I never touched it—I had so much pudding at dinner, and I was so worried about papa's books.” Her words began to tumble over each other. “It's got cake in it, and little meat pies, and jam tarts and buns, and oranges and red-currant wine, and figs and chocolate. I'll creep back to my room and get it this minute, and we'll eat it now.”

15.113.oldText: Sara almost reeled. When you are faint with hunger, the mention of food sometimes has a strange effect. She clutched Ermengarde's arm.

15.114.oldText: “Do you think—you COULD?” she burst out.

15.115.oldText: “I know I could,” answered Ermengarde, and she ran to the door—opened it softly—put her head out into the darkness, and listened. Then she went back to Sara. “The lights are out. Everyone's in bed. I can creep—and creep—and no one will hear.”

15.116.oldText: It was so delightful that they caught each other's hands, and a sudden light sprang into Sara's eyes.

15.117.oldText: “Ermie!” she said. “Let us PRETEND! Let us pretend it's a party! And oh, won't you invite the prisoner in the next cell?”

15.118.oldText: “Yes! Yes! Let us knock on the wall now. The jailer won't hear.”

15.119.oldText: Sara went to the wall. Through it she could hear poor Becky crying more softly. She knocked four times.

15.120.oldText: “That means, ‘Come to me through the secret passage under the wall,’” she explained. “‘I have something to tell you.’”

15.123.oldText: Almost immediately the door of the attic opened and Becky appeared. Her eyes were red and her cap was sliding off, and when she caught sight of Ermengarde she began to rub her face nervously with her apron.

15.124.oldText: “Don't mind me a bit, Becky!” cried Ermengarde.

15.125.oldText: “Miss Ermengarde has asked you to come in,” said Sara, “because she is going to bring a box of good things up here to us.”

15.126.oldText: Becky's cap almost fell off entirely, she broke in with such excitement.

15.127.oldText: “To eat, miss?” she said. “Things that's good to eat?”

15.128.oldText: “Yes,” answered Sara, “and we are going to pretend a party.”

15.129.oldText: “And you shall have as much as you WANT to eat,” put in Ermengarde. “I'll go this minute!”

15.130.oldText: She was in such a hurry that as she tiptoed out of the attic she dropped her red shawl and never noticed it had fallen. No one saw it for a minute or so. Becky was too overwhelmed by the good luck that had landed on her.

15.131.oldText: “Oh, miss! Oh, miss!” she gasped. “I know it was you who asked her to let me come. It—it makes me cry just thinking about it.” And she went to Sara's side and stood looking at her with worship in her eyes.

15.132.oldText: But in Sara's hungry eyes the old light had begun to shine and transform the world for her. Here in the attic—with the cold night outside—with the afternoon in the slushy streets barely behind them—with the memory of the dreadful starving look in the beggar child's eyes still fresh—this simple, cheerful thing had happened like something out of magic.

15.134.oldText: “Somehow, something always happens,” she said, “just before things get to the very worst. It's as if the Magic does it. If only I could remember that always. The worst thing never QUITE comes.”

15.135.oldText: She gave Becky a little cheerful shake.

15.136.oldText: “No, no! You mustn't cry!” she said. “We have to hurry and set the table.”

15.137.oldText: “Set the table, miss?” said Becky, looking around the room. “What'll we set it with?”

15.139.oldText: “There doesn't seem to be much,” she answered, half laughing.

15.141.oldText: “Here's the shawl,” she cried. “I know she won't mind. It will make a lovely red tablecloth.”

15.142.oldText: They pulled the old table forward and threw the shawl over it. Red is a wonderfully kind and comforting color. It made the room look furnished right away.

15.143.oldText: “How nice a red rug would look on the floor!” Sara exclaimed. “We have to pretend there is one!”

15.144.oldText: Her eye swept the bare boards with a quick glance of admiration. The rug was already laid down.

15.145.oldText: “How soft and thick it is!” she said, with the little laugh Becky knew the meaning of. She lifted her foot and set it down again carefully, as if she could feel something soft beneath it.

15.146.oldText: “Yes, miss,” answered Becky, watching her with serious wonder. She was always completely serious.

15.147.oldText: “What next, now?” said Sara. She stood still and put her hands over her eyes. “Something will come if I think and wait a little,” she said in a soft, expectant voice. “The Magic will tell me.”

15.148.oldText: One of her favorite ideas was that on “the outside,” as she called it, thoughts were waiting for people to call them. Becky had seen her stand and wait many times before, and knew that in a few seconds she would lower her hands and reveal a brightened, laughing face.

15.149.oldText: And in a moment she did.

15.150.oldText: “There!” she cried. “It has come! I know now! I have to look through the things in the old trunk I had when I was a princess.”

15.151.oldText: She flew to its corner and knelt down. The trunk hadn't been put in the attic for her—it was here because there was no room for it anywhere else. Nothing had been left in it but rubbish. But she knew she would find something. The Magic always arranged that kind of thing one way or another.

15.152.oldText: In a corner lay a package so small and plain-looking that it had been overlooked, and when she had found it herself she had kept it as a keepsake. It held a dozen small white handkerchiefs. She seized them joyfully and ran to the table. She began arranging them on the red tablecloth, patting and coaxing them into shape with the narrow lace edge curling outward, her Magic working its spells for her as she did it.

15.153.oldText: “These are the plates,” she said. “They are golden plates. These are the richly embroidered napkins. Nuns made them in convents in Spain.”

15.154.oldText: “Did they, miss?” breathed Becky, her very soul lifted by the news.

15.155.oldText: “You have to pretend it,” said Sara. “If you pretend it enough, you will see them.”

15.156.oldText: “Yes, miss,” said Becky. And as Sara went back to the trunk, she threw herself into the effort of achieving such a wonderful goal.

15.157.oldText: Sara turned suddenly and found her standing by the table, looking very strange indeed. Becky had shut her eyes and was twisting her face into odd, jerking contortions, her hands clenched stiffly at her sides. She looked as if she were trying to lift some enormous weight.

15.158.oldText: “What is the matter, Becky?” Sara cried. “What are you doing?”

15.160.oldText: “I was a-pretendin', miss,” she answered a little shyly. “I was tryin' to see it like you do. I almost did,” she added with a hopeful grin. “But it takes a lot o' strength.”

15.161.oldText: “Maybe it does, if you're not used to it,” said Sara, with friendly sympathy. “But you don't know how easy it is when you've done it often. I wouldn't try so hard at first. It will come to you after a while. I'll just tell you what things are. Look at these.”

15.162.oldText: She held an old summer hat in her hand which she had pulled out of the bottom of the trunk. There was a wreath of flowers on it. She pulled the wreath off.

15.163.oldText: “These are garlands for the feast,” she said grandly. “They fill all the air with perfume. There's a mug on the wash-stand, Becky. Oh—and bring the soap dish for a centerpiece.”

15.165.oldText: “What are they now, miss?” she asked. “You'd think they was made of crockery—but I know they ain't.”

15.166.oldText: “This is a carved flagon,” said Sara, arranging the wreath's tendrils around the mug. “And this”—bending tenderly over the soap dish and heaping it with roses—“is purest alabaster set with jewels.”

15.167.oldText: She touched the things gently, a happy smile on her lips that made her look like someone in a dream.

15.169.oldText: “If we just had something for candy dishes,” Sara murmured. “There!”—darting to the trunk again. “I remember I saw something just now.”

15.170.oldText: It was only a bundle of wool wrapped in red and white tissue paper, but the tissue paper was soon twisted into the shape of little dishes and combined with the leftover flowers to decorate the candlestick that would light the feast. Only the Magic could have made it more than an old table covered with a red shawl and set with junk from a long-unopened trunk. But Sara stepped back and gazed at it, seeing wonders. And Becky, after staring in delight, spoke in a hushed voice.

15.171.oldText: “This 'ere,” she suggested, glancing around the attic, “is it the Bastille now—or has it turned into somethin' different?”

15.172.oldText: “Oh, yes, yes!” said Sara. “Quite different. It's a banquet hall!”

15.173.oldText: “My eye, miss!” gasped Becky. “A blanket 'all!” And she turned to look at the splendors around her in awed bewilderment.

15.174.oldText: “A banquet hall,” said Sara. “A huge room where feasts are held. It has a vaulted ceiling, and a minstrels' gallery, and a huge fireplace filled with blazing oak logs, and it glows with wax candles twinkling on every side.”

15.175.oldText: “My eye, Miss Sara!” gasped Becky again.

15.176.oldText: Then the door opened, and Ermengarde came in, almost staggering under the weight of her hamper. She started back with a cry of joy. To come in from the chilly darkness outside and find herself standing in front of a totally unexpected feast, draped in red, decorated with white napkins and wreathed with flowers, was to feel that the preparations were truly brilliant.

15.177.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” she cried out. “You are the cleverest girl I ever saw!”

15.178.oldText: “Isn't it nice?” said Sara. “They are things from my old trunk. I asked my Magic, and it told me to go and look.”

15.179.oldText: “But oh, miss,” cried Becky, “wait till she's told you what they are! They ain't just—oh, miss, please tell her,” she begged, looking at Sara.

15.180.oldText: So Sara told her, and because her Magic helped her, she made her ALMOST see it all: the golden platters—the vaulted spaces—the blazing logs—the twinkling wax candles. As the things came out of the hamper—the frosted cakes—the fruits—the candies and the wine—the feast became something splendid.

15.181.oldText: “It's like a real party!” cried Ermengarde.

15.182.oldText: “It's like a queen's table,” sighed Becky.

15.184.oldText: “I'll tell you what, Sara,” she said. “Pretend you are a princess now and this is a royal feast.”

15.185.oldText: “But it's your feast,” said Sara. “You must be the princess, and we will be your maids of honor.”

15.186.oldText: “Oh, I can't,” said Ermengarde. “I'm too fat, and I don't know how. YOU be her.”

15.187.oldText: “Well, if you want me to,” said Sara.

15.189.oldText: “There's a lot of paper and rubbish stuffed in here!” she exclaimed. “If we light it, there'll be a bright blaze for a few minutes, and we'll feel like it's a real fire.” She struck a match and lit it up, and a bright, fake-looking glow filled the room.

15.190.oldText: “By the time it stops blazing,” Sara said, “we'll forget it isn't real.”

15.192.oldText: “Doesn't it LOOK real?” she said. “Now we'll begin the party.”

15.193.oldText: She led the way to the table. She waved her hand graciously to Ermengarde and Becky. She was deep inside her dream.

15.194.oldText: “Step forward, fair damsels,” she said in her happy dream-voice, “and be seated at the banquet table. My noble father, the king, who is away on a long journey, has commanded me to feast you.” She turned her head slightly toward the corner of the room. “What ho there, minstrels! Strike up with your viols and bassoons. Princesses,” she explained quickly to Ermengarde and Becky, “always had minstrels playing at their feasts. Pretend there's a minstrel gallery up there in the corner. Now we'll begin.”

15.195.oldText: They had barely had time to take their pieces of cake into their hands—not one of them had time to do more, when—all three sprang to their feet and turned pale faces toward the door—listening—listening.

15.196.oldText: Someone was coming up the stairs. There was no mistaking it. Each of them recognized the angry, climbing tread and knew that this was the end of everything.

15.197.oldText: “It's—the missus!” choked Becky, and dropped her piece of cake on the floor.

15.198.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara, her eyes growing shocked and large in her small white face. “Miss Minchin has found us out.”

15.199.oldText: Miss Minchin struck the door open with a blow of her hand. She was pale herself, but it was with rage. She looked from the frightened faces to the banquet table, and from the banquet table to the last flicker of burnt paper in the grate.

15.200.oldText: “I have suspected something of this sort,” she exclaimed. “But I never imagined such nerve. Lavinia was telling the truth.”

15.201.oldText: So they knew that Lavinia had somehow guessed their secret and betrayed them. Miss Minchin marched over to Becky and boxed her ears for the second time.

15.202.oldText: “You impudent creature!” she said. “You leave the house in the morning!”

15.203.oldText: Sara stood very still, her eyes growing larger, her face paler. Ermengarde burst into tears.

15.204.oldText: “Oh, don't send her away,” she sobbed. “My aunt sent me the hamper. We're—only—having a party.”

15.205.oldText: “So I see,” said Miss Minchin, scornfully. “With Princess Sara at the head of the table.” She turned fiercely on Sara. “This is your doing, I know,” she cried. “Ermengarde would never have thought of such a thing. You decorated the table, I suppose—with this rubbish.” She stamped her foot at Becky. “Go to your attic!” she commanded, and Becky crept away, her face hidden in her apron, her shoulders shaking.

15.207.oldText: “I will deal with you tomorrow. You shall have neither breakfast, dinner, nor supper!”

15.208.oldText: “I have not had either dinner or supper today, Miss Minchin,” said Sara, rather faintly.

15.209.oldText: “Then so much the better. You will have something to remember. Don't stand there. Put those things back into the hamper.”

15.210.oldText: She began sweeping them off the table into the hamper herself, and caught sight of Ermengarde's beautiful new books.

15.211.oldText: “And you”—to Ermengarde—“have brought your beautiful new books into this dirty attic. Pick them up and go back to bed. You will stay there all day tomorrow, and I will write to your papa. What would HE say if he knew where you were tonight?”

15.212.oldText: Something she saw in Sara's grave, fixed gaze at that moment made her turn on her fiercely.

15.213.oldText: “What are you thinking of?” she demanded. “Why do you look at me like that?”

15.214.oldText: “I was wondering,” answered Sara, just as she had answered that famous day in the schoolroom.

15.216.oldText: It was very like the scene in the schoolroom. There was no rudeness in Sara's manner. It was only sad and quiet.

15.217.oldText: “I was wondering,” she said in a low voice, “what MY papa would say if he knew where I am tonight.”

15.218.oldText: Miss Minchin was infuriated, just as before, and her anger came out, as before, in a violent way. She rushed at her and shook her.

15.219.oldText: “You insolent, unmanageable child!” she cried. “How dare you! How dare you!”

15.220.oldText: She picked up the books, swept the rest of the feast back into the hamper in a jumbled heap, thrust it into Ermengarde's arms, and pushed her ahead of her toward the door.

15.221.oldText: “I will leave you to wonder,” she said. “Go to bed this instant.” And she shut the door behind herself and poor stumbling Ermengarde, and left Sara standing all alone.

15.222.oldText: The dream was completely over. The last spark had died out of the paper in the grate and left only black ashes. The table was bare, the golden plates and richly embroidered napkins and the garlands had transformed back into old handkerchiefs, scraps of red and white paper, and discarded artificial flowers all scattered on the floor. The minstrels in the minstrel gallery had slipped away, and the viols and bassoons were silent. Emily was sitting with her back against the wall, staring very hard. Sara saw her, and went and picked her up with trembling hands.

15.223.oldText: “There isn't any banquet left, Emily,” she said. “And there isn't any princess. There is nothing left but the prisoners in the Bastille.” And she sat down and hid her face.

15.224.oldText: What would have happened if she hadn't hidden her face just then, and if she had happened to look up at the skylight at the wrong moment, I don't know—perhaps the end of this chapter would have been quite different—because if she had glanced up at the skylight she would certainly have been startled by what she would have seen. She would have seen exactly the same face pressed against the glass and peering in at her as had peered in earlier in the evening when she was talking to Ermengarde.

15.225.oldText: But she didn't look up. She sat with her little black head in her arms for some time. She always sat like that when she was trying to bear something in silence. Then she got up and went slowly to the bed.

15.226.oldText: “I can't pretend anything else—while I'm awake,” she said. “There wouldn't be any use in trying. If I go to sleep, perhaps a dream will come and pretend for me.”

15.227.oldText: She suddenly felt so tired—maybe from lack of food—that she sat down on the edge of the bed quite weakly.

15.228.oldText: “Suppose there was a bright fire in the grate, with lots of little dancing flames,” she murmured. “Suppose there was a comfortable chair in front of it—and suppose there was a small table near it, with a little hot—hot supper on it. And suppose”—as she pulled the thin coverings over her—“suppose this was a beautiful soft bed, with fleecy blankets and large downy pillows. Suppose—suppose—” And her very tiredness was good to her, for her eyes closed and she fell fast asleep.

15.229.oldText: She didn't know how long she slept. But she had been tired enough to sleep deeply and soundly—too deeply and soundly to be disturbed by anything, even by the squeaks and scampering of Melchisedec's entire family, if all his sons and daughters had chosen to come out of their hole to fight and tumble and play.

15.230.oldText: When she woke up, it was rather suddenly, and she didn't know that any particular thing had called her out of her sleep. The truth was, however, that it was a sound that had called her back—a real sound—the click of the skylight as it fell shut after a slim white figure who had slipped through it and was crouching down on the slates of the roof—just close enough to see what happened in the attic, but not close enough to be seen.

15.231.oldText: At first she didn't open her eyes. She felt too sleepy and—oddly enough—too warm and comfortable. She was so warm and comfortable, in fact, that she didn't believe she was really awake. She was never as warm and cozy as this except in some lovely vision.

15.232.oldText: “What a nice dream!” she murmured. “I feel quite warm. I—don't—want—to—wake—up.”

15.233.oldText: Of course it was a dream. She felt as if warm, delightful bedclothes were heaped on her. She could actually FEEL blankets, and when she put out her hand it touched something exactly like a satin-covered eider-down quilt. She mustn't wake up from this delight—she must stay very still and make it last.

15.234.oldText: But she couldn't—even though she kept her eyes closed tightly, she couldn't. Something was forcing her to wake up—something in the room. It was a sense of light, and a sound—the sound of a crackling, roaring little fire.

15.235.oldText: “Oh, I am waking up,” she said sadly. “I can't help it—I can't.”

15.236.oldText: Her eyes opened in spite of herself. And then she actually smiled—because what she saw she had never seen in the attic before, and knew she never should see.

15.237.oldText: “Oh, I HAVEN'T woken up,” she whispered, daring to lift herself onto her elbow and look all around her. “I'm dreaming still.” She knew it MUST be a dream, for if she were awake such things could not—could not be.

15.238.oldText: Do you wonder that she felt sure she hadn't come back to earth? This is what she saw. In the grate there was a glowing, blazing fire. On the hob was a little brass kettle hissing and boiling. Spread on the floor was a thick, warm crimson rug. Before the fire stood a folding-chair, unfolded, with cushions on it. By the chair was a small folding-table, unfolded, covered with a white cloth, and on it were small covered dishes, a cup, a saucer, a teapot. On the bed were new warm coverings and a satin-covered down quilt. At the foot of the bed lay a curious padded silk robe, a pair of quilted slippers, and some books. The room of her dream seemed transformed into fairyland—and it was flooded with warm light, for a bright lamp stood on the table covered with a rosy shade.

15.239.oldText: She sat up, leaning on her elbow, and her breathing came short and fast.

15.240.oldText: “It does not—melt away,” she panted. “Oh, I never had such a dream before.” She hardly dared to move; but at last she pushed the bedclothes aside, and put her feet on the floor with a rapturous smile.

15.241.oldText: “I am dreaming—I am getting out of bed,” she heard her own voice say. And then, as she stood up in the middle of it all, turning slowly from side to side—“I am dreaming it stays—real! I'm dreaming it FEELS real. It's bewitched—or I'm bewitched. I only THINK I see it all.” Her words began to hurry. “If I can only keep on thinking it,” she cried, “I don't care! I don't care!”

15.243.oldText: “Oh, it isn't true!” she said. “It CAN'T be true! But oh, how true it seems!”

15.244.oldText: The blazing fire drew her toward it, and she knelt down and held out her hands close to it—so close that the heat made her start back.

15.245.oldText: “A fire I only dreamed wouldn't be HOT,” she cried.

15.246.oldText: She sprang up, touched the table, the dishes, the rug. She went to the bed and touched the blankets. She took up the soft padded dressing-gown, and suddenly clutched it to her chest and held it to her cheek.

15.247.oldText: “It's warm. It's soft!” she almost sobbed. “It's real. It must be!”

15.249.oldText: “They are real, too. It's all real!” she cried. “I am NOT—I am NOT dreaming!”

15.250.oldText: She almost staggered to the books and opened the one that lay on top. Something was written on the flyleaf—just a few words, and they were these:

15.251.oldText: “To the little girl in the attic. From a friend.”

15.252.oldText: When she saw that—wasn't it a strange thing for her to do?—she put her face down on the page and burst into tears.

15.253.oldText: “I don't know who it is,” she said. “But somebody cares for me a little. I have a friend.”

15.254.oldText: She took her candle and crept out of her own room and into Becky's, and stood by her bedside.

15.255.oldText: “Becky, Becky!” she whispered as loudly as she dared. “Wake up!”

15.256.oldText: When Becky woke up and sat upright, staring in shock, her face still smudged with traces of tears, beside her stood a little figure in a luxurious padded robe of crimson silk. The face she saw was a shining, wonderful thing. The Princess Sara—as she remembered her—stood right at her bedside, holding a candle in her hand.

15.258.oldText: Becky was too frightened to speak. She simply got up and followed her, with her mouth and eyes wide open, and without a word.

15.259.oldText: And when they crossed the threshold, Sara shut the door gently and drew her into the warm, glowing midst of things that made her brain reel and her hungry senses faint. “It's true! It's true!” she cried. “I've touched them all. They're as real as we are. The Magic has come and done it, Becky, while we were asleep—the Magic that won't let those worst things EVER quite happen.”

16.0.oldText: Imagine, if you can, what the rest of the evening was like. How they huddled by the fire, which blazed and leaped and made so much of itself in the little grate. How they took the covers off the dishes and found rich, hot, savory soup that was a meal in itself, plus sandwiches, toast, and muffins enough for both of them. The mug from the washstand became Becky’s tea cup, and the tea was so delicious that there was no need to pretend it was anything but tea. They were warm and well-fed and happy, and it was just like Sara that, having found her strange good fortune real, she gave herself up to enjoying it as much as she possibly could. She had lived such a life of imaginings that she could accept any wonderful thing that happened, and almost stop, in a short time, finding it bewildering.

16.1.oldText: “I don’t know anyone in the world who could have done it,” she said. “But someone has. And here we are sitting by their fire—and—and—it’s true! And whoever it is—wherever they are—I have a friend, Becky. Someone is my friend.”

16.2.oldText: It can’t be denied that as they sat before the blazing fire, eating the warm, comforting food, they felt a kind of joyful awe. They looked into each other’s eyes with something almost like doubt.

16.3.oldText: “Do you think,” Becky faltered once, in a whisper, “do you think it could melt away, miss? Hadn’t we better be quick?” And she hastily crammed her sandwich into her mouth. If it was only a dream, kitchen manners would be overlooked.

16.4.oldText: “No, it won’t melt away,” said Sara. “I AM eating this muffin, and I can taste it. You never really eat things in dreams. You only think you’re going to eat them. Besides, I keep pinching myself, and I touched a hot piece of coal just now, on purpose.”

16.5.oldText: The sleepy comfort that finally almost overpowered them was a heavenly thing. It was the drowsiness of happy, well-fed childhood, and they sat in the firelight and luxuriated in it until Sara found herself turning to look at her transformed bed.

16.6.oldText: There were even enough blankets to share with Becky. The narrow couch in the next attic was more comfortable that night than its occupant had ever dreamed it could be.

16.7.oldText: As she was leaving the room, Becky turned at the doorway and looked around her with hungry eyes.

16.8.oldText: “If it ain’t here in the mornin’, miss,” she said, “it’s been here tonight, anyways, an’ I shan’t never forget it.” She looked at each particular thing, as if to memorize it. “The fire was THERE,” pointing with her finger, “an’ the table was before it; an’ the lamp was there, an’ the light looked rosy red; an’ there was a satin cover on your bed, an’ a warm rug on the floor, an’ everythin’ looked beautiful; an’”—she paused for a second and laid her hand tenderly on her stomach—“there WAS soup an’ sandwiches an’ muffins—there WAS.” And, with this conviction now a reality at least, she went away.

16.9.oldText: Through the mysterious way news travels in schools and among servants, by morning it was well known that Sara Crewe was in terrible disgrace, that Ermengarde was being punished, and that Becky would have been thrown out of the house before breakfast—except that a scullery maid couldn’t be replaced at a moment’s notice. The servants knew she was allowed to stay because Miss Minchin couldn’t easily find another creature helpless and humble enough to work like a bound slave for so few shillings a week. The older girls in the schoolroom knew that if Miss Minchin didn’t send Sara away, it was for practical reasons of her own.

16.10.oldText: “She’s growing so fast and learning so much, somehow,” said Jessie to Lavinia, “that she’ll be given classes soon, and Miss Minchin knows she’ll have to work for nothing. It was rather nasty of you, Lavvy, to tell on her for having fun in the garret. How did you find out?”

16.11.oldText: “I got it out of Lottie. She’s such a baby she didn’t know she was telling me. There was nothing nasty at all in speaking to Miss Minchin. I felt it was my duty”—primly. “She was being deceitful. And it’s ridiculous that she should look so grand and be made so much of, in her rags and tatters!”

16.12.oldText: “What were they doing when Miss Minchin caught them?”

16.13.oldText: “Pretending some silly thing. Ermengarde had taken her hamper up to share with Sara and Becky. She never invites US to share anything. Not that I care, but it’s rather vulgar of her to share with servant girls in attics. I’m surprised Miss Minchin didn’t throw Sara out—even if she does want her for a teacher.”

16.14.oldText: “If she was thrown out, where would she go?” asked Jessie, a little anxiously.

16.15.oldText: “How do I know?” snapped Lavinia. “She’ll look pretty strange when she comes into the schoolroom this morning, I should think—after what’s happened. She had no dinner yesterday, and she’s not to have any today.”

16.16.oldText: Jessie was not as mean as she was silly. She picked up her book with a little jerk.

16.17.oldText: “Well, I think it’s horrid,” she said. “They have no right to starve her to death.”

16.18.oldText: When Sara went into the kitchen that morning, the cook gave her a sideways look, and so did the housemaids; but she walked past them quickly. She had, in fact, overslept a little, and since Becky had done the same, neither had had time to see the other, and each had come downstairs in a hurry.

16.19.oldText: Sara went into the scullery. Becky was scrubbing a kettle furiously, and was actually humming a little song under her breath. She looked up with a wildly excited face.

16.20.oldText: “It was there when I woke up, miss—the blanket,” she whispered excitedly. “It was as real as it was last night.”

16.21.oldText: “So was mine,” said Sara. “It’s all there now—every bit of it. While I was getting dressed, I ate some of the cold things we left.”

16.22.oldText: “Oh, laws! Oh, laws!” Becky breathed the words in a sort of rapturous groan, and ducked her head over her kettle just in time, as the cook came in from the kitchen.

16.23.oldText: Miss Minchin had expected to see in Sara, when she appeared in the schoolroom, very much what Lavinia had expected to see. Sara had always been an annoying puzzle to her, because harshness never made her cry or look frightened. When she was scolded, she stood still and listened politely with a serious face. When she was punished, she did her extra tasks or went without her meals, never complaining or showing any outward sign of rebellion. The very fact that she never gave a rude answer seemed to Miss Minchin a kind of rudeness in itself. But after yesterday’s missed meals, the violent scene of last night, and the prospect of more hunger today, surely she must have broken down. It would be strange indeed if she didn’t come downstairs with pale cheeks and red eyes and an unhappy, humbled face.

16.24.oldText: Miss Minchin saw her for the first time when she entered the schoolroom to hear the little French class recite its lessons and oversee its exercises. And in came Sara with a springing step, color in her cheeks, and a smile hovering at the corners of her mouth. It was the most astonishing thing Miss Minchin had ever seen. It gave her quite a shock. What was the child made of? What could such a thing mean? She called her at once to her desk.

16.25.oldText: “You don’t look as if you realize that you are in disgrace,” she said. “Are you absolutely hardened?”

16.26.oldText: The truth is that when you’re still a child—or even when you’re grown up—and you’ve been well fed, and you’ve slept long and softly and warm; when you’ve fallen asleep in the middle of a fairy story and woken up to find it real, you can’t be unhappy or even look as if you are. And you couldn’t, even if you tried, keep a glow of joy out of your eyes. Miss Minchin was almost struck dumb by the look in Sara’s eyes when she gave her perfectly respectful answer.

16.27.oldText: “I beg your pardon, Miss Minchin,” she said. “I know I am in disgrace.”

16.28.oldText: “Be good enough not to forget it and look as if you’d come into a fortune. It is impertinent. And remember you are to have no food today.”

16.29.oldText: “Yes, Miss Minchin,” Sara answered. But as she turned away, her heart leaped with the memory of what yesterday had been. “If the Magic hadn’t saved me just in time,” she thought, “how horrible it would have been!”

16.30.oldText: “She can’t be very hungry,” whispered Lavinia. “Just look at her. Maybe she’s pretending she had a good breakfast”—with a spiteful laugh.

16.31.oldText: “She’s different from other people,” said Jessie, watching Sara with her class. “Sometimes I’m a bit frightened of her.”

16.33.oldText: All through the day the light was in Sara’s face, and the color in her cheeks. The servants cast puzzled glances at her and whispered to each other, and Miss Amelia’s small blue eyes wore an expression of bewilderment. What such a bold look of well-being, under official displeasure, could mean she couldn’t understand. It was, however, just like Sara’s strange stubborn way. She was probably determined to brave the matter out.

16.34.oldText: One thing Sara had decided, as she thought things over. The wonders that had happened must be kept a secret, if such a thing was possible. If Miss Minchin chose to climb up to the attic again, of course everything would be discovered. But it didn’t seem likely she would do so for some time at least, unless she was led there by suspicion. Ermengarde and Lottie would be watched so strictly that they wouldn’t dare sneak out of their beds again. Ermengarde could be told the story and trusted to keep it secret. If Lottie made any discoveries, she could be sworn to secrecy too. Perhaps the Magic itself would help to hide its own marvels.

16.35.oldText: “But whatever happens,” Sara kept telling herself all day—“WHATEVER happens, somewhere in the world there is a heavenly kind person who is my friend—my friend. If I never know who it is—if I can never even thank him—I shall never feel quite so lonely again. Oh, the Magic was GOOD to me!”

16.36.oldText: If it was possible for the weather to be worse than it had been the day before, it was worse this day—wetter, muddier, colder. There were more errands to be done, the cook was more irritable, and, knowing that Sara was in disgrace, she was crueler. But what does anything matter when your Magic has just proven itself your friend? Sara’s supper the night before had given her strength. She knew she would sleep well and warmly, and even though she had naturally started to be hungry again before evening, she felt she could bear it until breakfast time the next day, when her meals would surely be given to her again. It was quite late when she was finally allowed to go upstairs. She had been told to go into the schoolroom and study until ten o’clock, and she had become interested in her work and stayed over her books later.

16.37.oldText: When she reached the top flight of stairs and stood before the attic door, it must be admitted that her heart beat rather fast.

16.38.oldText: “Of course it MIGHT all have been taken away,” she whispered, trying to be brave. “It might only have been lent to me for that one awful night. But it WAS lent to me—I had it. It was real.”

16.39.oldText: She pushed the door open and went in. Once inside, she gasped slightly, shut the door, and stood with her back against it, looking from side to side.

16.40.oldText: The Magic had been there again. It really had, and it had done even more than before. The fire was blazing in lovely leaping flames, more cheerfully than ever. Several new things had been brought into the attic, so altering the look of it that, if she hadn’t been past doubting, she would have rubbed her eyes. On the low table another supper stood—this time with cups and plates for Becky as well as herself. A piece of bright, heavy, unusual embroidery covered the battered mantel, and ornaments had been placed on it. All the bare, ugly things that could be covered with draperies had been hidden and made to look quite pretty. Some unusual fabrics in rich colors had been fastened to the wall with fine, sharp tacks—so sharp that they could be pressed into the wood and plaster without hammering. Some brilliant fans were pinned up, and there were several large cushions, big and substantial enough to use as seats. A wooden box was covered with a rug, and some cushions lay on it, so that it had quite the look of a sofa.

16.41.oldText: Sara slowly moved away from the door and simply sat down and looked and looked again.

16.42.oldText: “It’s exactly like a fairy tale come true,” she said. “There isn’t the smallest difference. I feel as if I might wish for anything—diamonds or bags of gold—and they would appear! THAT wouldn’t be any stranger than this. Is this my garret? Am I the same cold, ragged, damp Sara? And to think I used to pretend and pretend and wish there were fairies! The one thing I always wanted was to see a fairy story come true. I am LIVING in a fairy story. I feel as if I might be a fairy myself, and able to turn things into anything else.”

16.44.oldText: When she walked in, she almost dropped in a heap on the floor. For a few seconds she completely lost her breath.

16.47.oldText: On this night Becky sat on a cushion on the hearth rug and had a cup and saucer of her own.

16.48.oldText: When Sara went to bed, she found she had a new thick mattress and big downy pillows. Her old mattress and pillow had been moved to Becky’s bedstead, and so, with these additions, Becky had been given a level of comfort she had never imagined.

16.49.oldText: “Where does it all come from?” Becky burst out at one point. “Laws, who does it, miss?”

16.50.oldText: “Don’t let’s even ASK,” said Sara. “If it weren’t that I want to say, ‘Oh, thank you,’ I would rather not know. It makes it more beautiful.”

16.51.oldText: From that time on, life became more wonderful day by day. The fairy story continued. Almost every day something new was done. Some new comfort or ornament appeared each time Sara opened the door at night, until in a short time the attic was a beautiful little room full of all sorts of strange and luxurious things. The ugly walls were gradually covered entirely with pictures and draperies. Clever pieces of folding furniture appeared. A bookshelf was hung up and filled with books. New comforts and conveniences appeared one by one, until there seemed to be nothing left to wish for. When Sara went downstairs in the morning, the remains of supper were on the table; and when she returned to the attic in the evening, the magician had taken them away and left another nice little meal. Miss Minchin was as harsh and insulting as ever, Miss Amelia as peevish, and the servants as vulgar and rude. Sara was sent on errands in all weathers, scolded and driven this way and that. She was hardly allowed to speak to Ermengarde and Lottie. Lavinia sneered at the increasing shabbiness of her clothes, and the other girls stared curiously at her when she appeared in the schoolroom. But what did any of it matter while she was living in this wonderful mysterious story? It was more romantic and delightful than anything she had ever invented to comfort her starved young soul and save herself from despair. Sometimes, when she was being scolded, she could hardly keep from smiling.

16.52.oldText: “If you only knew!” she was saying to herself. “If you only knew!”

16.53.oldText: The comfort and happiness she enjoyed were making her stronger, and she always had them to look forward to. If she came home from her errands wet and tired and hungry, she knew she would soon be warm and well fed once she had climbed the stairs. During the hardest day she could occupy herself blissfully by thinking of what she would see when she opened the attic door, and wondering what new delight had been prepared for her. In a very short time she began to look less thin. Color came into her cheeks, and her eyes no longer seemed too big for her face.

16.54.oldText: “Sara Crewe looks remarkably well,” Miss Minchin remarked disapprovingly to her sister.

16.55.oldText: “Yes,” answered poor, silly Miss Amelia. “She’s absolutely fattening up. She was beginning to look like a little starved crow.”

16.56.oldText: “Starved!” exclaimed Miss Minchin angrily. “There was no reason for her to look starved. She always had plenty to eat!”

16.57.oldText: “Of—of course,” Miss Amelia agreed humbly, alarmed to find that, as usual, she had said the wrong thing.

16.58.oldText: “There is something very disagreeable about seeing that sort of thing in a child of her age,” said Miss Minchin, with haughty vagueness.

16.60.oldText: “It might almost be called defiance,” answered Miss Minchin, annoyed because she knew the thing she resented was nothing like defiance, and she didn’t know what other unpleasant word to use. “The spirit and will of any other child would have been entirely humbled and broken by—by the changes she has had to endure. But, upon my word, she seems as little subdued as if—as if she were a princess.”

16.61.oldText: “Do you remember,” put in the unwise Miss Amelia, “what she said to you that day in the schoolroom about what you would do if you found out that she was—”

16.62.oldText: “No, I don’t,” said Miss Minchin. “Don’t talk nonsense.” But she remembered very clearly indeed.

16.63.oldText: Quite naturally, even Becky was beginning to look plumper and less frightened. She couldn’t help it. She had her share in the secret fairy story, too. She had two mattresses, two pillows, plenty of bedding, and every night a hot supper and a seat on the cushions by the fire. The Bastille had melted away; the prisoners no longer existed. Two comforted children sat in the middle of all these delights. Sometimes Sara read aloud from her books, sometimes she studied her own lessons, sometimes she sat and looked into the fire and tried to imagine who her friend could be, wishing she could say to him some of the things in her heart.

16.64.oldText: Then it happened that another wonderful thing occurred. A man came to the door and left several parcels. All of them were addressed in large letters: “To the Little Girl in the right-hand attic.”

16.65.oldText: Sara herself was sent to open the door and bring them in. She laid the two largest parcels on the hall table, and was looking at the address, when Miss Minchin came down the stairs and saw her.

16.66.oldText: “Take the things to the young lady they belong to,” she said sternly. “Don’t stand there staring at them.”

16.67.oldText: “They belong to me,” answered Sara quietly.

16.68.oldText: “To you?” exclaimed Miss Minchin. “What do you mean?”

16.69.oldText: “I don’t know where they come from,” said Sara, “but they’re addressed to me. I sleep in the right-hand attic. Becky has the other one.”

16.70.oldText: Miss Minchin came to her side and looked at the parcels with an excited expression.

16.74.oldText: Sara did as she was told. When the packages were unfolded, Miss Minchin’s face suddenly wore a strange expression. What she saw was pretty and comfortable clothing—clothing of various kinds: shoes, stockings, gloves, and a warm and beautiful coat. There was even a nice hat and an umbrella. They were all good and expensive things, and on the pocket of the coat was pinned a paper with these words written on it: “To be worn every day. Will be replaced by others when necessary.”

16.75.oldText: Miss Minchin was quite agitated. This was an incident that suggested strange things to her sordid mind. Could it be that she had made a mistake after all, and that the neglected child had some powerful, if eccentric, friend in the background—perhaps some previously unknown relation, who had suddenly traced her whereabouts and chose to provide for her in this mysterious and fantastic way? Relations were sometimes very odd—particularly rich old bachelor uncles, who didn’t care to have children near them. A man of that sort might prefer to look after his young relation from a distance. Such a person, however, would surely be cranky and hot-tempered enough to be easily offended. It would not be very pleasant if there were such a person, and he learned the whole truth about the thin, shabby clothes, the meager food, and the hard work. She felt very strange indeed, and very uncertain, and she gave Sara a sideways glance.

16.76.oldText: “Well,” she said, in a voice she had never used since the little girl lost her father, “someone is very kind to you. Since the things have been sent, and you’re to have new ones when they wear out, you may as well go and put them on and look respectable. After you’re dressed, you may come downstairs and study your lessons in the schoolroom. You needn’t go on any more errands today.”

16.77.oldText: About half an hour later, when the schoolroom door opened and Sara walked in, the entire seminary was struck dumb.

16.78.oldText: “My word!” exclaimed Jessie, jogging Lavinia’s elbow. “Look at the Princess Sara!”

16.79.oldText: Everybody was looking, and when Lavinia looked, she turned quite red.

16.80.oldText: It was Princess Sara indeed. At least, since the days when she had been a princess, Sara had never looked the way she did now. She didn’t seem like the Sara they had seen come down the back stairs a few hours ago. She was dressed in the kind of frock Lavinia had been used to envying her for owning. It was deep and warm in color, and beautifully made. Her slender feet looked the way they had when Jessie had admired them, and the hair, whose heavy locks had made her look rather like a Shetland pony when it fell loose around her small, odd face, was tied back with a ribbon.

16.81.oldText: “Maybe someone has left her a fortune,” Jessie whispered. “I always thought something would happen to her. She’s so strange.”

16.82.oldText: “Maybe the diamond mines have suddenly appeared again,” said Lavinia scathingly. “Don’t please her by staring at her like that, you silly thing.”

16.83.oldText: “Sara,” broke in Miss Minchin’s deep voice, “come and sit here.”

16.84.oldText: And while the whole schoolroom stared and nudged each other with their elbows, hardly making any effort to hide its excited curiosity, Sara went to her old seat of honor and bent her head over her books.

16.85.oldText: That night, when she went to her room, after she and Becky had eaten their supper, she sat and looked at the fire seriously for a long time.

16.86.oldText: “Are you making something up in your head, miss?” Becky asked respectfully and softly. When Sara sat in silence and looked into the coals with dreaming eyes, it usually meant she was making up a new story. But this time she wasn’t, and she shook her head.

16.87.oldText: “No,” she answered. “I’m wondering what I ought to do.”

16.89.oldText: “I can’t help thinking about my friend,” Sara explained. “If he wants to keep himself a secret, it would be rude to try to find out who he is. But I do so want him to know how thankful I am to him—and how happy he has made me. Anyone who is kind wants to know when people have been made happy. They care about that more than about being thanked. I wish—I do wish—”

16.90.oldText: She stopped short, because at that instant her eyes fell on something standing on a table in a corner. It was something she had found in the room when she came up to it only two days before. It was a little writing-case fitted with paper and envelopes and pens and ink.

16.91.oldText: “Oh,” she exclaimed, “why didn’t I think of that before?”

16.92.oldText: She got up and went to the corner and brought the case back to the fire.

16.93.oldText: “I can write to him,” she said joyfully, “and leave it on the table. Then perhaps the person who takes the things away will take it too. I won’t ask him anything. He won’t mind my thanking him, I’m sure.”

16.94.oldText: So she wrote a note. This is what she said:

16.95.oldText: I hope you will not think it is impolite that I should write this note to you when you wish to keep yourself a secret. Please believe I do not mean to be impolite or try to find out anything at all; only I want to thank you for being so kind to me—so heavenly kind—and making everything like a fairy story. I am so grateful to you, and I am so happy—and so is Becky. Becky feels just as thankful as I do—it is all just as beautiful and wonderful to her as it is to me. We used to be so lonely and cold and hungry, and now—oh, just think what you have done for us! Please let me say just these words. It seems as if I OUGHT to say them. THANK you—THANK you—THANK you!

16.97.oldText: The next morning she left this on the little table, and in the evening it had been taken away with the other things. So she knew the Magician had received it, and she was happier for the thought. She was reading one of her new books to Becky just before they went to their separate beds, when her attention was caught by a sound at the skylight. When she looked up from her page, she saw that Becky had heard the sound too, since she had turned her head to look and was listening rather nervously.

16.99.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara slowly. “It sounds—rather like a cat—trying to get in.”

16.100.oldText: She left her chair and went to the skylight. It was a strange little sound she heard—like a soft scratching. She suddenly remembered something and laughed. She remembered a quaint little intruder who had once before made his way into the attic. She had seen him that very afternoon, sitting miserably on a table by a window in the Indian gentleman’s house.

16.101.oldText: “Suppose,” she whispered in pleased excitement—“just suppose it was the monkey who got away again. Oh, I wish it was!”

16.102.oldText: She climbed onto a chair, very cautiously raised the skylight, and peeped out. It had been snowing all day, and on the snow, quite near her, crouched a tiny, shivering figure, whose small black face wrinkled itself piteously at the sight of her.

16.103.oldText: “It is the monkey,” she cried out. “He has crept out of the Lascar’s attic, and he saw the light.”

16.105.oldText: “Are you going to let him in, miss?” she said.

16.106.oldText: “Yes,” Sara answered joyfully. “It’s too cold for monkeys to be out. They’re delicate. I’ll coax him in.”

16.107.oldText: She put a hand out gently, speaking in a coaxing voice—the way she spoke to the sparrows and to Melchisedec—as if she were some friendly little animal herself.

16.108.oldText: “Come along, monkey darling,” she said. “I won’t hurt you.”

16.109.oldText: He knew she wouldn’t hurt him. He knew it before she laid her soft, caressing little paw on him and drew him toward her. He had felt human love in the slim brown hands of Ram Dass, and he felt it in hers. He let her lift him through the skylight, and when he found himself in her arms, he cuddled up to her chest and looked up into her face.

16.110.oldText: “Nice monkey! Nice monkey!” she crooned, kissing his funny head. “Oh, I do love little animal things.”

16.111.oldText: He was clearly glad to get to the fire, and when she sat down and held him on her knee, he looked from her to Becky with a mixture of interest and appreciation.

16.112.oldText: “He IS plain-looking, miss, ain’t he?” said Becky.

16.113.oldText: “He looks like a very ugly baby,” laughed Sara. “I beg your pardon, monkey; but I’m glad you’re not a baby. Your mother COULDN’T be proud of you, and no one would dare say you looked like any of your relations. Oh, I do like you!”

16.115.oldText: “Maybe he’s sorry he’s so ugly,” she said, “and it’s always on his mind. I wonder if he HAS a mind. Monkey, my love, do you have a mind?”

16.116.oldText: But the monkey only put up a tiny paw and scratched his head.

16.117.oldText: “What will you do with him?” Becky asked.

16.118.oldText: “I’ll let him sleep with me tonight, and then take him back to the Indian gentleman tomorrow. I’m sorry to take you back, monkey; but you must go. You ought to be fondest of your own family; and I’m not a REAL relation.”

16.119.oldText: And when she went to bed, she made him a nest at her feet, and he curled up and slept there as if he were a baby and very pleased with his quarters.
