17.0.oldText: The next afternoon, three members of the Large Family sat in the Indian gentleman's library, doing their best to cheer him up. They had been allowed to come and do this because he had specially invited them. He had been living in suspense for some time, and today he was waiting anxiously for a particular event. The event was the return of Mr. Carmichael from Moscow. His stay there had stretched on from week to week. When he first arrived, he had not been able to track down the family he had gone to find. When he finally felt sure he had located them and went to their house, he was told they were away on a journey. His efforts to reach them had failed, so he had decided to stay in Moscow until they returned. Mr. Carrisford sat in his reclining chair, and Janet sat on the floor beside him. He was very fond of Janet. Nora had found a footstool, and Donald was straddling the head of the tiger that decorated the rug made from the animal's skin. It must be admitted that he was riding it rather wildly.

17.1.oldText: “Don't whoop so loud, Donald,” Janet said. “When you come to cheer up a sick person, you don't cheer them up at the top of your voice. Maybe cheering up is too loud, Mr. Carrisford?” she asked, turning to the Indian gentleman.

17.3.oldText: “No, it isn't,” he answered. “And it keeps me from thinking too much.”

17.4.oldText: “I'm going to be quiet,” Donald shouted. “We'll all be as quiet as mice.”

17.5.oldText: “Mice don't make noise like that,” said Janet.

17.6.oldText: Donald made a bridle out of his handkerchief and bounced up and down on the tiger's head.

17.7.oldText: “A whole lot of mice might,” he said cheerfully. “A thousand mice might.”

17.8.oldText: “I don't believe fifty thousand mice would,” said Janet sternly. “And we have to be as quiet as one mouse.”

17.10.oldText: “Papa won't be very long now,” she said. “May we talk about the lost little girl?”

17.11.oldText: “I don't think I could talk about much else right now,” the Indian gentleman answered, knitting his brow with a tired look.

17.12.oldText: “We like her so much,” said Nora. “We call her the little un-fairy princess.”

17.13.oldText: “Why?” the Indian gentleman asked, because the imaginings of the Large Family always made him forget things a little.

17.15.oldText: “It's because, even though she isn't exactly a fairy, she'll be so rich when she's found that she'll be like a princess in a fairy tale. We called her the fairy princess at first, but it didn't quite fit.”

17.16.oldText: “Is it true,” said Nora, “that her papa gave all his money to a friend to put into a mine that had diamonds in it, and then the friend thought he had lost it all and ran away because he felt as if he were a robber?”

17.17.oldText: “But he wasn't really, you know,” Janet put in quickly.

17.18.oldText: The Indian gentleman took hold of her hand suddenly.

17.20.oldText: “I feel sorry for the friend,” Janet said. “I can't help it. He didn't mean to do it, and it would break his heart. I'm sure it would break his heart.”

17.21.oldText: “You are an understanding little woman, Janet,” the Indian gentleman said, and he held her hand close.

17.22.oldText: “Did you tell Mr. Carrisford,” Donald shouted again, “about the little-girl-who-isn't-a-beggar? Did you tell him she has nice new clothes? Maybe somebody found her when she was lost.”

17.23.oldText: “There's a cab!” exclaimed Janet. “It's stopping in front of the door. It's papa!”

17.24.oldText: All three of them ran to the windows to look out.

17.25.oldText: “Yes, it's papa,” Donald announced. “But there is no little girl.”

17.26.oldText: All three of them rushed out of the room and tumbled into the hall. This was how they always welcomed their father. You could hear them jumping up and down, clapping their hands, and being scooped up and kissed.

17.27.oldText: Mr. Carrisford tried to stand up and sank back down again.

17.28.oldText: “It's no use,” he said. “What a wreck I am!”

17.29.oldText: Mr. Carmichael's voice approached the door.

17.30.oldText: “No, children,” he was saying. “You may come in after I've talked to Mr. Carrisford. Go and play with Ram Dass.”

17.31.oldText: Then the door opened and he came in. He looked rosier than ever, and brought an atmosphere of freshness and health with him. But his eyes were disappointed and worried as they met the invalid's eager, questioning look, even as the two men grasped each other's hands.

17.32.oldText: “What news?” Mr. Carrisford asked. “The child the Russian people adopted?”

17.33.oldText: “She is not the child we are looking for,” was Mr. Carmichael's answer. “She is much younger than Captain Crewe's little girl. Her name is Emily Carew. I have seen her and talked to her. The Russians were able to give me every detail.”

17.34.oldText: How weary and miserable the Indian gentleman looked! His hand dropped from Mr. Carmichael's.

17.35.oldText: “Then the search has to begin all over again,” he said. “That is all. Please sit down.”

17.36.oldText: Mr. Carmichael took a seat. Somehow, he had gradually grown fond of this unhappy man. He himself was so well and happy, and so surrounded by cheerfulness and love, that loneliness and broken health seemed pitifully unbearable. If there had been the sound of just one bright little high-pitched voice in the house, it would have been so much less forlorn. And the thought that a man should be forced to carry around the belief that he had wronged and abandoned a child was not something one could face.

17.37.oldText: “Come, come,” he said in his cheery voice. “We'll find her yet.”

17.38.oldText: “We must begin at once. No time must be lost,” Mr. Carrisford fretted. “Do you have any new suggestion to make—any at all?”

17.39.oldText: Mr. Carmichael felt rather restless. He stood up and began to pace the room with a thoughtful, uncertain face.

17.40.oldText: “Well, perhaps,” he said. “I don't know what it may be worth. The fact is, an idea came to me as I was thinking it over on the train ride from Dover.”

17.41.oldText: “What was it? If she is alive, she is somewhere.”

17.42.oldText: “Yes, she is somewhere. We have searched the schools in Paris. Let us give up Paris and begin in London. That was my idea—to search London.”

17.43.oldText: “There are plenty of schools in London,” said Mr. Carrisford. Then he gave a small start, jolted by a memory. “By the way, there is one right next door.”

17.44.oldText: “Then we will begin there. We cannot begin nearer than next door.”

17.45.oldText: “No,” said Carrisford. “There is a child there who interests me, but she is not a pupil. And she is a little dark, forlorn creature, as unlike poor Crewe as a child could possibly be.”

17.46.oldText: Perhaps the Magic was at work again at that very moment—the beautiful Magic. It really seemed as if it might be. What was it that brought Ram Dass into the room—even as his master was speaking—bowing respectfully, but with a barely hidden flicker of excitement in his dark, flashing eyes?

17.47.oldText: “Sahib,” he said, “the child herself has come—the child the sahib felt pity for. She brings back the monkey, who had run away again to her attic under the roof. I have asked that she remain. I thought it would please the sahib to see her and speak with her.”

17.49.oldText: “God knows,” Mr. Carrisford answered. “She is the child I spoke of. A little drudge at the school.” He waved his hand to Ram Dass and addressed him. “Yes, I should like to see her. Go and bring her in.” Then he turned to Mr. Carmichael. “While you have been away,” he explained, “I have been desperate. The days were so dark and long. Ram Dass told me about this child's miseries, and together we invented a romantic plan to help her. I suppose it was a childish thing to do, but it gave me something to plan and think about. Without the help of a quick, soft-footed Easterner like Ram Dass, however, it could not have been done.”

17.50.oldText: Then Sara came into the room. She carried the monkey in her arms, and he clearly had no intention of leaving her if it could be helped. He was clinging to her and chattering, and the strange excitement of finding herself in the Indian gentleman's room had brought a flush to Sara's cheeks.

17.51.oldText: “Your monkey ran away again,” she said in her pretty voice. “He came to my garret window last night, and I took him in because it was so cold. I would have brought him back if it hadn't been so late. I knew you were ill and might not like to be disturbed.”

17.53.oldText: “That was very thoughtful of you,” he said.

17.55.oldText: “Shall I give him to the Lascar?” she asked.

17.56.oldText: “How do you know he is a Lascar?” said the Indian gentleman, smiling a little.

17.57.oldText: “Oh, I know Lascars,” Sara said, handing over the unwilling monkey. “I was born in India.”

17.58.oldText: The Indian gentleman sat upright so suddenly, and with such a change of expression, that for a moment she was quite startled.

17.59.oldText: “You were born in India,” he exclaimed. “Were you? Come here.” And he held out his hand.

17.60.oldText: Sara went to him and laid her hand in his, since he seemed to want to take it. She stood still, and her green-gray eyes met his with wonder. Something seemed to be the matter with him.

17.62.oldText: “Yes; I live at Miss Minchin's seminary.”

17.63.oldText: “But you are not one of her pupils?”

17.64.oldText: A strange little smile hovered around Sara's mouth. She hesitated for a moment.

17.65.oldText: “I don't think I know exactly what I am,” she replied.

17.67.oldText: “At first I was a pupil, and a parlor boarder; but now—”

17.68.oldText: “You were a pupil! What are you now?”

17.69.oldText: The odd little sad smile was on Sara's lips again.

17.70.oldText: “I sleep in the attic, next to the scullery maid,” she said. “I run errands for the cook—I do anything she tells me; and I teach the little ones their lessons.”

17.71.oldText: “Question her, Carmichael,” said Mr. Carrisford, sinking back as if he had lost his strength. “Question her; I cannot.”

17.72.oldText: The big, kind father of the Large Family knew how to question little girls. Sara could tell how much practice he had had when he spoke to her in his nice, encouraging voice.

17.73.oldText: “What do you mean by ‘at first,’ my child?” he asked.

17.74.oldText: “When I was first taken there by my papa.”

17.76.oldText: “He died,” said Sara, very quietly. “He lost all his money and there was none left for me. There was no one to take care of me or to pay Miss Minchin.”

17.77.oldText: “Carmichael!” the Indian gentleman cried out loudly. “Carmichael!”

17.78.oldText: “We must not frighten her,” Mr. Carmichael said aside to him in a quick, low voice. And he added aloud to Sara, “So you were sent up into the attic, and made into a little drudge. That was about it, wasn't it?”

17.79.oldText: “There was no one to take care of me,” said Sara. “There was no money; I belong to nobody.”

17.80.oldText: “How did your father lose his money?” the Indian gentleman broke in breathlessly.

17.81.oldText: “He did not lose it himself,” Sara answered, growing more puzzled by the moment. “He had a friend he was very fond of—he was very fond of him. It was his friend who took his money. He trusted his friend too much.”

17.82.oldText: The Indian gentleman's breath came more quickly.

17.83.oldText: “The friend might have meant to do no harm,” he said. “It might have happened through a mistake.”

17.84.oldText: Sara did not realize how unforgiving her quiet young voice sounded as she answered. If she had known, she would surely have tried to soften it for the Indian gentleman's sake.

17.85.oldText: “The suffering was just as bad for my papa,” she said. “It killed him.”

17.86.oldText: “What was your father's name?” the Indian gentleman said. “Tell me.”

17.87.oldText: “His name was Ralph Crewe,” Sara answered, feeling startled. “Captain Crewe. He died in India.”

17.88.oldText: The haggard face contracted, and Ram Dass sprang to his master's side.

17.89.oldText: “Carmichael,” the invalid gasped, “it is the child—the child!”

17.90.oldText: For a moment Sara thought he was going to die. Ram Dass poured out drops from a bottle and held them to his lips. Sara stood near, trembling a little. She looked in a bewildered way at Mr. Carmichael.

17.92.oldText: “He was your father's friend,” Mr. Carmichael answered her. “Don't be frightened. We have been looking for you for two years.”

17.93.oldText: Sara put her hand up to her forehead, and her mouth trembled. She spoke as if she were in a dream.

17.94.oldText: “And I was at Miss Minchin's the whole time,” she half whispered. “Just on the other side of the wall.”

18.0.oldText: It was kind, comfortable Mrs. Carmichael who explained everything. She was sent for at once and came across the square to take Sara into her warm arms and make clear to her all that had happened. The excitement of the totally unexpected discovery had been almost overwhelming for Mr. Carrisford in his weak condition.

18.1.oldText: “Honestly,” he said faintly to Mr. Carmichael, when it was suggested that the little girl should go into another room, “I feel as if I do not want to lose sight of her.”

18.2.oldText: “I will take care of her,” Janet said, “and mamma will come in a few minutes.” And it was Janet who led her away.

18.3.oldText: “We are so glad you are found,” she said. “You don’t know how glad we are that you are found.”

18.4.oldText: Donald stood with his hands in his pockets and gazed at Sara with thoughtful, guilty eyes.

18.5.oldText: “If I had just asked what your name was when I gave you my sixpence,” he said, “you would have told me it was Sara Crewe, and then you would have been found in a minute.” Then Mrs. Carmichael came in. She looked very moved, and suddenly she took Sara in her arms and kissed her.

18.6.oldText: “You look bewildered, poor child,” she said. “And no wonder.”

18.7.oldText: Sara could only think of one thing.

18.8.oldText: “Was he,” she said, with a glance toward the closed door of the library—“was HE the wicked friend? Oh, please tell me!”

18.9.oldText: Mrs. Carmichael was crying as she kissed her again. She felt as if Sara ought to be kissed very often, because she had not been kissed for so long.

18.10.oldText: “He was not wicked, my dear,” she answered. “He did not really lose your papa’s money. He only thought he had lost it. And because he loved your papa so much, his grief made him so ill that for a time he was not in his right mind. He almost died of brain fever, and long before he began to recover, your poor papa was already dead.”

18.11.oldText: “And he did not know where to find me,” murmured Sara. “And I was so near.” Somehow, she could not forget that she had been so close.

18.12.oldText: “He believed you were at school in France,” Mrs. Carmichael explained. “And he was constantly misled by false clues. He has looked for you everywhere. When he saw you pass by, looking so sad and neglected, he did not dream that you were his friend’s poor child. But because you were a little girl, he was sorry for you and wanted to make you happier. And he told Ram Dass to climb into your attic window and try to make you comfortable.”

18.13.oldText: Sara gave a start of joy; her whole face changed.

18.14.oldText: “Did Ram Dass bring the things?” she cried out. “Did HE tell Ram Dass to do it? Did HE make the dream that came true?”

18.15.oldText: “Yes, my dear—yes! He is kind and good, and he was sorry for you, for little lost Sara Crewe’s sake.”

18.16.oldText: The library door opened and Mr. Carmichael appeared, calling Sara to him with a gesture.

18.17.oldText: “Mr. Carrisford is better already,” he said. “He wants you to come to him.”

18.18.oldText: Sara did not wait. When the Indian gentleman looked at her as she entered, he saw that her face was glowing.

18.19.oldText: She went and stood before his chair, with her hands clasped together against her chest.

18.20.oldText: “You sent the things to me,” she said, in a joyful little voice full of feeling, “the beautiful, beautiful things? YOU sent them!”

18.21.oldText: “Yes, poor, dear child, I did,” he answered her. He was weak and worn out from long illness and trouble, but he looked at her with the look she remembered in her father’s eyes—that look of loving her and wanting to take her in his arms. It made her kneel down by him, just as she used to kneel by her father when they were the dearest friends in the world.

18.22.oldText: “Then it is you who are my friend,” she said. “It is you who are my friend!” And she dropped her face on his thin hand and kissed it again and again.

18.23.oldText: “The man will be himself again in three weeks,” Mr. Carmichael said quietly to his wife. “Look at his face already.”

18.24.oldText: In fact, he did look changed. Here was the “Little Missus,” and he had new things to think about and plan for already. In the first place, there was Miss Minchin. She must be visited and told about the change in her pupil’s fortunes.

18.25.oldText: Sara was not to return to the seminary at all. The Indian gentleman was very firm on that point. She must stay where she was, and Mr. Carmichael would go and see Miss Minchin himself.

18.26.oldText: “I am glad I do not need to go back,” said Sara. “She will be very angry. She does not like me—though perhaps it is my fault, because I do not like her.”

18.27.oldText: But, oddly enough, Miss Minchin made it unnecessary for Mr. Carmichael to go to her, by actually coming to look for her pupil herself. She had wanted Sara for something, and on asking around she had heard an astonishing thing. One of the housemaids had seen her sneak out of the basement with something hidden under her cloak, and had also seen her go up the steps next door and enter the house.

18.28.oldText: “What does she mean by it!” cried Miss Minchin to Miss Amelia.

18.29.oldText: “I really don’t know, sister,” answered Miss Amelia. “Unless she has made friends with him because he has lived in India.”

18.30.oldText: “It would be just like her to push herself on him and try to win his sympathy in some such rude way,” said Miss Minchin. “She must have been in the house for two hours. I will not allow such cheek. I shall go and ask about it, and apologize for her intrusion.”

18.31.oldText: Sara was sitting on a footstool close to Mr. Carrisford’s knee, listening to some of the many things he felt he had to try to explain to her, when Ram Dass announced the visitor’s arrival.

18.32.oldText: Sara rose without thinking, and turned rather pale. But Mr. Carrisford saw that she stood quietly, and showed none of the usual signs of a child’s fear.

18.33.oldText: Miss Minchin entered the room with a sternly dignified manner. She was correctly and well dressed, and stiffly polite.

18.34.oldText: “I am sorry to disturb Mr. Carrisford,” she said. “But I have explanations to make. I am Miss Minchin, the owner of the Young Ladies’ Seminary next door.”

18.35.oldText: The Indian gentleman looked at her for a moment in silent study. He was a man with a naturally quick temper, and he did not want it to get the better of him.

18.36.oldText: “So you are Miss Minchin?” he said.

18.38.oldText: “In that case,” the Indian gentleman replied, “you have arrived at the right time. My lawyer, Mr. Carmichael, was just about to go and see you.”

18.39.oldText: Mr. Carmichael bowed slightly, and Miss Minchin looked from him to Mr. Carrisford in amazement.

18.40.oldText: “Your lawyer!” she said. “I do not understand. I have come here as a matter of duty. I have just discovered that you have been intruded upon by the boldness of one of my pupils—a charity pupil. I came to explain that she intruded without my knowledge.” She turned on Sara. “Go home at once,” she ordered angrily. “You shall be severely punished. Go home at once.”

18.43.oldText: Miss Minchin felt rather as if she must be losing her mind.

18.45.oldText: “No,” said Mr. Carrisford. “She is not going home—if you call your house that. Her home from now on will be with me.”

18.46.oldText: Miss Minchin stepped back in amazed indignation.

18.47.oldText: “With YOU! With YOU, sir! What does this mean?”

18.48.oldText: “Kindly explain the matter, Carmichael,” said the Indian gentleman, “and get it over as quickly as possible.” And he made Sara sit down again and held her hands in his—which was another habit of her papa’s.

18.49.oldText: Then Mr. Carmichael explained—in the quiet, level, steady manner of a man who knew his subject and all its legal weight, which was something Miss Minchin understood as a businesswoman, and did not enjoy.

18.50.oldText: “Mr. Carrisford, madam,” he said, “was a close friend of the late Captain Crewe. He was his partner in certain large investments. The fortune which Captain Crewe believed he had lost has been recovered, and is now in Mr. Carrisford’s hands.”

18.51.oldText: “The fortune!” cried Miss Minchin; and she really lost color as she said the word. “Sara’s fortune!”

18.52.oldText: “It WILL be Sara’s fortune,” replied Mr. Carmichael, rather coldly. “In fact, it is Sara’s fortune now. Certain events have increased it enormously. The diamond mines have come back to life.”

18.53.oldText: “The diamond mines!” Miss Minchin gasped out. If this was true, nothing so horrible, she felt, had ever happened to her since she was born.

18.54.oldText: “The diamond mines,” Mr. Carmichael repeated, and he could not help adding, with a rather sly, un-lawyer-like smile, “There are not many princesses, Miss Minchin, who are richer than your little charity pupil, Sara Crewe, will be. Mr. Carrisford has been searching for her for nearly two years. He has found her at last, and he will keep her.”

18.55.oldText: After that he asked Miss Minchin to sit down while he explained matters to her fully, and went into as much detail as was necessary to make it quite clear to her that Sara’s future was secure, and that what had seemed to be lost was to be returned to her ten times over. Also, that she had in Mr. Carrisford a guardian as well as a friend.

18.56.oldText: Miss Minchin was not a clever woman, and in her shock she was silly enough to make one desperate attempt to win back what she could not help seeing she had lost through her own greed and folly.

18.57.oldText: “He found her under my care,” she protested. “I have done everything for her. If it weren’t for me, she would have starved in the streets.”

18.58.oldText: Here the Indian gentleman lost his temper.

18.59.oldText: “As for starving in the streets,” he said, “she might have starved more comfortably there than in your attic.”

18.60.oldText: “Captain Crewe left her in my charge,” Miss Minchin argued. “She must return to it until she is of age. She can be a parlor boarder again. She must finish her education. The law will step in on my behalf.”

18.61.oldText: “Come, come, Miss Minchin,” Mr. Carmichael cut in, “the law will do nothing of the sort. If Sara herself wishes to return to you, I dare say Mr. Carrisford might not refuse to allow it. But that rests with Sara.”

18.62.oldText: “Then,” said Miss Minchin, “I appeal to Sara. I have not spoiled you, perhaps,” she said awkwardly to the little girl; “but you know that your papa was pleased with your progress. And—ahem—I have always been fond of you.”

18.63.oldText: Sara’s green-gray eyes fixed themselves on her with the quiet, clear look Miss Minchin particularly disliked.

18.64.oldText: “Have YOU, Miss Minchin?” she said. “I did not know that.”

18.66.oldText: “You ought to have known it,” she said. “But children, unfortunately, never know what is best for them. Amelia and I always said you were the cleverest child in the school. Will you not do your duty to your poor papa and come home with me?”

18.67.oldText: Sara took a step toward her and stood still. She was thinking of the day she had been told she belonged to nobody, and was in danger of being thrown out into the street. She was thinking of the cold, hungry hours she had spent alone with Emily and Melchisedec in the attic. She looked Miss Minchin steadily in the face.

18.68.oldText: “You know why I will not go home with you, Miss Minchin,” she said. “You know quite well.”

18.69.oldText: A hot flush showed on Miss Minchin’s hard, angry face.

18.70.oldText: “You will never see your friends again,” she began. “I will see that Ermengarde and Lottie are kept away—”

18.71.oldText: Mr. Carmichael stopped her with polite firmness.

18.72.oldText: “Excuse me,” he said. “She will see anyone she wishes to see. The parents of Miss Crewe’s schoolmates are not likely to refuse her invitations to visit her at her guardian’s house. Mr. Carrisford will see to that.”

18.73.oldText: It must be admitted that even Miss Minchin flinched. This was worse than the eccentric bachelor uncle who might have a peppery temper and be easily offended at how his niece had been treated. A woman with a low mind could easily believe that most people would not refuse to let their children stay friends with a little heiress of diamond mines. And if Mr. Carrisford chose to tell certain of her customers how unhappy Sara Crewe had been made, many unpleasant things might happen.

18.74.oldText: “You have not taken on an easy charge,” she said to the Indian gentleman, as she turned to leave the room. “You will discover that very soon. The child is neither truthful nor grateful. I suppose”—to Sara—“that you feel now that you are a princess again.”

18.75.oldText: Sara looked down and flushed a little, because she thought her favorite idea might not be easy for strangers—even nice ones—to understand at first.

18.76.oldText: “I—TRIED not to be anything else,” she answered in a low voice—“even when I was coldest and hungriest—I tried not to be.”

18.77.oldText: “Now it will not be necessary to try,” said Miss Minchin sourly, as Ram Dass bowed her out of the room.

18.78.oldText: She returned home and, going to her sitting room, sent at once for Miss Amelia. She sat shut in with her for the rest of the afternoon, and it must be admitted that poor Miss Amelia went through more than one bad quarter of an hour. She shed many tears, and dabbed her eyes a great deal. One of her unfortunate remarks almost caused her sister to bite her head off, but it ended in an unusual way.

18.79.oldText: “I’m not as clever as you, sister,” she said, “and I am always afraid to say things to you for fear of making you angry. Perhaps if I were not so timid it would be better for the school and for both of us. I must say I have often thought it would have been better if you had been less harsh with Sara Crewe, and had seen that she was decently dressed and more comfortable. I KNOW she was worked too hard for a child of her age, and I know she was only half fed—”

18.80.oldText: “How dare you say such a thing!” exclaimed Miss Minchin.

18.81.oldText: “I don’t know how I dare,” Miss Amelia answered, with a kind of reckless courage; “but now I’ve begun I may as well finish, whatever happens to me. The child was a clever child and a good child—and she would have paid you back for any kindness you had shown her. But you didn’t show her any. The fact was, she was too clever for you, and you always disliked her for that reason. She used to see right through us both—”

18.82.oldText: “Amelia!” gasped her furious elder sister, looking as if she would box her ears and knock her cap off, as she had often done to Becky.

18.83.oldText: But Miss Amelia’s disappointment had made her hysterical enough not to care what happened next.

18.84.oldText: “She did! She did!” she cried. “She saw right through us both. She saw that you were a hard-hearted, worldly woman, and that I was a weak fool, and that we were both of us vulgar and mean enough to grovel on our knees for her money, and to treat her badly because it was taken from her—even though she behaved like a little princess even when she was a beggar. She did—she did—like a little princess!” And her hysterics got the better of the poor woman, and she began to laugh and cry both at once, and rock herself backward and forward.

18.85.oldText: “And now you’ve lost her,” she cried wildly. “Some other school will get her and her money. And if she were like any other child she’d tell how she has been treated, and all our pupils would be taken away and we should be ruined. And it serves us right—but it serves you right more than it does me, for you are a hard woman, Maria Minchin, you are a hard, selfish, worldly woman!”

18.86.oldText: She was in danger of making so much noise with her hysterical chokes and gurgles that her sister was forced to go to her and apply smelling salts and sal volatile to quiet her, instead of pouring out her anger at Amelia’s boldness.

18.87.oldText: And from that time forward, it must be said, the elder Miss Minchin actually began to be a little afraid of a sister who, while she looked so foolish, was clearly not quite as foolish as she looked, and might therefore burst out and speak truths people did not want to hear.

18.88.oldText: That evening, when the pupils were gathered around the schoolroom fire, as was their custom before going to bed, Ermengarde came in with a letter in her hand and a strange look on her round face. It was strange because, while it was a look of delighted excitement, it was mixed with such amazement as seemed to belong to a kind of shock just received.

18.89.oldText: “What IS the matter?” cried two or three voices at once.

18.90.oldText: “Has it anything to do with the row that has been going on?” said Lavinia eagerly. “There has been such a row in Miss Minchin’s room, Miss Amelia has had something like hysterics and has had to go to bed.”

18.92.oldText: “I have just had this letter from Sara,” she said, holding it out to let them see what a long letter it was.

18.93.oldText: “From Sara!” Every voice joined in that exclamation.

18.95.oldText: “Next door,” said Ermengarde, “with the Indian gentleman.”

18.96.oldText: “Where? Where? Has she been sent away? Does Miss Minchin know? Was the row about that? Why did she write? Tell us! Tell us!”

18.97.oldText: There was a perfect uproar, and Lottie began to cry mournfully.

18.98.oldText: Ermengarde answered them slowly, as if she were half lost in what, at the moment, seemed the most important and self-explaining thing.

18.99.oldText: “There WERE diamond mines,” she said firmly. “There WERE!” Open mouths and open eyes faced her.

18.100.oldText: “They were real,” she hurried on. “It was all a mistake about them. Something happened for a time, and Mr. Carrisford thought they were ruined—”

18.102.oldText: “The Indian gentleman. And Captain Crewe thought so, too—and he died. And Mr. Carrisford had brain fever and ran away, and HE almost died. And he did not know where Sara was. And it turned out that there were millions and millions of diamonds in the mines—and half of them belong to Sara. And they belonged to her when she was living in the attic with no one but Melchisedec for a friend, and the cook ordering her about. And Mr. Carrisford found her this afternoon, and he has got her in his home—and she will never come back—and she will be more a princess than she ever was—a hundred and fifty thousand times more. And I am going to see her tomorrow afternoon. There!”

18.103.oldText: Even Miss Minchin herself could scarcely have controlled the uproar after this; and though she heard the noise, she did not try. She was in no mood to face anything more than she was facing in her room, while Miss Amelia was weeping in bed. She knew that the news had somehow worked its way through the walls, and that every servant and every child would go to bed talking about it.

18.104.oldText: So until almost midnight the entire seminary, sensing somehow that all rules had been set aside, crowded round Ermengarde in the schoolroom and heard read and re-read the letter containing a story which was quite as wonderful as any Sara herself had ever invented, and which had the amazing charm of having happened to Sara herself and the mysterious Indian gentleman in the very next house.

18.105.oldText: Becky, who had heard it too, managed to creep upstairs earlier than usual. She wanted to get away from people and go and look at the little magic room once more. She did not know what would happen to it. It was not likely it would be left to Miss Minchin. It would be taken away, and the attic would be bare and empty again. As glad as she was for Sara’s sake, she went up the last flight of stairs with a lump in her throat and tears blurring her sight. There would be no fire tonight, and no rosy lamp; no supper, and no princess sitting in the glow reading or telling stories—no princess!

18.106.oldText: She choked down a sob as she pushed the attic door open, and then she broke into a low cry.

18.107.oldText: The lamp was filling the room with light, the fire was blazing, the supper was waiting—and Ram Dass was standing smiling into her startled face.

18.108.oldText: “Missee sahib remembered,” he said. “She told the sahib all. She wished you to know the good fortune that has come to her. Look, a letter on the tray. She has written. She did not wish that you should go to sleep unhappy. The sahib commands you to come to him tomorrow. You are to be the attendant of missee sahib. Tonight I take these things back over the roof.”

18.109.oldText: And having said this with a beaming face, he made a little salaam and slipped through the skylight with an agile, silent ease of movement which showed Becky how easily he had done it before.

19.0.oldText: Never had such joy filled the nursery of the Large Family. Never had they imagined such delights as came from getting to know the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar. The mere fact of her sufferings and adventures made her a priceless treasure. Everyone wanted to be told over and over again the things that had happened to her. When you sat by a warm fire in a big, glowing room, it was quite delightful to hear how cold an attic could be. It must be admitted that the attic was rather enjoyed, and that its coldness and bareness sank into insignificance when Melchisedec was remembered, and you heard about the sparrows and the things you could see if you climbed onto the table and stuck your head and shoulders out of the skylight.

19.1.oldText: Of course, the thing they loved best was the story of the banquet and the dream that came true. Sara told it for the first time the day after she had been found. Several members of the Large Family came to take tea with her, and as they sat or curled up on the hearth-rug, she told the story in her own way, and the Indian gentleman listened and watched her. When she had finished, she looked up at him and put her hand on his knee.

19.2.oldText: “That is my part,” she said. “Now won't you tell your part of it, Uncle Tom?” He had asked her always to call him “Uncle Tom.” “I don't know your part yet, and it must be beautiful.”

19.3.oldText: So he told them how, when he sat alone, ill and dull and irritable, Ram Dass had tried to distract him by describing the people walking by, and there was one child who passed more often than anyone else. He had begun to be interested in her—partly perhaps because he was thinking a great deal about a little girl, and partly because Ram Dass had been able to relate the incident of his visit to the attic chasing the monkey. He had described its cheerless look, and the bearing of the child, who seemed as if she were not of the class of those treated as drudges and servants. Bit by bit, Ram Dass had made discoveries about the wretchedness of her life. He had found out how easy it was to climb across the few yards of roof to the skylight, and this fact had been the beginning of all that followed.

19.4.oldText: “Sahib,” he had said one day, “I could cross the slates and make the child a fire when she is out on some errand. When she returned, wet and cold, to find it blazing, she would think a magician had done it.”

19.5.oldText: The idea had been so fanciful that Mr. Carrisford's sad face had lit up with a smile, and Ram Dass had been so filled with delight that he had expanded on it and explained to his master how simple it would be to do many other things. He had shown a childlike pleasure and inventiveness, and the preparations for carrying out the plan had filled many a day with interest that would otherwise have dragged wearily. On the night of the ruined banquet, Ram Dass had kept watch, all his packages ready in the attic that was his own. The person who was to help him had waited with him, as interested as he was in the strange adventure. Ram Dass had been lying flat on the slates, looking in at the skylight, when the banquet had come to its disastrous end. He had been sure of how deeply Sara was sleeping in her exhaustion. Then, with a dark lantern, he had crept into the room, while his companion remained outside and handed the things in to him. When Sara had stirred even faintly, Ram Dass had closed the lantern-slide and lain flat on the floor. These and many other exciting things the children found out by asking a thousand questions.

19.6.oldText: “I am so glad,” Sara said. “I am so glad it was you who were my friend!”

19.7.oldText: There were never such friends as these two became. Somehow, they seemed to suit each other in a wonderful way. The Indian gentleman had never had a companion he liked quite as much as he liked Sara. Within a month, he was, as Mr. Carmichael had predicted, a new man. He was always amused and interested, and he began to find an actual pleasure in owning the wealth he had imagined he hated being burdened with. There were so many charming things to plan for Sara. There was a little joke between them that he was a magician, and one of his pleasures was inventing things to surprise her. She found beautiful new flowers growing in her room, whimsical little gifts tucked under pillows, and once, as they sat together in the evening, they heard the scratch of a heavy paw on the door. When Sara went to find out what it was, there stood a great dog—a splendid Russian boarhound—with a grand silver and gold collar bearing an inscription. “I am Boris,” it read. “I serve the Princess Sara.”

19.8.oldText: There was nothing the Indian gentleman loved more than remembering the little princess in rags and tatters. The afternoons when the Large Family, or Ermengarde and Lottie, gathered to celebrate together were very delightful. But the hours when Sara and the Indian gentleman sat alone reading or talking had a special charm of their own. During those hours many interesting things happened.

19.9.oldText: One evening, Mr. Carrisford, looking up from his book, noticed that his companion had not stirred for some time, but sat gazing into the fire.

19.11.oldText: Sara looked up, with a bright color on her cheek.

19.12.oldText: “I was supposing,” she said. “I was remembering that hungry day, and a child I saw.”

19.13.oldText: “But there were a great many hungry days,” said the Indian gentleman, with a rather sad tone in his voice. “Which hungry day was it?”

19.14.oldText: “I forgot you didn't know,” said Sara. “It was the day the dream came true.”

19.15.oldText: Then she told him the story of the bun shop, and the fourpence she picked up out of the sloppy mud, and the child who was hungrier than she was. She told it quite simply, and in as few words as possible; but somehow the Indian gentleman found it necessary to shade his eyes with his hand and look down at the carpet.

19.16.oldText: “And I was supposing a kind of plan,” she said when she had finished. “I was thinking I would like to do something.”

19.17.oldText: “What was it?” said Mr. Carrisford in a low tone. “You may do anything you like, princess.”

19.18.oldText: “I was wondering,” Sara hesitated—“you know, you say I have so much money—I was wondering if I could go to see the bun-woman, and tell her that if hungry children come and sit on the steps, or look in at the window—particularly on those dreadful days—she could just call them in and give them something to eat, and send the bills to me. Could I do that?”

19.19.oldText: “You shall do it tomorrow morning,” said the Indian gentleman.

19.20.oldText: “Thank you,” said Sara. “You see, I know what it is to be hungry, and it is very hard when you cannot even pretend it away.”

19.21.oldText: “Yes, yes, my dear,” said the Indian gentleman. “Yes, yes, it must be. Try to forget it. Come and sit on this footstool near my knee, and only remember you are a princess.”

19.22.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara, smiling; “and I can give buns and bread to the populace.” And she went and sat on the stool, and the Indian gentleman (he sometimes liked her to call him that, too) drew her small dark head down on his knee and stroked her hair.

19.23.oldText: The next morning, Miss Minchin, looking out of her window, saw the things she perhaps least enjoyed seeing. The Indian gentleman's carriage, with its tall horses, drew up before the door of the next house, and its owner and a little figure, warm in soft, rich furs, came down the steps to get into it. The little figure was a familiar one, and reminded Miss Minchin of days in the past. It was followed by another familiar sight—one she found very irritating. It was Becky, who, in the role of delighted attendant, always accompanied her young mistress to her carriage, carrying wraps and belongings. Already Becky had a pink, round face.

19.24.oldText: A little later the carriage drew up before the door of the baker's shop, and its occupants got out, oddly enough, just as the bun-woman was putting a tray of steaming-hot buns into the window.

19.25.oldText: When Sara entered the shop, the woman turned and looked at her, and, leaving the buns, came and stood behind the counter. For a moment she looked at Sara very hard indeed, and then her good-natured face lit up.

19.26.oldText: “I'm sure I remember you, miss,” she said. “And yet—”

19.27.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara. “Once you gave me six buns for fourpence, and—”

19.28.oldText: “And you gave five of them to a beggar child,” the woman broke in. “I've always remembered it. I couldn't make it out at first.” She turned to the Indian gentleman and spoke her next words to him. “I beg your pardon, sir, but there aren't many young people who notice a hungry face the way she did; and I've thought of it many a time. Excuse the liberty, miss”—to Sara—“but you look rosier and—well, better than you did that—that—”

19.29.oldText: “I am better, thank you,” said Sara. “And—I am much happier—and I have come to ask you to do something for me.”

19.30.oldText: “Me, miss!” exclaimed the bun-woman, smiling cheerfully. “Why, bless you! Yes, miss. What can I do?”

19.31.oldText: And then Sara, leaning on the counter, made her little proposal about the dreadful days and the hungry waifs and the buns.

19.32.oldText: The woman watched her, and listened with an astonished face.

19.33.oldText: “Why, bless me!” she said again when she had heard it all. “It'll be a pleasure to me to do it. I am a working woman myself and cannot afford to do much on my own, and there's plenty of trouble on every side; but, if you'll excuse me, I'm bound to say I've given away many a bit of bread since that wet afternoon, just from thinking of you—and how wet and cold you were, and how hungry you looked; and yet you gave away your hot buns as if you were a princess.”

19.34.oldText: The Indian gentleman smiled at this without meaning to, and Sara smiled a little, too, remembering what she had said to herself when she put the buns down on the ravenous child's ragged lap.

19.35.oldText: “She looked so hungry,” she said. “She was even hungrier than I was.”

19.36.oldText: “She was starving,” said the woman. “Many's the time she's told me of it since—how she sat there in the wet, and felt as if a wolf was tearing at her poor young insides.”

19.37.oldText: “Oh, have you seen her since then?” exclaimed Sara. “Do you know where she is?”

19.38.oldText: “Yes, I do,” answered the woman, smiling more good-naturedly than ever. “Why, she's in that back room there, miss, and has been for a month. She's going to turn out a decent, well-meaning girl, and she's such a help to me in the shop and in the kitchen as you'd scarcely believe, knowing how she's lived.”

19.39.oldText: She stepped to the door of the little back parlor and spoke; and the next minute a girl came out and followed her behind the counter. And there she actually was—the beggar-child, clean and neatly clothed, and looking as if she had not been hungry for a long time. She looked shy, but she had a nice face, now that she was no longer wild, and the savage look had gone from her eyes. She knew Sara in an instant, and stood and looked at her as if she could never look enough.

19.40.oldText: “You see,” said the woman, “I told her to come when she was hungry, and that when she came I'd give her odd jobs to do. And I found she was willing, and somehow I got to like her; and the end of it was, I've given her a place and a home, and she helps me, and behaves well, and is as thankful as a girl can be. Her name's Anne. She has no other.”

19.41.oldText: The children stood and looked at each other for a few minutes; and then Sara took her hand out of her muff and held it out across the counter, and Anne took it, and they looked straight into each other's eyes.

19.42.oldText: “I am so glad,” Sara said. “And I have just thought of something. Perhaps Mrs. Brown will let you be the one to give the buns and bread to the children. Perhaps you would like to do it because you know what it is to be hungry, too.”

19.44.oldText: And, somehow, Sara felt as if she understood her, though Anne said so little, and only stood still and looked and looked after her as she went out of the shop with the Indian gentleman, and they got into the carriage and drove away.

1.0.oldText: En mørk vinterdag kørte en lille pige med et usædvanligt ansigt langsomt gennem Londons brede gader i en droske, ved siden af sin far. Den gule tåge lå så tyk og tung over byen, at gadelygterne var tændt, og der skinnede gaslys fra butiksvinduerne, ligesom om natten.

1.1.oldText: Hun sad med fødderne trukket op under sig og lænede sig ind til sin far, der havde en arm om hende. Hun så på de mennesker, der gik forbi uden for vinduet, og i hendes store øjne lå et underligt, tankefuldt udtryk, som lignede en meget ældre persons.

1.2.oldText: Et sådant udtryk var uventet i ansigtet på så lille en pige. Det ville have set gammelt ud selv hos et barn på tolv, og Sara Crewe var kun syv. Men hun drømte altid og tænkte sære tanker. Hun kunne ikke huske nogen tid, hvor hun ikke havde undret sig over de voksne og den verden, de levede i. Hun følte, som om hun allerede havde levet i meget, meget lang tid.

1.3.oldText: Lige nu tænkte hun på rejsen fra Bombay sammen med sin far, kaptajn Crewe. Hun huskede det store skib, de indiske sømænd, lascarerne, der gik tavse frem og tilbage over det, og børnene, der legede på det varme dæk. Hun huskede også de unge officersfruer, som plejede at få hende i snak og lo af det, hun fortalte dem.

1.4.oldText: Mest af alt undrede hun sig over, hvor mærkeligt det var at være i Indiens brændende sol det ene øjeblik, så midt ude på havet, og så køre i en fremmed vogn gennem fremmede gader, hvor dagslyset var lige så sort som natten. Det forvirrede hende så meget, at hun rykkede lidt tættere på sin far.

1.5.oldText: »Papa,« sagde hun med en lav, hemmelighedsfuld lille stemme, der næsten var en hvisken, »papa.«

1.6.oldText: »Hvad er der, min skat?« svarede kaptajn Crewe og holdt hende tættere ind til sig og så ned i hendes ansigt. »Hvad tænker Sara på?«

1.7.oldText: »Er det her stedet?« hviskede Sara og krøb endnu tættere ind til ham. »Er det, papa?«

1.8.oldText: »Ja, lille Sara, det er her. Nu er vi endelig fremme.« Hun var kun syv år, men hun kunne høre sorgen i hans stemme.

1.9.oldText: Det føltes som mange år siden, at han begyndte at forberede hende på »stedet«, som hun altid kaldte det. Hendes mor var død, da hun blev født, så hun havde hverken kendt hende eller savnet hende. Hendes far, der var ung og køn og rig og altid kælede for hende, var den eneste slægtning, hun havde i hele verden. De havde altid leget sammen og holdt af at være sammen. Hun vidste kun, at han var rig, fordi folk sagde det, når de troede, at hun ikke kunne høre det. Hun havde også hørt dem sige, at hun selv ville blive rig, når hun blev stor. Hvad det egentlig ville sige at være rig, forstod hun ikke helt. Hun havde altid boet i en dejlig bungalow fuld af tjenere, som bukkede for hende, kaldte hende »Missee Sahib« og lod hende få sin vilje i alt. Hun havde legetøj og kæledyr og en ayah, en indisk barnepige, som elskede hende højt. Lidt efter lidt havde hun forstået, at rige mennesker har den slags ting. Mere vidste hun ikke om det.

1.10.oldText: Der havde kun været én bekymring i hendes korte liv: »stedet«, som hun en dag skulle af sted til. Man mente, at Indiens klima var meget usundt for børn, og de blev sendt væk, så snart det kunne lade sig gøre — som regel til skole i England. Andre børn var rejst for øjnene af hende, og hun havde hørt deres forældre tale om de breve, der kom fra dem. Hun havde altid vidst, at turen også ville komme til hende. Nogle gange fik farens fortællinger om rejsen og det nye land hende til at ville se det hele, men det plagede hende, at han ikke kunne blive hos hende.

1.11.oldText: »Kunne du ikke tage med til det sted, papa?« havde hun spurgt, da hun var fem år gammel. »Kunne du ikke også gå i skole? Jeg ville hjælpe dig med dine lektier.«

1.12.oldText: »Men du skal ikke blive der i særlig lang tid, lille Sara,« havde han altid sagt. »Du skal til et rart hus, hvor der vil være mange små piger, og I skal lege sammen, og jeg vil sende dig masser af bøger. Du vokser så hurtigt, at det næppe vil føles som et år, før du er stor nok og klog nok til at komme tilbage og passe papa.«

1.13.oldText: Det havde hun kunnet lide at tænke på. At holde hus for sin far; at ride med ham og sidde for bordenden, når han havde middagsselskaber; at tale med ham og læse hans bøger — det ville være det, hun mest af alt ville ønske sig i verden. Og hvis man måtte rejse til »stedet« i England for at opnå det, så måtte hun beslutte sig for at tage af sted. Hun brød sig ikke videre om andre små piger, men hvis hun havde masser af bøger, kunne hun trøste sig selv. Hun holdt mere af bøger end af noget andet og var i virkeligheden altid ved at finde på historier om smukke ting og fortælle dem til sig selv. Sommetider havde hun fortalt dem til sin far, og han havde syntes lige så godt om dem, som hun selv gjorde.

1.14.oldText: »Nå, papa,« sagde hun blidt, »hvis vi er her, så må vi vel finde os i det.«

1.15.oldText: Han lo af hendes gammelkloge ord og kyssede hende. Egentlig følte han slet ikke, at han kunne finde sig i det, men han vidste, at hun ikke måtte se det. Hans sære lille Sara havde været et vidunderligt selskab. Han tænkte på, hvor ensom han ville blive, når han kom tilbage til Indien og gik ind i sin bungalow, uden at nogen lille skikkelse i en hvid kjole løb hen for at tage imod ham. Da drosken drejede ind på den store, dystre plads, hvor de skulle hen, holdt han hende tæt ind til sig med begge arme.

1.16.oldText: Det store, dystre hus var bygget af mursten, ligesom alle de andre i rækken. Det eneste, der adskilte det fra dem, var en blank messingplade på hoveddøren med disse ord i sort:

1.19.oldText: »Så er vi her, Sara,« sagde kaptajn Crewe og lagde så meget munterhed i stemmen, som han kunne. Han løftede hende ned fra drosken, og sammen gik de op ad trappen og ringede på. Senere tænkte Sara ofte på, hvor nøjagtigt huset lignede Miss Minchin. Det var respektabelt og havde gode møbler, men alt var grimt. Selv lænestolene så ud, som om de havde hårde knogler indeni. Hallen var fuld af hårdhed og blank politur, og på det høje ur i hjørnet så månefacens røde kinder strenge ud under lakken. De blev vist ind i en dagligstue med et tæppe med firkantet mønster og firkantede stole. Et tungt marmorur stod på en lige så tung marmorkamin.

1.20.oldText: Sara satte sig i en af de stive mahognistole og lod sit hurtige, vågne blik glide rundt i rummet.

1.21.oldText: »Jeg kan ikke lide det, papa,« sagde hun. »Men jeg tror egentlig heller ikke, at soldater KAN LIDE at gå i kamp — ikke engang de modige.«

1.22.oldText: Kaptajn Crewe brød ud i latter. Han var ung og glad, og han blev aldrig træt af at høre Saras sære bemærkninger.

1.23.oldText: »Åh, lille Sara,« sagde han, »hvad skal der blive af mig, når du ikke er der til at sige højtidelige ting? Ingen andre kan være helt så højtidelige som dig.«

1.25.oldText: »Fordi du er så morsom, når du siger det,« svarede han og lo endnu højere. Så trak han hende pludselig ind i sine arme og kyssede hende inderligt. Latteren hørte op med det samme, og hans øjne så næsten ud, som om de fyldtes med tårer.

1.26.oldText: I samme øjeblik kom Miss Minchin ind. Sara syntes, at hun lignede huset påfaldende meget: høj, trist, respektabel og grim. Hendes øjne var store, kolde og fiskeagtige, og det samme var hendes smil. Da hun så kaptajn Crewe og Sara, blev smilet enormt bredt. Damen, der havde anbefalet hendes skole, havde fortalt hende mange behagelige ting om den unge soldat. Blandt andet at han var rig og villig til at bruge en meget stor sum på sin lille pige.

1.27.oldText: »Det vil være en stor ære at tage sig af så smukt og lovende et barn, kaptajn Crewe,« sagde hun, mens hun tog Saras hånd og strøg den. »Lady Meredith har fortalt mig om hendes usædvanlige begavelse. For en skole som min er et klogt barn en rigtig skat.«

1.28.oldText: Sara sad stille og sagde ingenting, men holdt blikket på Miss Minchins ansigt. Som sædvanlig gik der en underlig tanke gennem hendes hoved.

1.29.oldText: »Hvorfor siger hun, at jeg er et smukt barn?« tænkte hun. »Jeg er slet ikke smuk. Oberst Granges lille pige, Isobel, er smuk. Hun har rosenrøde kinder, smilehuller og langt, gyldent hår. Jeg har kort, sort hår og grønne øjne. Desuden er jeg tynd og slet ikke lys. Næsten ingen børn, jeg har set, er så grimme som mig. Hun fortæller en løgn lige fra starten.«

1.30.oldText: Men Sara tog fejl, når hun mente, at hun var grim. Hun lignede slet ikke Isobel Grange, regimentets lille skønhed, men hun havde en helt egen, sær charme. Hun var slank og yndefuld og ret høj til sin alder, med et lille ansigt, der var intenst og indtagende. Hendes tykke hår var helt sort og krøllede kun i spidserne. Hendes øjne var rigtignok grågrønne, men det var store, usædvanlige øjne med lange sorte vipper. Sara kunne ikke lide deres farve, men mange andre kunne lide den meget. Alligevel var hun fast overbevist om, at hun var en grim lille pige, og Miss Minchins kompliment løftede slet ikke hendes humør.

1.31.oldText: »Jeg ville sige en løgn, hvis jeg sagde, hun var smuk,« tænkte hun; »og jeg ville vide, at jeg sagde en løgn. Jeg tror, jeg er lige så grim som hun er — på min måde. Hvorfor sagde hun det?«

1.32.oldText: Efterhånden som Sara lærte Miss Minchin bedre at kende, forstod hun, hvorfor hun havde sagt det. Hun opdagede, at alle fædre og mødre, der kom med et barn til skolen, fik præcis det samme kompliment.

1.33.oldText: Sara stod ved sin fars side og lyttede til hans samtale med Miss Minchin. Han havde valgt skolen, fordi Lady Meredith havde sendt begge sine små piger dertil, og kaptajn Crewe stolede meget på hendes erfaring. Sara skulle være det, man kaldte »saloneleve«, med endnu flere privilegier, end sådanne elever ellers fik. Hun skulle have et pænt soveværelse og en dagligstue helt for sig selv, en pony med vogn og en tjenestepige i stedet for den ayah, der havde passet hende i Indien.

1.34.oldText: »Jeg er slet ikke bekymret for hendes skolegang,« sagde kaptajn Crewe med sin muntre latter og klappede Saras hånd. »Dit problem bliver at hindre hende i at lære for meget og for hurtigt. Hun sidder altid med sin lille næse begravet i en bog. Hun læser ikke bøger, Miss Minchin, hun sluger dem, som en lille ulv i stedet for en lille pige. Hun er altid sulten efter mere, og hun vil have voksenbøger: store, tykke bind på fransk og tysk såvel som engelsk, historie, biografier, digtere og alt muligt andet. Når hun læser for meget, så træk hende væk fra bøgerne. Send hende ud at ride på sin pony på ridestien Rotten Row, eller ud at købe en ny dukke. Hun burde lege mere med dukker.«

1.35.oldText: »Men papa,« forklarede Sara, »hvis jeg købte en ny dukke hvert par dage, ville jeg snart have flere dukker, end jeg kunne holde af. De burde være nære venner. Det er det, Emily skal være for mig.«

1.36.oldText: Kaptajn Crewe så på Miss Minchin, og Miss Minchin så på kaptajn Crewe.

1.39.oldText: Saras grågrønne øjne blev meget alvorlige og også bløde, da hun svarede.

1.40.oldText: »Hun er en dukke, som jeg ikke har endnu,« forklarede hun. »Papa skal købe hende til mig, og vi skal ud og finde hende sammen. Jeg har kaldt hende Emily. Når papa er rejst, skal hun være min ven. Jeg har brug for hende, så jeg kan tale med hende om ham.«

1.41.oldText: Miss Minchins store, fiskeagtige smil fik nu et direkte beundrende udtryk.

1.42.oldText: »Sikke et usædvanligt barn!« udbrød hun. »Sikke et yndigt lille væsen!«

1.43.oldText: »Ja,« sagde kaptajn Crewe og trak Sara tæt ind til sig. »Hun er et yndigt lille væsen. Pas godt på hende for mig, Miss Minchin.«

1.44.oldText: Sara boede nogle dage hos sin far på hans hotel; faktisk blev hun hos ham lige til den dag, han rejste til Indien. Sammen gik de fra den ene store butik til den anden og købte en utrolig masse ting — langt mere, end hun overhovedet kunne få brug for. Men kaptajn Crewe var en impulsiv, troskyldig ung mand. Alt, hvad hans lille pige beundrede, og alt, hvad han selv beundrede, ville han give hende. Sammen fik de samlet en garderobe, der var alt for flot til en syvårig. Der var fløjlskjoler med kanter af dyrt pelsværk, kjoler af blonder, kjoler med broderi, hatte med store, bløde strudsefjer, hermelinskåber og muffer og æsker fulde af små handsker, lommetørklæder og silkestrømper i enorme mængder. Bag disken hviskede de høflige unge ekspeditricer sammen: den mærkelige lille pige med de store, alvorlige øjne måtte da mindst være en udenlandsk prinsesse — måske en indisk rajas lille datter.

1.45.oldText: Til sidst fandt de Emily, men først måtte de besøge flere legetøjsbutikker og se på rigtig mange dukker, før hun dukkede op.

1.46.oldText: »Jeg vil have hende til at se ud, som om hun ikke rigtig var en dukke,« sagde Sara. »Jeg vil have hende til at se ud, som om hun LYTTER, når jeg taler til hende. Det ærgerlige ved dukker, papa« — og hun lagde hovedet på skrå og overvejede, mens hun sagde det — »det ærgerlige ved dukker er, at de aldrig synes at HØRE.« Så de kiggede på store og små — på dukker med sorte øjne og dukker med blå — på dukker med brune krøller og dukker med gyldne fletninger, dukker med tøj og dukker uden tøj.

1.47.oldText: »Ser du,« sagde Sara, mens de kiggede på en dukke uden tøj, »hvis den, jeg finder, ikke har nogen kjoler, kan vi gå til en syerske og få syet nogle, der er lavet specielt til hende. De passer meget bedre, hvis hun prøver dem på.«

1.50.oldText: Farven steg op i hendes kinder. Hendes grågrønne øjne fik det udtryk, man har, når man uventet får øje på en elsket og velkendt ven.

1.51.oldText: »Hun har ventet lige derinde på os!« sagde Sara. »Lad os gå ind til hende.«

1.53.oldText: »Du må præsentere mig, og jeg vil præsentere dig,« sagde Sara. »Men jeg kendte hende, det øjeblik jeg så hende — så måske kendte hun også mig.«

1.54.oldText: Måske havde Emily virkelig genkendt hende. Hun havde i hvert fald et meget intelligent udtryk i øjnene, da Sara tog hende i sine arme. Hun var en stor dukke, men ikke for stor til, at man let kunne bære hende. Hendes gyldenbrune hår krøllede af sig selv og faldt som en kappe rundt om hende. Hendes øjne var dybe, klare og gråblå med bløde, tykke vipper — rigtige vipper og ikke bare streger malet på ansigtet.

1.55.oldText: »Selvfølgelig,« sagde Sara og kiggede ind i hendes ansigt, mens hun holdt hende på skødet, »selvfølgelig, papa, det er Emily.«

1.57.oldText: »Jeg vil gerne have, at hun altid ser ud som et barn, hvis mor passer godt på hende,« sagde Sara. »Jeg er hendes mor, selvom jeg også vil have hende som min veninde.«

1.58.oldText: Kaptajn Crewe kunne have nydt alle indkøbene enormt, hvis ikke en trist tanke blev ved med at trække i hans hjerte. Hvert eneste køb betød, at afskeden fra hans kære, sære lille ven kom nærmere.

1.59.oldText: Han stod op midt om natten og gik hen og kiggede ned på Sara, der lå og sov med Emily i armene. Saras sorte hår lå spredt over puden og blandede sig med Emilys gyldenbrune krøller. Begge havde de natkjoler med blondekanter, og begge havde de lange vipper, der hvilede mod kinderne og krøllede opad. Emily lignede et rigtigt barn så meget, at kaptajn Crewe var glad for, at hun var der. Han sukkede dybt og hev i sit overskæg med et drengeagtigt udtryk i ansigtet.

1.60.oldText: »Å ja, lille Sara!« mumlede han for sig selv. »Jeg tror ikke, du ved, hvor frygteligt din papa kommer til at savne dig.«

1.61.oldText: Dagen efter kørte han Sara over til Miss Minchin og overlod hende i hendes varetægt. Hans skib skulle sejle næste morgen. Han fortalte Miss Minchin, at hans sager i England blev varetaget af hans advokater, herrerne Barrow & Skipworth. De ville give hende alle de råd, hun måtte få brug for, og betale de regninger, hun sendte for Sara. Han ville skrive to breve til sin datter hver uge, og hun måtte få al den fornøjelse, hun bad om.

1.62.oldText: »Hun er et fornuftigt lille væsen,« forklarede han, »og hun beder aldrig om noget, som det ville være farligt at give hende.«

1.63.oldText: Bagefter gik han med Sara op i hendes lille dagligstue for at sige farvel. Hun sad på hans skød med sine små hænder knyttet om opslagene på hans frakke og kiggede længe og intenst på hans ansigt.

1.65.oldText: »Nej,« svarede hun. »Jeg kan dig udenad. Du er inden i mit hjerte.« Og de slog armene om hinanden og kyssede, som om de aldrig ville give slip på hinanden.

1.66.oldText: Da drosken kørte væk, sad Sara på gulvet i sin dagligstue med hagen hvilende i hænderne og fulgte den med øjnene, indtil den forsvandt om et hjørne af pladsen. Emily sad ved siden af hende og så den også køre væk. Miss Minchin sendte sin søster, Miss Amelia, op for at finde ud af, hvad barnet lavede. Da Miss Amelia kom derop, ville døren ikke åbne sig.

1.67.oldText: »Jeg har låst døren,« lød en sær, høflig lille stemme indefra. »Vær så venlig — jeg vil gerne være helt alene.«

1.68.oldText: Miss Amelia var tyk og lille, og hun stod i stor ærefrygt for sin søster. Hun var i virkeligheden den venligste af de to, men hun ville aldrig gå imod Miss Minchin. Hun gik ned ad trappen igen og så næsten forskrækket ud.

1.69.oldText: »Søster, jeg har aldrig mødt et så mærkeligt, gammelklogt barn,« sagde hun. »Hun har låst sig inde på sit værelse, og der kommer ikke den mindste lyd fra hende.«

1.70.oldText: »Det er meget bedre, end hvis hun sparkede og skreg, sådan som nogle af dem gør,« svarede Miss Minchin. »Jeg havde forventet, at et barn så forkælet som hun ville sætte hele huset på den anden ende. Hvis nogensinde et barn har fået sin vilje i alt, så er det hende.«

1.71.oldText: »Jeg har pakket hendes kufferter ud og lagt hendes ting på plads,« sagde Miss Amelia. »Jeg har aldrig set noget lignende — frakker med kanter af sobel og hermelin og ægte Valenciennes-blonder på hendes undertøj. Du har selv set noget af hendes tøj. Hvad SYNES du om det?«

1.72.oldText: »Jeg synes, det er fuldstændig latterligt,« svarede Miss Minchin skarpt; »men det vil tage sig pænt ud i spidsen af rækken, når vi tager skolebørnene med i kirke om søndagen. Hun er blevet udstyret, som om hun var en lille prinsesse.«

2.0.oldText: Da Sara trådte ind i klasselokalet næste morgen, så alle pigerne på hende med store, nysgerrige øjne. De havde allerede hørt en hel del om hende, lige fra Lavinia Herbert, der var næsten tretten og mente, at hun var helt voksen, til fireårige Lottie Legh, skolens lille baby. De vidste uden tvivl, at Miss Minchin ville vise hende frem som noget, skolen kunne være stolt af. En eller to havde endda fået et glimt af hendes franske kammerpige, Mariette, som var kommet aftenen før. Lavinia havde sørget for at gå forbi Saras åbne dør og havde set Mariette pakke en kasse ud, der var blevet leveret sent fra en af butikkerne.

2.1.oldText: »Den var fuld af underkjoler med blondefrynser — rækker på rækker af dem,« hviskede hun til sin veninde Jessie, mens hun bøjede sig over sin geografi. »Jeg så hende ryste dem ud. Jeg hørte Miss Minchin sige til Miss Amelia, at tøjet var så fint, at det var latterligt for et barn. Min mama siger, at børn skal klæde sig enkelt. Hun har en af de underkjoler på lige nu. Jeg så det, da hun satte sig.«

2.2.oldText: »Hun har silkestrømper på!« hviskede Jessie, der også bøjede sig over sin geografi. »Og hvor små fødder! Jeg har aldrig set så små fødder.«

2.3.oldText: »Åh,« fnyste Lavinia ondskabsfuldt, »det er bare sådan, hendes tøfler er lavet. Min mama siger, at en dygtig skomager kan få selv store fødder til at se små ud. Jeg synes slet ikke, hun er smuk. Hun har en mærkelig farve øjne.«

2.4.oldText: »Hun er ikke smuk på den sædvanlige måde,« sagde Jessie og kastede endnu et blik på hende i smug henover rummet. »Men man får lyst til at se på hende igen. Hun har utroligt lange vipper, selv om hendes øjne er næsten grønne.«

2.5.oldText: Sara sad stille på sin plads tæt ved Miss Minchins kateder og ventede på besked. Alle de stirrende øjne gjorde hende slet ikke forlegen. Hun var selv nysgerrig og så roligt tilbage på de andre børn. Hvad mon de tænkte? Kunne de lide Miss Minchin? Syntes de om at have timer? Og var der nogen af dem, der havde en papa, der lignede hendes? Tidligere samme morgen havde hun talt længe med Emily om sin far.

2.6.oldText: »Han er på havet nu, Emily,« havde hun sagt til hende. »Du og jeg må være de allerbedste venner og fortælle hinanden alt. Se på mig, Emily. Ingen har pænere øjne end dig — men jeg ville ønske, du kunne tale.«

2.7.oldText: Hendes hoved var fuldt af fantasiverdener og mærkelige idéer. En af dem var, at det kunne være til stor trøst bare at lade som om, at Emily var levende og virkelig kunne høre og forstå. Mariette havde klædt hende i en mørkeblå kjole til timerne og sat et mørkeblåt bånd i hendes hår. Så gik Sara hen til Emily, der sad i sin egen stol, og rakte hende en bog.

2.8.oldText: »Her er noget at læse i, mens jeg er nedenunder,« sagde hun til Emily. Da hun så, at Mariette kiggede nysgerrigt på hende, vendte hun sig om og forklarede det med et meget alvorligt lille ansigt.

2.9.oldText: »Jeg tror, at dukker kan gøre alle mulige ting, som de skjuler for os,« sagde hun. »Måske kan Emily i virkeligheden både læse og tale og gå, men hun venter, til alle har forladt værelset, før hun gør noget af det. Det er hendes hemmelighed. Hvis folk fandt ud af, hvad dukker kunne, ville de jo sætte dem i arbejde. Måske har dukkerne alle lovet hinanden aldrig at sladre. Så længe du er her, vil Emily bare sidde og stirre. Men når du går, begynder hun måske at læse eller går hen og kigger ud ad vinduet. Hvis hun hørte en af os komme tilbage, ville hun skynde sig hen til sin stol, hoppe op i den og lade som om, hun havde siddet der hele tiden.«

2.10.oldText: »Comme elle est drôle!« tænkte Mariette, og senere, nedenunder, fortalte hun historien til overstuepigen. Men hun var allerede begyndt at holde af den usædvanlige lille pige med det kloge lille ansigt og de fejlfri manerer. Andre børn, hun havde passet, havde været langt mindre høflige. Sara var en meget fin lille person. Der var noget dejligt i den milde taknemmelighed, hvormed hun sagde »Vær så venlig, Mariette« og »Tak, Mariette«. Som Mariette forklarede overstuepigen, takkede barnet hende nøjagtig, som hun ville have takket en dame.

2.11.oldText: »Elle a l'air d'une princesse, cette petite,« sagde hun. Faktisk var hun meget glad for sin nye lille frue og henrykt over sin plads.

2.12.oldText: Der gik nogle minutter, mens Sara sad under de andre elevers blikke. Så bankede Miss Minchin værdigt på sit kateder for at få opmærksomhed.

2.13.oldText: »Unge damer,« sagde hun, »lad mig præsentere jer for jeres nye kammerat.« Alle de små piger rejste sig ved deres pladser, og Sara rejste sig også. »Jeg forventer, at I alle vil være meget venlige over for Miss Crewe. Hun har rejst meget langt for at komme til os — helt fra Indien, faktisk. Når timerne er slut, må I lære hinanden at kende.«

2.14.oldText: Eleverne bukkede formelt, og Sara svarede med et lille kniks. Så satte alle sig og begyndte igen at kigge på hinanden.

2.15.oldText: »Sara,« sagde Miss Minchin med sin lærerstemme, »kom herhen til mig.«

2.16.oldText: Hun havde taget en bog fra katederet og bladede i dens sider. Sara gik høfligt hen til hende.

2.17.oldText: »Eftersom din papa har ansat en fransk kammerpige til dig,« begyndte hun, »går jeg ud fra, at han ønsker, at du skal lægge særlig vægt på at lære fransk.«

2.19.oldText: »Jeg tror, han ansatte hende,« sagde hun, »fordi han — han troede, jeg ville kunne lide hende, Miss Minchin.«

2.20.oldText: »Jeg er bange for,« sagde Miss Minchin med et svagt surt smil, »at du har været en meget forkælet lille pige. Du tror altid, at tingene bliver ordnet, bare for at glæde dig. Jeg tror, din papa har ment, at du skulle lære fransk.«

2.21.oldText: Hvis Sara havde været lidt ældre, eller mindre fast besluttet på at være perfekt høflig over for alle, ville nogle få ord have opklaret misforståelsen. I stedet mærkede hun, at hendes kinder blev varme. Miss Minchin var streng og imponerende. Hun virkede så helt sikker på, at Sara slet ikke kunne fransk, at det føltes næsten uhøfligt at sige hende imod. Sara kunne faktisk ikke huske nogen tid, hvor fransk havde virket fremmed for hende. Hendes far havde ofte talt det til hende, selv da hun var baby. Hendes mor havde været fransk, og kaptajn Crewe elskede hendes sprog. Derfor havde Sara altid hørt fransk omkring sig og var vokset op med det.

2.22.oldText: »Jeg — jeg har ikke ligefrem læst fransk, men — men —« begyndte hun og prøvede forsagt at forklare.

2.23.oldText: Det var en af Miss Minchins mest generende hemmeligheder, at hun ikke selv kunne tale fransk, og hun ville gerne holde det skjult. Hun havde ikke lyst til at tale mere om emnet og risikere uskyldige spørgsmål fra en lille elev, der først lige var kommet.

2.24.oldText: »Nok,« sagde hun, syrlig under sin høflighed. »Hvis du aldrig har lært det, må du begynde med det samme. Monsieur Dufarge, vores franskunderviser, kommer om et par minutter. Tag denne bog og læs i den, mens du venter på ham.«

2.25.oldText: Med brændende kinder gik Sara tilbage til sin plads og åbnede bogen. Med et alvorligt ansigt læste hun den første side. Hun vidste, at det ville være uhøfligt at smile, og hun var fast besluttet på ikke at være uhøflig. Men hvor var det mærkeligt at blive sat til at læse en side, der forklarede, at »le père« var »faderen«, og »la mère« var »moderen«.

2.26.oldText: Miss Minchin kastede et forskende blik på hende.

2.27.oldText: »Du ser temmelig sur ud, Sara,« sagde hun. »Det gør mig ondt, at du ikke kan lide tanken om at lære fransk.«

2.28.oldText: »Jeg kan rigtig godt lide det,« svarede Sara, der besluttede at prøve igen; »men —«

2.29.oldText: »Når man får besked på at gøre noget, må man ikke svare ›men‹,« sagde Miss Minchin. »Læs i din bog igen.«

2.30.oldText: Sara adlød. Hun lod være med at smile, selv da hun læste, at »le fils« var »sønnen«, og »le frère« var »broderen«.

2.31.oldText: »Når monsieur Dufarge kommer,« tænkte hun, »kan jeg forklare det for ham.«

2.32.oldText: Monsieur Dufarge ankom meget kort tid efter. Han var en meget rar, intelligent, midaldrende franskmand, og han så interesseret ud, da hans øjne faldt på Sara, der høfligt forsøgte at virke fordybet i sin lille bog med vendinger.

2.33.oldText: »Har De en ny elev til mig, madame?« spurgte han Miss Minchin. »Jeg håber, jeg er så heldig.«

2.34.oldText: Miss Minchin svarede: »Hendes papa, kaptajn Crewe, er meget ivrig efter, at hun begynder at lære sproget. Desværre ser hun ud til at have en barnlig modvilje mod det. Jeg er bange for, at hun viser ringe vilje til at lære.«

2.35.oldText: »Det gør mig ondt at høre, mademoiselle,« sagde han venligt til Sara. »Måske, når vi begynder at studere sammen, kan jeg vise dig, at det er et charmerende sprog.«

2.36.oldText: Den lille Sara rejste sig. Hun var ved at blive helt fortvivlet, for hun følte, at hun næsten var kommet i unåde. Hun løftede sine store grøngrå øjne mod monsieur Dufarges ansigt og så på ham med et uskyldigt, bønfaldende blik. Hun vidste, at han ville forstå, så snart hun talte. På smukt, flydende fransk forklarede hun det helt enkelt. Madame havde misforstået hende. Hun havde ikke ligefrem lært fransk — ikke fra bøger — men hendes papa og andre mennesker havde altid talt det til hende, og hun havde læst og skrevet det, ligesom hun havde læst og skrevet engelsk. Hendes papa elskede sproget, og hun elskede det for hans skyld. Hendes kære mama, der var død, da hun blev født, var fransk. Hun ville gerne lære alt, hvad monsieur ville lære hende. Det, hun bare havde villet sige til madame, var, at ordene i netop denne bog allerede var kendt for hende. Mens hun sagde det, rakte hun ham den lille bog med vendinger.

2.37.oldText: Ved Saras første ord fór Miss Minchin voldsomt sammen. Hun stirrede over sine briller, næsten fornærmet, og blev ved med at stirre, til forklaringen var slut. Monsieur Dufarge begyndte imens at smile, og man kunne tydeligt se hans glæde. Den søde barnestemme, der talte hans eget sprog så naturligt og charmerende, fik ham næsten til at føle sig hjemme igen. På Londons mørke, tågede dage kunne hans fødeland føles utrolig langt væk. Da Sara holdt op med at tale, tog han bogen med vendinger imod med et næsten kærligt blik. Det var dog til Miss Minchin, han talte.

2.38.oldText: »Åh, madame,« sagde han, »der er ikke meget, jeg kan lære hende. Hun har ikke LÆRT fransk; hun ER fransk. Hvilken smuk udtale.«

2.39.oldText: »Du skulle have forklaret mig det,« udbrød Miss Minchin, dybt forlegen, og vendte sig mod Sara.

2.40.oldText: »Jeg — jeg prøvede,« sagde Sara. »Måske begyndte jeg ikke på den rigtige måde.«

2.41.oldText: Miss Minchin vidste, at hun havde forsøgt, og at det ikke havde været hendes skyld, at hun ikke havde fået lov at forklare sig. Og da hun så, at eleverne havde lyttet, og at Lavinia og Jessie fnisede bag deres franske grammatikker, blev hun rasende.

2.43.oldText: Og fra det øjeblik begyndte hun at nære en slags nag mod sin paradeelev.

3.0.oldText: Den første morgen, mens Sara sad ved siden af Miss Minchin, og hele klassen travlt studerede hende, lagde hun snart mærke til en lille pige på omtrent hendes egen alder. Pigen stirrede intenst på hende med et par blege, ret matte, blå øjne. Hun var buttet og så slet ikke klog ud, men hendes mund var godmodigt trutten. Det lyse hår var flettet i en stram fletning med et bånd om enden. Hun havde trukket fletningen om foran på halsen og tyggede på enden af båndet, mens hun støttede albuerne på pulten og stirrede forundret på den nye pige. Da Monsieur Dufarge begyndte at tale til Sara, så hun ret forskrækket ud. Så trådte Sara frem, løftede sine uskyldige, bedende øjne mod ham og svarede ham på fransk, helt uden varsel. Den buttede pige gav et forskrækket hop og blev helt rød af målløs beundring. I flere uger havde hun grædt fortvivlede tårer over at skulle huske, at »la mère« betød »moderen« og »le père« betød »faderen« — når ethvert fornuftigt menneske talte almindeligt engelsk. Nu sad der en pige på hendes egen alder, som ikke bare kendte de ord helt perfekt, men tydeligvis kendte mange flere og kastede dem ind i sætninger med verber, som om det ingenting var. Det var næsten for meget for hende.

3.1.oldText: Hun stirrede så stift og tyggede så hurtigt på båndet, at hun fangede Miss Minchins blik. Miss Minchin var i meget dårligt humør netop da og slog straks ned på hende.

3.2.oldText: »Miss St. John!« udbrød hun skarpt. »Hvad skal denne opførsel betyde? Tag albuerne af pulten! Tag det bånd ud af munden! Sid ret op — med det samme!«

3.3.oldText: Ved det gav Miss St. John endnu et hop, og da Lavinia og Jessie fnisede, blev hun rødere end nogensinde — så rød, at hun næsten havde tårer i sine stakkels, matte, barnlige øjne. Sara så det og fik så ondt af hende, at hun begyndte at kunne lide hende og ville være hendes veninde. Sådan havde hun altid været: Hun ville kaste sig ind i enhver strid, hvor nogen blev gjort elendig tilmode.

3.4.oldText: »Hvis Sara havde været en dreng og levet for nogle hundrede år siden,« plejede hendes far at sige, »ville hun have redet rundt i hele landet med draget sværd og reddet og forsvaret enhver i nød. Så snart hun ser nogen i vanskeligheder, vil hun kæmpe.«

3.5.oldText: Sara kom til at kunne lide den buttede, langsomme lille Miss St. John og kiggede over til hende hele formiddagen. Hun kunne se, at det ikke var let for pigen at lære noget, og at ingen nogensinde ville løbe den risiko at forkæle hende ved at behandle hende som en stjerneelev. Hendes franskundervisning var ynkelig. Hendes udtale fik selv Monsieur Dufarge til at smile mod sin vilje, og Lavinia og Jessie og de andre, mere heldige piger fnisede eller stirrede på hende med forbløffet foragt. Sara lo aldrig. Hun gjorde sit bedste for at se ud, som om hun ikke havde hørt det, da Miss St. John sagde »le bon pain« som »lee bong pang«. Hun havde selv et hidsigt lille temperament, og når hun hørte fniseriet og så det stakkels, langsomme, ulykkelige ansigt, blev hun helt rasende.

3.6.oldText: »Det er virkelig ikke morsomt,« sagde hun mellem sammenbidte tænder, mens hun bøjede sig over sin bog. »De burde ikke le.«

3.7.oldText: Da timerne var slut, og pigerne samlede sig i små grupper for at snakke, gik Sara hen for at finde Miss St. John. Hun fandt hende ret trist og sammensunket i et vinduessæde, gik over til hende og talte til hende. Hun sagde bare det, små piger altid siger for at starte et venskab, men der var noget varmt ved Sara, og det mærkede folk altid.

3.9.oldText: For at forstå Miss St. Johns forbløffelse må man huske, at en ny elev i et stykke tid er noget af et mysterium. Hele skolen havde snakket om denne nye pige aftenen før, til alle faldt i søvn, trætte af spænding og modstridende historier. En ny elev med vogn og pony og sin egen tjenestepige og en rejse over havet fra Indien at fortælle om var slet ikke en almindelig person at møde.

3.11.oldText: »Jeg hedder Sara Crewe,« sagde Sara. »Dit er meget kønt. Det lyder som noget fra en historiebog.«

3.12.oldText: »Synes du om det?« sagde Ermengarde forvirret. »Jeg — jeg synes om dit.«

3.13.oldText: Det største problem i Miss St. Johns liv var, at hun havde en klog far. Nogle gange føltes det som en forfærdelig ulykke. Når ens far ved alt, taler syv eller otte sprog og har tusindvis af bøger, som han tilsyneladende kan udenad, forventer han som regel, at man i det mindste kender indholdet af sine egne skolebøger. Han synes nok også, at man burde kunne huske nogle begivenheder fra historien og skrive en fransk stil. Ermengarde var en stor skuffelse for Mr. St. John. Han kunne ikke forstå, hvordan et barn af ham kunne være så åbenlyst og håbløst tungnemt og aldrig udmærke sig i noget.

3.14.oldText: »Du godeste!« havde han mere end én gang sagt, mens han stirrede på hende. »Nogle gange tror jeg, at hun er lige så dum som hendes tante Eliza!«
